common_errors: Averaging the two individual speeds ($10$ km/h and $6$ km/h): it gives $8$ km/h here only because the two stages take EQUAL time, so the shortcut fails on any journey with unequal times — always use total distance $\div$ total time.

exam_questions.statement:
A train travels $234$ km in $2$ hours $36$ minutes.
(a) Write $2$ hours $36$ minutes as a decimal number of hours. [1]
(b) Find the average speed of the train in km/h. [2]
(c) Change your answer to part (b) into m/s, correct to $3$ significant figures. [2]
mark_scheme: (b) M1 for the division $234\div2.6$ (using a correct decimal-hours value, follow through from (a) if needed); A1 for $90$
(c) M1 for dividing the speed in km/h by $3.6$; A1 for $25.0$ m/s
common_errors: In (a), writing $2.36$ by copying the minutes straight after the decimal point instead of dividing by $60$.

exam_questions.statement:
A cyclist's journey has two stages. In the first stage she rides $40$ km at an average speed of $20$ km/h. In the second stage she rides a further $40$ km at an average speed of $40$ km/h.
(a) Find the time taken for each stage. [2]
(b) Find the average speed for the whole journey. [2]
(c) Explain why the average speed for the whole journey is not $30$ km/h. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Stage 1: $2$ h; Stage 2: $1$ h (b) $26.7$ km/h (3 s.f.) (c) Because more time was spent at the slower speed.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $40\div20=2$ h; $40\div40=1$ h. (b) Total distance $=80$ km, total time $=3$ h, so average speed $=80\div3=26.666\ldots=26.7$ km/h (3 s.f.). (c) $30$ km/h would be the mean of $20$ and $40$, which is only correct if EQUAL TIME is spent at each speed; here the cyclist spends twice as long (2 h against 1 h) at the slower speed, which pulls the true average down below $30$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for a correct method (distance $\div$ speed) for at least one stage; A1 for both times correct
(b) M1 for $80\div3$ using correct total distance and total time; A1 for $26.7$ km/h (accept $26\tfrac23$ or $80/3$)
(c) B1 for identifying that unequal time is spent at each speed; B1 for stating that more time is spent at the slower speed, which lowers the average below the simple mean
common_errors: In (b), averaging $20$ and $40$ to give $30$ km/h directly, skipping the total-distance-over-total-time method entirely.

exam_questions.statement:
A metal sphere has mass $680$ g and volume $80$ cm$^3$.
(a) Calculate the density of the sphere, giving the correct unit. [2]
(b) A second sphere is made of the same metal and has volume $125$ cm$^3$. Calculate its mass. [2]
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for the division $680\div80$; A1 for $8.5$ g/cm$^3$ with the unit stated (the unit is required for the final mark)
(b) M1 for multiplying the density from (a) by $125$; A1 for $1\,062.5$ g (or $1.0625$ kg)
common_errors: Omitting the unit g/cm$^3$ in part (a), which loses the accuracy mark even when the number $8.5$ is correct.

challenge_questions.statement: A car drives to a village at $60$ km/h and returns along the same road at $40$ km/h. Show that the average speed for the round trip is $48$ km/h, not $50$ km/h.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Let the one-way distance be $d$. Time out $=d/60$, time back $=d/40$; total time $=d\left(\tfrac1{60}+\tfrac1{40}\right)=\tfrac{d}{24}$. Total distance $=2d$, so average speed $=2d\div\tfrac d{24}=48$ km/h. The car spends longer travelling at the slower speed, which pulls the average below the simple mean of $60$ and $40$ (which is $50$).
common_errors: Averaging $60$ and $40$ to get $50$ km/h, the same error as averaging two unequal-time speeds anywhere else in the lesson.

challenge_questions.statement: A train $150$ m long travels at $72$ km/h. How long does it take to pass a signal? How long does it take to pass completely through a tunnel of length $450$ m?
challenge_questions.full_solution: $72$ km/h $=20$ m/s. Passing a signal (a point) means the whole train's length must go past: $150\div20=7.5$ s. Through the tunnel, the FRONT of the train travels the tunnel's length plus the train's own length before the BACK clears the tunnel: $150+450=600$ m, so $600\div20=30$ s.
common_errors: Using only the tunnel's length ($450$ m) for the tunnel calculation, forgetting that the train's own length must also be added before it has fully passed through.

challenge_questions.statement: A mixture is made of $60$ cm$^3$ of metal A (density $8$ g/cm$^3$) and $40$ cm$^3$ of metal B (density $3$ g/cm$^3$). Find the density of the mixture, assuming the volumes just add.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Mass $=60\times8+40\times3=480+120=600$ g; volume $=60+40=100$ cm$^3$; density of the mixture $=600\div100=6$ g/cm$^3$.
common_errors: Averaging the two densities ($8$ and $3$) to get $5.5$ g/cm$^3$, instead of combining the actual total mass and total volume — the same 'averaging a rate' error as with average speed.

challenge_questions.statement: Tap A fills a tank in $20$ minutes and tap B fills it in $30$ minutes. How long does it take when both are open?
challenge_questions.full_solution: In one minute, tap A fills $\tfrac1{20}$ of the tank and tap B fills $\tfrac1{30}$; together they fill $\tfrac1{20}+\tfrac1{30}=\tfrac{3+2}{60}=\tfrac1{12}$ of the tank per minute, so the whole tank takes $12$ minutes.
common_errors: Adding the two times directly ($20+30=50$) or averaging them ($25$), instead of adding the two FLOW RATES (fraction of the tank per minute).

challenge_questions.statement: Car A uses $6.5$ litres per $100$ km with petrol at $\pounds1.55$ per litre. Car B uses $5.2$ litres per $100$ km with petrol at $\pounds1.72$ per litre. Which is cheaper per $100$ km and by how much?
challenge_questions.answer: Car B is cheaper, by about $\pounds1.13$ per $100$ km.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Car A: $6.5\times1.55=\pounds10.075\approx\pounds10.08$ per $100$ km. Car B: $5.2\times1.72=\pounds8.944\approx\pounds8.94$ per $100$ km. Car B is cheaper by $10.075-8.944=\pounds1.131\approx\pounds1.13$ per $100$ km.
common_errors: Comparing only the fuel-consumption rates (lower litres per 100 km) without multiplying by the different petrol PRICES, which can reverse which car is actually cheaper to run.

mcq.stem: A lorry travels $100$ km at $50$ km/h and a further $100$ km at $25$ km/h. What is its average speed for the whole journey?

options.why_wrong: This is the simple mean of $50$ and $25$; it ignores that the lorry spends twice as long travelling at the slower speed.
This is just the faster of the two speeds; because part of the journey is at only $25$ km/h, the average speed must be less than $50$ km/h.
This adds the two speeds ($50+25$) instead of combining distance and time correctly; an average speed faster than either stage is impossible.

mcq.explanation: Time for stage 1: $100\div50=2$ h; stage 2: $100\div25=4$ h. Total distance $=200$ km, total time $=6$ h, so average speed $=200\div6=33.3$ km/h (3 s.f.).

mcq.stem: A journey takes $4$ hours $12$ minutes. Written as a decimal number of hours, this is:

options.why_wrong: This copies the minutes straight after the decimal point, treating time as base-$10$ instead of dividing $12$ by $60$.
This would be the decimal form of $4$ h $45$ min, not $4$ h $12$ min.
This divides $12$ by $20$ rather than by $60$.

mcq.stem: The exchange rate is $\pounds1=\$1.35$. To change $\$270$ into pounds, you should:

options.why_wrong: This always multiplies by the rate regardless of direction; going back to the currency worth the number $1$ needs division, not multiplication.
This divides the rate by the amount, the wrong way round, and would give a tiny, meaningless number of pounds.
Currency conversion is always a multiplication or division by the rate, never an addition.

mcq.explanation: Dollars are the currency with the bigger number in the rate, so converting back to pounds (the number-$1$ currency) means dividing: $270\div1.35=\pounds200$.

mcq.stem: A block has mass $0.6$ kg and volume $200$ cm$^3$. What is its density in g/cm$^3$?

options.why_wrong: This divides $0.6$ (still in kg) by $200$ without converting to grams first, mixing two different mass units.
This divides $200$ by $0.6$, the wrong way round for density (mass $\div$ volume, not volume $\div$ mass).
This multiplies $0.6$ by $200$ instead of dividing.

mcq.explanation: Convert the mass to grams first: $0.6$ kg $=600$ g. Then density $=600\div200=3$ g/cm$^3$.

mcq.stem: Which calculation correctly converts $25$ m/s into km/h?

options.why_wrong: This divides instead of multiplying; dividing is the correct operation for km/h to m/s, not the reverse.
This scales up by $1000$ as if converting metres to kilometres alone, without also converting the TIME unit (seconds to hours).
Unit conversion between km/h and m/s is always a multiplication or division, never an addition.

mcq.explanation: To go from m/s to km/h, multiply by $3.6$: $25\times3.6=90$ km/h.

flashcards.front: What does 'per' mean in a rate such as '$\pounds8.50$ per hour'?
flashcards.back: 'For each one' — it signals a division: total $\div$ number of units gives the rate.

flashcards.front: Speed, distance, time: the three rearrangements
flashcards.back: $\text{speed}=D/T$, $\text{distance}=S\times T$, $\text{time}=D/S$.

flashcards.front: Average speed of a whole journey
flashcards.back: $\dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$ — never the mean of the individual speeds.

flashcards.front: True or false: the average speed of a two-stage journey is the mean of the two speeds.
flashcards.back: False, in general. It only equals the mean when EQUAL TIME is spent at each speed; otherwise use total distance $\div$ total time.

flashcards.front: $3$ h $45$ min as a decimal number of hours
Converting km/h ↔ m/s
flashcards.back: km/h $\to$ m/s: divide by $3.6$. m/s $\to$ km/h: multiply by $3.6$.

flashcards.front: Density, pressure, population density (all given in the exam)
flashcards.back: density $=$ mass$/$volume (g/cm$^3$); pressure $=$ force$/$area (N/m$^2$); population density $=$ population$/$area (people/km$^2$).

flashcards.front: Speed formula vs. density/pressure formulas — which must you memorise?
flashcards.back: Speed $=$ distance$/$time must be known from memory; density, pressure and population-density formulas are always GIVEN in the exam question.

flashcards.front: Currency rate direction: when do you multiply, when do you divide?
flashcards.back: Multiply to convert INTO the currency with the bigger number in the rate; divide to convert BACK into the currency worth $1$ unit.

flashcards.front: Check method for any rate answer
flashcards.back: Run the calculation in reverse: multiply your rate answer by the amount to see if it reproduces the original total.

flashcards.front: A tap fills a tank in $20$ min, another in $30$ min — how fast do they fill it together?
flashcards.back: Add the FLOW RATES (fraction of the tank per minute), not the times: $\tfrac1{20}+\tfrac1{30}=\tfrac1{12}$, so together they take $12$ minutes.

flashcards.front: A train of length $L$ passes completely through a tunnel of length $T$ — what distance does the front of the train travel?
flashcards.back: $L+T$: the front must travel the length of the tunnel PLUS the train's own length before the back clears the tunnel.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The average speed of a journey made of two different speeds is the simple average (mean) of those two speeds.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Averaging two numbers by adding and halving is such a familiar, general-purpose procedure that it gets applied here automatically, without checking whether the TIME spent at each speed is actually equal.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: For a journey of $60$ km at $60$ km/h then $60$ km at $30$ km/h, the learner answers $45$ km/h (the mean of $60$ and $30$) instead of $40$ km/h.
misconceptions.correct_model: Average speed is always $\dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$. Averaging the speeds only happens to give the right answer when EQUAL TIMES (not equal distances) are spent at each speed, which is rarely the case in an exam question.
misconceptions.remediation: Always find the time for each stage separately ($\text{distance}\div\text{speed}$), add the times, add the distances, and divide — never average the speed values themselves.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A time written as hours-and-minutes can be read straight into a decimal, so $3$ h $45$ min becomes $3.45$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Every other decimal measurement in school maths (money, length) runs in base $10$, so it feels natural to treat the minutes after the point the same way, instead of remembering that time alone runs in base $60$.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner computes a speed as $45\div3.45$ instead of $45\div3.75$, giving an answer around $13.0$ km/h instead of the correct $12$ km/h.
misconceptions.correct_model: Minutes must be divided by $60$ to become a decimal fraction of an hour: $45$ min $=45\div60=0.75$ h, so $3$ h $45$ min $=3.75$ h, not $3.45$ h.
misconceptions.remediation: Before using any time in a speed/rate formula, convert it fully to decimal hours first and write that decimal value down as a separate step, so the base-$60$ conversion cannot be skipped.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The exchange rate is always multiplied by, regardless of which currency you are starting from or converting into.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A rate is usually introduced as 'multiply by the rate', and the REVERSE direction (dividing to undo a multiplication) is a separate idea that is easy to forget under exam pressure, especially when the rate is given as '$\pounds1=X$' rather than symmetrically.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner multiplies a dollar amount by the rate when converting dollars back to pounds, giving an answer that is far too large (e.g. treating $\$500$ as if it were worth MORE than $500$ pounds).
misconceptions.correct_model: Changing INTO the currency that has the bigger number in the rate statement means multiplying; changing BACK into the currency that has the number $1$ means dividing by the same rate.
misconceptions.remediation: Before calculating, write the rate as a sentence ('$1$ pound buys $1.28$ dollars') and ask which currency the answer should be bigger or smaller in; this sense check catches the wrong operation before it is used.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A rate calculation can mix whatever units the question happens to give (minutes with km/h, grams with kg, cm$^3$ with litres) without converting first.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The question often gives the two quantities in different units because that is how the real-world data naturally comes, and converting feels like an extra, skippable step when a calculator will accept any numbers typed into it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner divides a time given in minutes directly by a speed given in km/h, or mixes grams and kilograms in a density calculation, producing an answer that is wrong by a factor of $60$, $1000$, or similar.
misconceptions.correct_model: Convert both quantities to consistent units FIRST (both in hours, or both in grams, etc.), and only then apply the rate formula; the unit of the final answer should match the units you actually divided.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the units of every quantity next to its value before calculating, circle any mismatch, and convert it before doing the division or multiplication.

common_mistakes.mistake: Averaging two speeds to find the average speed of a two-stage journey.
common_mistakes.why: Averaging two given numbers feels like the natural shortcut, and it happens to give the right answer whenever the TIME spent at each speed is equal, which can mask the error until an unequal-time question appears.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always find the time for each stage separately, add the distances and the times, and divide total distance by total time.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing an hours-and-minutes time directly as a decimal (e.g. $3$ h $45$ min as $3.45$).
common_mistakes.why: Every other everyday decimal (money, length) runs in base $10$, so minutes feel like they should too.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always divide the minutes by $60$ to get the decimal part: $45\div60=0.75$, so $3$ h $45$ min $=3.75$ h.

common_mistakes.mistake: Omitting the compound unit (g/cm$^3$, N/m$^2$, people/km$^2$) from a density/pressure/population-density answer.
common_mistakes.why: The number feels like 'the answer' once the division is done, and the unit can feel like an afterthought.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Write the unit as soon as you set up the division (mass in g over volume in cm$^3$ gives g/cm$^3$), not only at the very end.

exam_notes: The speed $=$ distance $\div$ time formula must be known from memory; density, pressure and population-density formulas are always given in the question, but you still lose marks for the wrong compound unit.
Write compound units exactly in the form asked (m/s, g/cm$^3$, people/km$^2$) — a correct number with no unit, or the wrong unit, loses the final accuracy mark.
Give money to $2$ decimal places and other non-exact answers to $3$ significant figures unless the question says otherwise.
Show the division or multiplication itself (e.g. '$45\div3.75$') before writing the final answer: this is where the method mark sits, even if the final number then goes wrong.

For an average-speed question with more than one stage, write out the time for EACH stage separately before combining — a marker can award method marks for this step even if the final division is wrong.

summary.big_idea: A rate is a division that can be run both ways: divide to find the rate, multiply by the rate to predict a total — and average speed is always total distance over total time, never the mean of the individual speeds.
key_points: Speed $=$ distance $\div$ time (and its two rearrangements) must be memorised; density, pressure and population-density formulas are always given, but the correct compound unit is still required.
Time must be converted to decimal hours (minutes $\div60$) before it is used in any speed calculation — $3$ h $45$ min is $3.75$ h, not $3.45$ h.
Average speed for a multi-stage journey is total distance $\div$ total time; averaging the individual speeds only works by coincidence when the times happen to be equal.
A currency rate is multiplied to convert TOWARDS the bigger-number currency and divided to convert BACK; a sense check on the size of the answer catches the wrong direction.
km/h $\leftrightarrow$ m/s: divide by $3.6$ to get m/s, multiply by $3.6$ to get km/h.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: For any rate problem, decide which direction you are converting (multiply to scale up towards a total, divide to find the rate or go back), always convert time to decimal hours first, and for average speed always use total distance $\div$ total time — never average the speeds themselves.

11_Percentages.json.title: Percentages
11_Percentages.json.subject: Mathematics
11_Percentages.json.course_label: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 · Number · Core + Extended

objectives.statement: Find a percentage of a quantity, and write one quantity as a percentage of another.
Increase or decrease a quantity by a percentage using a multiplier, and calculate a percentage change, including percentages over $100\%$.
Solve problems on discount, profit and loss, deposits and earnings.
Find the original quantity when the value after a percentage change is known (reverse percentages).

prerequisites.statement: Convert fluently between a percentage, a decimal and a fraction (e.g. $35\%=0.35=\tfrac{35}{100}$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every calculation in this lesson starts by turning a percentage into a decimal multiplier; without this conversion step the whole multiplier method cannot get started.

prerequisites.statement: Multiply and divide decimals accurately, including with a calculator.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Once the percentage is written as a decimal, finding a percentage of an amount, increasing/decreasing a value, or reversing a percentage are all single multiplications or divisions, so an arithmetic slip here is the most common cause of a wrong final answer.

prerequisites.statement: Identify which of two quantities in a word problem is the 'whole' (the $100\%$ amount) and which is the 'part'.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every percentage statement is really a statement about $100\%$ of something; choosing the wrong quantity as the whole (for example the selling price instead of the cost price for a profit question) gives a plausible-looking but wrong answer.

prerequisites.statement: Round a money answer correctly to $2$ decimal places.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Almost every worked context in this lesson is money, and the exam expects money answers rounded to the nearest penny/cent, not left as a long decimal or rounded to $3$ significant figures.

diagnostic_items.question: What is the multiplier for a decrease of $35\%$? For an increase of $130\%$?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Decrease of $35\%$: multiplier $1-0.35=0.65$. Increase of $130\%$: multiplier $1+1.30=2.3$.

common_wrong_answers.answer: $0.35$ for the decrease, and $1.30$ for the increase.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Uses the percentage itself (converted to a decimal) as the multiplier, instead of combining it with the starting $100\%$ ($1-0.35$ or $1+1.30$) first.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner understands a multiplier as '$100\%$ plus or minus the change', or has only memorised 'convert the percentage to a decimal' without the $1\pm$ step — this error would make every increase/decrease calculation in the lesson wrong.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Build the multiplier from the sentence '$100\%$ of the original, $\pm$ the change': for $-35\%$, that is $100\%-35\%=65\%=0.65$; for $+130\%$, that is $100\%+130\%=230\%=2.3$.

diagnostic_items.question: A price is increased by $10\%$ and then decreased by $10\%$. Is it back to the original? Why?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No. The combined multiplier is $1.1\times0.9=0.99$, so the price ends $1\%$ LOWER than it started: the $10\%$ decrease is taken from the larger, already-increased price, not from the original.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, because $+10\%$ and $-10\%$ cancel each other out.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Treats the two percentage changes as if they applied to the SAME fixed base each time, rather than recognising that the second change is applied to the new, already-changed amount.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This is the single most tested misconception in the whole lesson: it checks whether the learner understands that each percentage change is taken of the CURRENT value, not of a fixed original.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Work through a concrete number: $100\to110$ (after $+10\%$) $\to99$ (after $-10\%$ of $110$, not of $100$); show explicitly that $10\%$ of $110$ is $11$, more than the $10$ gained, so the price ends lower.

diagnostic_items.question: A shirt costs $\pounds36$ after a $25\%$ reduction. Is the original price $\pounds36+25\%$ of $36$? Explain.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No. The $\pounds36$ is $75\%$ of the ORIGINAL price, so the original is $36\div0.75=\pounds48$. Adding $25\%$ of the new, smaller value ($\pounds36$) gives a different (smaller) result, because $25\%$ of the original is not the same amount as $25\%$ of the reduced price.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, $\pounds36+25\%$ of $36=\pounds45$.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Assumes that adding back the SAME percentage, taken of the NEW (reduced) value, undoes the original reduction — this is the reverse-percentage misconception, since the $25\%$ reduction was of a bigger base in the first place.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This diagnostic previews the Extended reverse-percentages topic: it checks whether the learner already senses that 'adding the percentage back to the new value' is not the same operation as 'reversing the original percentage change', before the formal method is taught.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: State explicitly that the reduced price $\pounds36$ represents $100\%-25\%=75\%$ of the ORIGINAL, so the correct reverse operation is $36\div0.75$, not $36+0.25\times36$.

diagnostic_items.question: Profit is calculated as a percentage of which price?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The cost price (the price the trader paid), unless the question explicitly says otherwise.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The selling price, since that is the price the item was sold for.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Chooses the more prominent or final number in the question as the 'whole', rather than identifying which quantity the percentage is conventionally measured against.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner has a fixed convention for percentage profit/loss (always the cost price) rather than guessing between the two prices given in a typical question.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: State the convention explicitly and test it on a concrete pair of prices, comparing the two different percentages you would get using the cost price versus the selling price as the base, to show they are genuinely different numbers.

theory_blocks.title: A percentage is a fraction out of 100 — decide the 100% first
theory_blocks.body: A percentage is a fraction with denominator $100$: $35\%=\tfrac{35}{100}=0.35$. Every percentage problem is a statement about $100\%$ — the whole, or BASE, amount. The single most important step in any percentage question is deciding [[blue:which quantity plays the role of $100\%$]]; once that is fixed, everything else follows by scaling that quantity up or down.

theory_blocks.title: Percentage of a quantity
theory_blocks.body: To find a percentage of a quantity, convert the percentage to a decimal (divide by $100$) and multiply: $p\%$ of $A=\dfrac{p}{100}\times A$. A double number line — one line marked in percentages, one marked in the actual quantity — makes the scaling visible: if $100\%$ corresponds to $\pounds80$, then $1\%$ is $\pounds0.80$, and $35\%$ is $35\times0.80=\pounds28$.

assets.caption: A double number line: $100\%$ lines up with $\pounds80$, so $35\%$ lines up with $\pounds28$.
assets.purpose: Make the proportional scaling behind 'percentage of a quantity' visible before the decimal-multiplier method is stated formally.

theory_blocks.title: Mental shortcuts without a calculator
theory_blocks.body: Useful shortcuts without a calculator: $50\%=\tfrac12$, $25\%=\tfrac14$, $10\%=$ divide by $10$, $1\%=$ divide by $100$. Build other percentages by combining these: $15\%=10\%+5\%$, $35\%=25\%+10\%$, $17.5\%=10\%+5\%+2.5\%$.

theory_blocks.title: One quantity as a percentage of another
theory_blocks.body:
$$\text{percentage}=\frac{\text{part}}{\text{whole}}\times100\%.$$
The "whole" is the quantity that comes after "of" in the question — the thing you are comparing WITH. If the two quantities are given in different units, convert them to the SAME unit before dividing.

theory_blocks.title: Percentage increase and decrease: the multiplier
theory_blocks.body:
To increase a quantity by $p\%$, multiply by $1+\dfrac p{100}$; to decrease by $p\%$, multiply by $1-\dfrac p{100}$. This single number is the **multiplier**: it does in one step what 'find $p\%$, then add or subtract it' does in two.

| Change | Multiplier | Change | Multiplier |
|---|---|---|---|
| increase by $20\%$ | $1.20$ | decrease by $20\%$ | $0.80$ |
| increase by $3.5\%$ | $1.035$ | decrease by $12\%$ | $0.88$ |
| increase by $100\%$ | $2$ | decrease by $35\%$ | $0.65$ |
| increase by $130\%$ | $2.3$ | decrease by $0.5\%$ | $0.995$ |

theory_blocks.title: Percentage change
theory_blocks.body:
$$\text{percentage change}=\frac{\text{actual change}}{\text{original value}}\times100\%.$$
The change is **new $-$ original** (positive for an increase, negative for a decrease), and the **original** value is always the denominator — never the new value.

theory_blocks.title: Three common percentage mistakes
theory_blocks.body:
- Dividing by the NEW value instead of the ORIGINAL: a rise from $\pounds40$ to $\pounds46$ is [[green:$6/40=15\%$]], not [[red:$6/46\approx13\%$]].
- Believing that $+25\%$ followed by $-25\%$ returns to the start. If $100$ increases by $25\%$ it becomes $125$; $25\%$ of $125$ is $31.25$, so the result is $93.75$, not $100$ — the second percentage is of a DIFFERENT base.
- Confusing "$40\%$ off" (multiplier $0.6$) with "costs $40\%$" (multiplier $0.4$).

theory_blocks.title: Percentages over 100%
theory_blocks.body: A percentage CAN be more than $100\%$ — it simply means "more than the original". Increasing by $130\%$ gives $230\%$ of the original (multiplier $2.3$). Likewise, a new value can be expressed as a percentage greater than $100\%$ of an old one: $240$ is $\dfrac{240}{150}\times100=160\%$ of $150$.

theory_blocks.title: Contexts: profit, discount, deposit, earnings
theory_blocks.body:
- **Profit** $=$ selling price $-$ cost price; **loss** $=$ cost price $-$ selling price. Percentage profit (or loss) is $\dfrac{\text{profit (loss)}}{\text{cost price}}\times100\%$ — always measured against the cost price, unless told otherwise.
- **Discount**: the price is reduced by a percentage; the sale price is the multiplier times the original.
- **Deposit**: an initial payment made as a percentage of the price; the balance is the rest.
- **Earnings**: wages, salaries and commission can be raised (or taxed) by a percentage, using exactly the same multiplier method.

theory_blocks.title: Check your answer for size
theory_blocks.body: Test your answer for size. After a discount the answer must be SMALLER than the original; after an increase it must be LARGER. For percentage change, check: $46$ is $115\%$ of $40$, so the change is $+15\%$, matching the division you did. For percentages of a whole, the parts you find must add up to the whole.

theory_blocks.title: Reverse percentages: divide by the multiplier
theory_blocks.body:
Sometimes the value AFTER a percentage change is known and you must find the ORIGINAL. The known value is a percentage of the original, not of itself, so the original is found by **dividing** by the multiplier — never by taking a percentage of the new value.
$$\text{forward: original}\times\text{multiplier}=\text{new value},\qquad \text{reverse: new value}\div\text{multiplier}=\text{original}.$$

assets.caption: The forward step multiplies the original by the multiplier; the reverse step divides the new value by the SAME multiplier to recover the original.
assets.purpose: Make the forward/reverse pair of operations visible as mirror images of each other, built on the same multiplier.

theory_blocks.title: Do not add the percentage of the new value
theory_blocks.body: Do not work out a percentage of the KNOWN value and add it back. If a jacket costs $\pounds68$ after a $20\%$ discount, $68+20\%$ of $68=68+13.60=\pounds81.60$ is WRONG, because the $20\%$ discount was taken from the ORIGINAL (larger) price, not from $\pounds68$. Always ask: "the amount I am told is what percentage of the original?", then divide by that percentage's multiplier.

keywords.definition: A fraction with denominator $100$, written with the symbol $\%$.
The single number you multiply by to increase or decrease a quantity by a given percentage, e.g. $1.2$ for a $20\%$ increase.
The actual change in a quantity, divided by its ORIGINAL value, expressed as a percentage.
Selling price minus cost price, when the selling price is greater.
Cost price minus selling price, when the cost price is greater.
A reduction in the normal price of an item, usually given as a percentage.
An initial payment made as a percentage of the total price, with the remainder paid later.
Finding the original quantity when only the value after a percentage change is known, by dividing by the multiplier.
The price a trader pays to buy or make an item, before it is sold on.
The price an item is actually sold for.

worked_examples.statement: Percentage of an amount. Find (a) $35\%$ of $\pounds80$; (b) $7.5\%$ of $64$ kg; (c) $12\tfrac12\%$ of $360$.
reasoning: Convert each percentage to a decimal and multiply by the quantity.
For (c), recognise $12.5\%=\tfrac18$ as a shortcut instead of multiplying by $0.125$ directly.
worked_examples.interpretation: Converting a percentage to a decimal (or a known friendly fraction) and multiplying is the single method behind every 'percentage of a quantity' question, however the numbers are dressed up.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting to move the decimal point two places when converting the percentage (e.g. using $3.5$ instead of $0.035$ for $3.5\%$).

worked_examples.statement: Expressing as a percentage. (a) Write $18$ out of $24$ as a percentage. (b) Write $45$ cm as a percentage of $1.5$ m.
reasoning: (a) Divide the part by the whole and multiply by $100$.
(b) Convert both quantities to the SAME unit before dividing.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $\dfrac{18}{24}\times100=75\%$. (b) Same units first: $1.5$ m $=150$ cm. Then $\dfrac{45}{150}\times100=30\%$.
worked_examples.interpretation: The 'part over whole, times $100$' formula only gives a meaningful answer once both quantities are expressed in the same unit.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing $45\div1.5$ in part (b) without converting units first, which compares centimetres with metres and gives a nonsensical percentage.

worked_examples.statement: Increase and decrease. (a) Increase $350$ by $20\%$. (b) A laptop costing $\pounds650$ is reduced by $12\%$ in a sale. Find the sale price.
reasoning: (a) Multiplier for $+20\%$ is $1.20$.
(b) Multiplier for $-12\%$ is $0.88$.
worked_examples.interpretation: The multiplier method does in one multiplication what the two-step 'find the percentage, then add or subtract it' does in two — both give the same answer, but the multiplier is faster and less error-prone.
worked_examples.common_mistake: In (b), multiplying by $0.12$ (the percentage removed) and stopping there, giving the DISCOUNT instead of the sale price.

worked_examples.statement: Percentage change. A price rises from $\pounds40$ to $\pounds46$. Find the percentage increase.
reasoning: Find the actual change: $46-40$.
Divide the change by the ORIGINAL value and multiply by $100$.
worked_examples.solution: Change $=46-40=6$. Percentage increase $=\dfrac{6}{40}\times100=15\%$.
worked_examples.interpretation: The ORIGINAL value is always the denominator in a percentage-change calculation, regardless of which value (original or new) is bigger.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing by $46$ (the new value) instead of $40$ (the original), giving $13.0\%$ instead of the correct $15\%$.

worked_examples.statement: Profit. A trader buys a coat for $\pounds120$ and sells it for $\pounds150$. Find the percentage profit.
reasoning: Profit $=$ selling price $-$ cost price.
Percentage profit $=$ profit $\div$ COST PRICE $\times100$.
worked_examples.solution: Profit $=150-120=\pounds30$. Percentage profit $=\dfrac{30}{120}\times100=25\%$ (of the cost price).
worked_examples.interpretation: Percentage profit always uses the COST price as the base, never the selling price — this is a fixed convention, not a choice to make each time.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing by $150$ (the selling price) instead of $120$ (the cost price), giving $20\%$ instead of the correct $25\%$.

worked_examples.statement: Deposit and salary. (a) A sofa costs $\pounds860$. A customer pays a $15\%$ deposit. How much is the deposit, and how much remains to pay? (b) A salary of $\pounds24\,000$ is increased by $3.5\%$. Find the new salary.
reasoning: (a) Deposit $=15\%$ of $860$; remainder $=$ total $-$ deposit.
(b) New salary $=$ old salary $\times$ multiplier for $+3.5\%$.
worked_examples.solution: (a) Deposit $=0.15\times860=\pounds129$. Remainder $=860-129=\pounds731$. (b) $24\,000\times1.035=\pounds24\,840$.
worked_examples.interpretation: A deposit splits a total into two percentages (the deposit percentage and its complement); a salary rise is the ordinary multiplier method applied to earnings instead of a price.
worked_examples.common_mistake: In (a), finding the deposit correctly but then forgetting to subtract it from the total to find the remaining balance.

worked_examples.statement: Sale price to original. In a sale all prices are reduced by $20\%$. A jacket costs $\pounds68$ in the sale. What was the original price?
reasoning: The sale price is $100\%-20\%=80\%$ of the original.
Set up $0.80\times x=68$ and solve for $x$ by dividing.
worked_examples.interpretation: The reverse-percentage method is just the forward multiplier equation solved backwards: if multiplier $\times$ original $=$ new, then original $=$ new $\div$ multiplier.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Adding $20\%$ of $68$ back on to get $\pounds81.60$, which incorrectly treats the known $\pounds68$ as the base for the $20\%$ instead of the (larger) original price.

worked_examples.statement: After an increase. After an $8\%$ pay rise, Mia earns $\pounds486$ per week. What did she earn before the rise?
reasoning: New $=108\%$ of old, multiplier $1.08$.
Divide the new value by the multiplier to recover the old value.
worked_examples.solution: $\text{old}=486\div1.08=\pounds450$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Reverse percentages work identically for an increase as for a decrease: divide by the multiplier that CREATED the known value, whatever that multiplier was.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing by $1.8$ (confusing an $8\%$ increase's multiplier $1.08$ with $180\%$), or subtracting $8\%$ of $486$ instead of dividing.

worked_examples.statement: Cost price from profit. A shop sells a bicycle for $\pounds168$, making a profit of $40\%$ on the cost price. Find the cost price.
reasoning: Selling price $=100\%+40\%=140\%$ of the cost price.
Divide the selling price by the multiplier $1.40$.
worked_examples.solution: $\text{cost}=168\div1.40=\pounds120$.
worked_examples.interpretation: A profit is really a percentage INCREASE on the cost price, so a 'find the cost price from the selling price and the profit percentage' question is a reverse-percentage question wearing a different context.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Working out $40\%$ of $168$ and subtracting it from $168$, instead of dividing by $1.40$ — the $40\%$ profit was of the (smaller) cost price, not of the selling price.

guided_exercises.statement: A price of $\pounds220$ is increased by $15\%$ and then, in a later sale, decreased by $15\%$. Find the final price, and explain why it is not $\pounds220$.
hints: Apply the two multipliers one after another, in order: first $\times1.15$, then $\times0.85$.
Think about what each $15\%$ is actually taken of — are they the same base amount?
guided_exercises.full_solution: $220\times1.15=253$, then $253\times0.85=215.05$. The $15\%$ decrease is taken from the LARGER, already-increased price ($253$), so it removes more than the original increase added — the combined multiplier is $1.15\times0.85=0.9775$, just under $1$.
common_errors: Assuming the two $15\%$ changes cancel exactly and answering $\pounds220$.

guided_exercises.statement: A trader buys a bicycle for $\pounds84$ and sells it for $\pounds105$. Find the percentage profit.
hints: Find the profit as an amount first (selling price minus cost price).
Divide the profit by the COST price, not the selling price, before multiplying by $100$.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Profit $=105-84=\pounds21$. Percentage profit $=\dfrac{21}{84}\times100=25\%$.
common_errors: Dividing the profit by $105$ (the selling price) instead of $84$ (the cost price).

guided_exercises.statement: After a $15\%$ discount, a television costs $\pounds425$. Find the original price.
hints: Write what percentage of the original the sale price represents ($100\%-15\%$).
Divide the sale price by the multiplier for that percentage — do not add $15\%$ of $425$ back on.
guided_exercises.full_solution: The sale price is $85\%$ of the original: $0.85\times x=425$, so $x=425\div0.85=\pounds500$. Check: $15\%$ of $500=75$, and $500-75=425$. ✓
common_errors: Adding $15\%$ of $425$ ($=63.75$) to $425$, giving $\pounds488.75$, instead of dividing by the multiplier.
Misplacing the decimal point when converting $7.5\%$ to $0.075$.

exercises.statement: Write (a) $45$ out of $60$; (b) $27$ out of $180$ as percentages.
common_errors: Dividing the whole by the part instead of the part by the whole.

exercises.statement: Increase $350$ by $20\%$.
common_errors: Multiplying by $0.2$ and stopping there, giving the increase amount rather than the new total.

exercises.statement: Decrease $84$ by $35\%$.
common_errors: Using multiplier $0.35$ instead of $0.65$, finding the amount removed rather than what remains.

exercises.statement: The price of a ticket rises from $\pounds25$ to $\pounds31$. Find the percentage increase.
common_errors: Dividing by $31$ (the new value) instead of $25$ (the original).

exercises.statement: A shirt costing $\pounds36$ is reduced by $25\%$ in a sale. Find the sale price.
exercises.full_solution: $36\times0.75=\pounds27$.
common_errors: Multiplying by $0.25$ and giving the amount of the discount instead of the sale price.

exercises.statement: A trader buys an item for $\pounds250$ and sells it for $\pounds200$. Find the percentage loss.
common_errors: Dividing the loss by the selling price ($200$) instead of the cost price ($250$).

exercises.statement: A salary of $\pounds24\,000$ is increased by $3.5\%$. Find the new salary.
common_errors: Using multiplier $1.35$ instead of $1.035$, misplacing the decimal point in $3.5\%$.

exercises.statement: A car costs $\pounds14\,500$. A customer pays a $12\%$ deposit. Find the deposit and the amount still to pay.
common_errors: Finding the deposit but forgetting to subtract it from the total to find the remaining balance.

exercises.statement: The population of a town increases from $8\,000$ to $10\,400$. Find the percentage increase.
common_errors: Dividing the change by $10\,400$ (the new value) instead of $8\,000$ (the original).

exercises.statement: Express $240$ as a percentage of $150$.
common_errors: Assuming a percentage 'of another' can never exceed $100\%$, and so reporting it incorrectly as $62.5\%$ (the reciprocal calculation) instead.

exercises.statement: A phone costs $\pounds320$. Its price is increased by $130\%$. Find the new price.
exercises.full_solution: Multiplier $=1+1.30=2.3$. $320\times2.3=\pounds736$.
common_errors: Using multiplier $1.3$ instead of $2.3$, forgetting that the $100\%$ starting value must still be included.

exercises.statement: In a sale all prices are reduced by $28\%$. A coat costs $\pounds57.60$ in the sale. Find its original price.
exercises.full_solution: Sale price is $72\%$ of original: $57.60\div0.72=\pounds80$.
common_errors: Adding $28\%$ of $57.60$ back on instead of dividing by the multiplier $0.72$.

exercises.statement: After a $6\%$ pay rise a worker earns $\pounds31\,800$ per year. Find the salary before the rise.
common_errors: Subtracting $6\%$ of $31\,800$ from $31\,800$ instead of dividing by $1.06$.

exercises.statement: A shop sells a table for $\pounds168$, making a $40\%$ profit on the cost price. Find the cost price.
common_errors: Finding $40\%$ of $168$ and subtracting it from $168$, instead of dividing by $1.4$.

exercises.statement: The population of a village falls by $15\%$ to $4\,250$. What was it before?
common_errors: Adding $15\%$ of $4\,250$ back to $4\,250$ instead of dividing by $0.85$.

exercises.statement: The price of a meal including $20\%$ VAT is $\pounds150$. Find the price before VAT.
common_errors: Finding $20\%$ of $150$ and subtracting it from $150$, instead of dividing by $1.2$ (the VAT was added to the ORIGINAL price, not to $150$).

exercises.statement: A trader sells a watch for $\pounds340$ at a loss of $15\%$. Find the cost price.
exercises.full_solution: Selling price is $85\%$ of cost: $340\div0.85=\pounds400$.
common_errors: Adding $15\%$ of $340$ to $340$ to try to recover the cost price, instead of dividing by $0.85$.

exam_questions.statement:
A shop buys bicycles for $\pounds140$ each and sells them for $\pounds189$ each.
(a) Calculate the percentage profit. [2]
(b) In a clearance sale, the shop reduces the selling price by $15\%$. Calculate the new selling price. [2]
(c) Is the shop still making a profit at the sale price? Give a reason. [1]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Profit $=189-140=49$; percentage profit $=\dfrac{49}{140}\times100=35\%$. (b) $189\times0.85=\pounds160.65$. (c) $\pounds160.65$ is still more than the $\pounds140$ cost price, so the shop is still making a profit (of $\pounds20.65$).
mark_scheme: (b) M1 for multiplying $189$ by $0.85$ (or finding $15\%$ of $189$ and subtracting); A1 for $\pounds160.65$
(c) B1 for 'yes' with a comparison to the $\pounds140$ cost price stated
common_errors: In (a), dividing the profit by $189$ (the selling price) instead of $140$ (the cost price).

exam_questions.statement:
A price of $\pounds180$ is increased by $20\%$ and then the new price is decreased by $20\%$.
(a) Find the price after both changes. [2]
(b) Explain why the final price is not $\pounds180$. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\pounds172.80$ (b) The $20\%$ decrease is taken from the larger, already-increased price, so it removes more than the increase added.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $180\times1.2\times0.8=\pounds172.80$. (b) The increase takes $180$ to $216$; the decrease then removes $20\%$ of $216$ ($=43.20$), which is more than the $36$ gained in the increase, so the combined multiplier $1.2\times0.8=0.96$ is less than $1$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for multiplying by both $1.2$ and $0.8$ in sequence (or finding $0.96\times180$); A1 for $\pounds172.80$
(b) B1 for stating that the second change acts on a different (larger) base than the original $\pounds180$; B1 for a correct supporting calculation or comparison of amounts
common_errors: Claiming the two $20\%$ changes cancel out exactly, giving $\pounds180$ as the final answer.

exam_questions.statement:
A company's profits increased by $8\%$ in 2023 and then by a further $5\%$ in 2024. The profit at the end of 2024 was $\$226\,800$.
(a) Find the profit at the end of 2022 (before either increase). [3]
(b) Find the overall percentage increase in profit from the end of 2022 to the end of 2024. [2]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Combined multiplier $=1.08\times1.05=1.134$; profit at end of 2022 $=226\,800\div1.134=\$200\,000$. (b) Overall multiplier $1.134$ corresponds to an increase of $13.4\%$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for forming the combined multiplier $1.08\times1.05$; M1 for dividing $226\,800$ by that multiplier; A1 for $\$200\,000$
(b) M1 for $(1.134-1)\times100$ or equivalent; A1 for $13.4\%$
common_errors: Adding the two percentages ($8\%+5\%=13\%$) and dividing $226\,800$ by $1.13$, or dividing by only ONE of the two multipliers, instead of dividing by both $1.08$ and $1.05$ (in either order) or by their product $1.134$.

challenge_questions.statement: A price is increased by $25\%$ and then decreased by $20\%$. Show that the final price equals the original. Explain why a $25\%$ increase followed by a $25\%$ decrease does not.
challenge_questions.answer: $1.25\times0.8=1$, so the price is unchanged; but $1.25\times0.75=0.9375$, a $6.25\%$ fall.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $1.25\times0.8=1$, so after the $25\%$ increase and $20\%$ decrease the price is exactly unchanged (this is because $0.8=\tfrac45$ is the exact reciprocal multiplier of $1.25=\tfrac54$). But $1.25\times0.75=0.9375$: the $25\%$ decrease is taken of the larger, increased price, so the final price is $6.25\%$ LOWER than the original, not unchanged.
common_errors: Assuming any 'increase by $p\%$, then decrease by $p\%$' pair cancels, without checking whether the two multipliers are genuine reciprocals of each other.

challenge_questions.statement: A shop buys an item for $\pounds80$, marks it up by $60\%$, and then sells it in a sale with $25\%$ off the marked price. Find the shop's percentage profit.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Marked price $=80\times1.6=\pounds128$; sale price $=128\times0.75=\pounds96$; profit $=96-80=\pounds16$; percentage profit $=16\div80\times100=20\%$.
common_errors: Combining the $+60\%$ and $-25\%$ as if they applied to the SAME base (giving a wrong combined multiplier of $1.35$), rather than applying the mark-up to the cost price and the discount to the marked price in sequence.

challenge_questions.statement: Ana says that a $30\%$ reduction followed by a further $20\%$ reduction is the same as a $50\%$ reduction. Show that she is wrong and find the true overall percentage reduction.
challenge_questions.answer: The true overall reduction is $44\%$, not $50\%$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Combined multiplier $=0.7\times0.8=0.56$: the price is $56\%$ of the original, an overall reduction of $44\%$ — not $50\%$, because the second $20\%$ is taken of the ALREADY-reduced price.
common_errors: Adding the two percentages ($30\%+20\%=50\%$) directly, the same error as adding or subtracting multiplied percentage changes anywhere in the lesson.

challenge_questions.statement: In a class of $40$, $60\%$ are girls. $25\%$ of the girls and $50\%$ of the boys walk to school. What percentage of the class walk?
challenge_questions.full_solution: Girls $=0.6\times40=24$; boys $=16$. Walkers: $0.25\times24=6$ girls and $0.5\times16=8$ boys, total $14$. Percentage of the class: $14\div40\times100=35\%$.
common_errors: Averaging the two given percentages ($25\%$ and $50\%$) directly to get $37.5\%$, ignoring that the two groups (girls and boys) are different sizes.

challenge_questions.statement: A house value rises by $10\%$ in each of two years to $\pounds4\,840$. Find its value at the start of the first year, and the overall percentage increase.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Combined multiplier over two years $=1.1^2=1.21$. Starting value $=4\,840\div1.21=\pounds4\,000$. Overall increase $=21\%$ (not $20\%$, because the second year's $10\%$ is of the already-increased value).
common_errors: Dividing $4\,840$ by $1.2$ (adding the two $10\%$s to get $20\%$) instead of using the correctly compounded multiplier $1.21$.

mcq.stem: A plant's height increases from $25$ cm to $32$ cm. What is the percentage increase?

options.why_wrong: This divides the change by the NEW height ($32$) instead of the original height ($25$).
This computes $25\div32\times100$, the wrong ratio entirely (original as a percentage of new, inverted).
This states the raw change in cm ($7$) as if it were already a percentage, without dividing by the original height at all.

mcq.explanation: Change $=32-25=7$. Percentage increase $=\dfrac{7}{25}\times100=28\%$.

mcq.stem: A price rises by $30\%$ and is then reduced by $30\%$. Compared with the original price, the final price is:

options.why_wrong: This assumes a percentage rise and an equal percentage fall always cancel; in fact the combined multiplier is $1.3\times0.7=0.91$, below $1$.
A rise followed by a fall of the SAME percentage always finishes lower, never higher: the fall is taken of the larger, risen price, so it removes more than the rise added.

options.text: impossible to say without knowing the original price
options.why_wrong: The combined multiplier ($0.91$) is the same fraction of the original regardless of what the original price actually is, so the direction and size of the overall change can be found without it.

mcq.explanation: Combined multiplier $=1.3\times0.7=0.91$, a $9\%$ overall FALL — the $30\%$ decrease is of the larger, risen price, so it removes more than the rise added.

mcq.stem: A shop advertises "$30\%$ off" one item and "now costs $30\%$ of the original price" for another. The two multipliers needed are:

options.why_wrong: This treats '$30\%$ off' and 'costs $30\%$' as the same statement; '$30\%$ off' means $70\%$ REMAINS, multiplier $0.7$, not $0.3$.
This correctly finds the multiplier for '$30\%$ off' but then reuses it for 'costs $30\%$', which should use $0.3$ directly.
'$30\%$ off' is a decrease, so its multiplier must be LESS than $1$, not $1.3$.

mcq.explanation: "$30\%$ off" leaves $100\%-30\%=70\%$, multiplier $0.7$. "Costs $30\%$ of the original" means the multiplier IS $0.3$ directly — the two phrases are complementary, not interchangeable.

mcq.stem: A number is increased by $150\%$. The multiplier used is:

options.why_wrong: This converts $150\%$ to a decimal but forgets to add the starting $100\%$ ($1+1.5$).
This treats the question as a DECREASE, but $150\%$ is an INCREASE, so the multiplier must be greater than $1$.
This divides $150$ by $10$ instead of by $100$ and forgets to add the starting $100\%$; the multiplier for any increase is $1$ plus the percentage written as a decimal.

mcq.explanation: Multiplier for an increase of $150\%$ is $1+1.50=2.5$.

mcq.stem: After a $12\%$ discount, a chair costs $\pounds220$. What was the original price?

options.why_wrong: This adds $12\%$ of $\pounds220$ back on to $220$, instead of dividing by the multiplier $0.88$; the $12\%$ discount was of the larger ORIGINAL price, not of $\pounds220$.
This multiplies $220$ by $0.88$ instead of dividing, applying the discount a second time rather than reversing it.
This adds a flat $\pounds12$ (treating $12\%$ as if it were $\pounds12$) instead of calculating a genuine percentage.

mcq.explanation: The sale price is $88\%$ of the original: $220\div0.88=\pounds250$.

mcq.stem: A trader sells a lamp for $\pounds90$ at a profit of $20\%$ on the cost price. Which calculation correctly finds the cost price?

options.why_wrong: This applies a $20\%$ DECREASE multiplier to the selling price; a profit is an increase on the cost price, so a decrease multiplier is the wrong operation entirely.
This subtracts $20\%$ of the SELLING price ($90$), but the $20\%$ profit was measured against the smaller COST price, not the selling price.
This increases the selling price further, moving away from the cost price instead of reversing back towards it.

mcq.explanation: Selling price $=120\%$ of cost price, so cost price $=90\div1.2=\pounds75$.

flashcards.front: What is a percentage?
flashcards.back: A fraction with denominator $100$: $p\%=\dfrac{p}{100}$.

flashcards.front: Multiplier for an increase/decrease of $p\%$
flashcards.back: Increase: $1+\dfrac{p}{100}$. Decrease: $1-\dfrac{p}{100}$.

flashcards.front: Percentage change formula
flashcards.back: $\dfrac{\text{actual change}}{\text{ORIGINAL value}}\times100\%$ — original is always the denominator.

flashcards.front: True or false: a $20\%$ rise followed by a $20\%$ fall returns a price to its original value.
flashcards.back: False. $1.2\times0.8=0.96$, a $4\%$ overall FALL — the fall is taken of the larger, risen price.

flashcards.front: '$40\%$ off' vs. 'costs $40\%$' — same multiplier?
flashcards.back: No. '$40\%$ off' $\to$ multiplier $0.6$ ($100\%-40\%$ remains). 'Costs $40\%$' $\to$ multiplier $0.4$ directly.

flashcards.front: Percentage profit or loss — as a percentage of WHICH price?
flashcards.back: Always the COST price, unless the question states otherwise.

flashcards.front: Reverse percentages: finding the original
flashcards.back: $\text{original}=\text{known (new) value}\div\text{multiplier}$ — divide, never add or subtract a percentage of the known value.

flashcards.front: A jacket costs $\pounds68$ after a $20\%$ discount. Is the original $68+20\%$ of $68$?
flashcards.back: No. $\pounds68$ is $80\%$ of the ORIGINAL; divide: $68\div0.8=\pounds85$.

flashcards.front: How do you express $240$ as a percentage of $150$?
flashcards.back: $240\div150\times100=160\%$ — percentages CAN exceed $100\%$.

flashcards.front: Two successive percentage changes — how do you combine them?
flashcards.back: Multiply the two multipliers together; never add or subtract the percentages directly.

flashcards.front: Deposit + remaining balance
flashcards.back: Deposit $=$ percentage $\times$ total price; remaining $=$ total $-$ deposit.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Percentage change is always calculated by dividing the change by the NEW value, not the original value.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The new value is usually the more recently calculated, more 'in focus' number, and in many everyday situations (a current price, say) it is the number that is easiest to reach for when dividing.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: For a price rising from $\pounds40$ to $\pounds46$, the learner computes $6\div46=13.0\%$ instead of $6\div40=15\%$.
misconceptions.correct_model: Percentage change $=\dfrac{\text{actual change}}{\text{ORIGINAL value}}\times100\%$ — the ORIGINAL (starting) value is always the denominator, never the new value.
misconceptions.remediation: Before dividing, label the two values 'original' and 'new' explicitly in the working, and underline the word 'original' as the one that goes on the bottom of the fraction.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A percentage increase of $p\%$ followed by a percentage decrease of the same $p\%$ (or vice versa) returns a quantity to its original value.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Addition and subtraction of the same amount cancel out, and it is natural to expect the same 'undo' behaviour from percentages, without noticing that each percentage change is taken of a DIFFERENT (already-changed) base.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner claims a $10\%$ rise followed by a $10\%$ fall leaves a price unchanged, or computes the combined multiplier as $1+0.10-0.10=1$ instead of multiplying the two multipliers together.
misconceptions.correct_model: Combine percentage changes by MULTIPLYING the multipliers, never by adding or subtracting the percentages: $1.1\times0.9=0.99$, an overall $1\%$ FALL, because the second change acts on the larger, already-increased amount.
misconceptions.remediation: Always convert each change to its own multiplier and multiply them together in sequence; test with a concrete starting value (e.g. $100$) to see the actual overall effect before trusting any shortcut.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: '$40\%$ off' and 'costs $40\%$' describe the same multiplier.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both phrases contain the number $40\%$ and both describe a price that is smaller than the original, so without pausing to find the complementary percentage they can feel interchangeable.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner uses the multiplier $0.4$ for a '$40\%$ off' question (which actually needs $0.6$), or $0.6$ for a 'the sale price is $40\%$ of the original' question (which actually needs $0.4$).
misconceptions.correct_model: '$40\%$ OFF' means you keep $100\%-40\%=60\%$, multiplier $0.6$. 'COSTS $40\%$' (of the original) means the multiplier IS $0.4$ directly. The two phrases are complementary, not identical.
misconceptions.remediation: Rewrite the phrase as 'the new price is ___ \% of the original' before choosing a multiplier; for 'off', that requires the subtraction step ($100-40$) first.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: To reverse a percentage change, work out the percentage of the NEW value and add it back on (or take it off), instead of dividing by the multiplier.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Addition/subtraction feels like a natural 'opposite' of the addition/subtraction that seemed to create the change in the first place, and the reverse-percentage method (dividing by a multiplier) is a genuinely new idea that is easy to skip under time pressure in favour of a familiar-looking shortcut.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: For a jacket costing $\pounds68$ after a $20\%$ reduction, the learner computes $20\%$ of $68$ ($=13.60$) and adds it back to get $\pounds81.60$, instead of dividing $68$ by $0.8$ to get $\pounds85$.
misconceptions.correct_model: The known value is a percentage of the ORIGINAL, not of itself, so the original is found by DIVIDING the known value by the multiplier: $\text{original}=\text{known value}\div\text{multiplier}$.
misconceptions.remediation: Always ask first: 'what percentage of the ORIGINAL does the value I have represent?' (e.g. $80\%$ after a $20\%$ reduction), write the multiplier for that percentage, and then DIVIDE by it — never add or subtract a percentage of the known value.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dividing by the new value instead of the original value when finding a percentage change.
common_mistakes.why: The new value is usually the number most recently calculated or most 'in view', so it is the one reached for first.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Label 'original' and 'new' explicitly before dividing, and always put the ORIGINAL on the bottom of the fraction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding or subtracting percentages directly instead of multiplying the multipliers.
common_mistakes.why: Addition/subtraction of the same percentage feels like it should 'cancel', mirroring how adding and subtracting the same NUMBER cancels.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always convert each percentage change to its own multiplier and multiply them together in sequence; test with a concrete value if unsure.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding a percentage of the known (new) value back on to reverse a percentage change.
common_mistakes.why: Addition/subtraction feels like the natural 'opposite' of whatever operation seemed to create the change.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always divide the known value by the multiplier that created it — never add or subtract a percentage of the known value itself.

exam_notes: Non-calculator papers use friendly percentages (multiples of $5\%$ or $10\%$); on the calculator paper, keep the multiplier exact (e.g. $0.88$) and round only at the end, to $2$ d.p. for money.
The command word 'show that' requires the FULL working with the multiplier or the percentage-change fraction written out — a bare final answer, even if correct, does not earn full marks.
For 'percentage profit' always divide by the COST price, unless the question states otherwise — state which price you are using as the base as part of your working.

For a reverse-percentage question, write the known value as a percentage of the original FIRST (e.g. 'the sale price is $80\%$ of the original') before dividing — this line itself earns a method mark even if the final division then goes wrong.

summary.big_idea: Every percentage statement is about $100\%$ of some base quantity; convert the percentage to a multiplier ($1\pm p/100$) to go forward (find a new value from an original), and divide by that same multiplier to go backward (find the original from a known new value) — never add or subtract a percentage of the wrong base.
key_points: $p\%$ of $A=\dfrac{p}{100}\times A$; one quantity as a percentage of another is $\dfrac{\text{part}}{\text{whole}}\times100\%$, with both quantities in the SAME unit.
Increase/decrease by $p\%$: multiply by $1\pm p/100$. Percentage change: $\dfrac{\text{change}}{\text{ORIGINAL}}\times100\%$, never divided by the new value.
Two successive percentage changes combine by MULTIPLYING the multipliers, not by adding or subtracting the percentages — a rise and an equal fall do not generally cancel.
Percentage profit/loss is always measured against the COST price; percentages can validly exceed $100\%$.
Extended: reverse percentages find the original by DIVIDING the known value by the multiplier that created it, never by adding/subtracting a percentage of the known value.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Decide which quantity is the $100\%$ (the original/base), convert the percentage to a multiplier, and multiply to go forward or divide to go backward — never add or subtract a percentage of the wrong quantity.

epistemic_overrides.note: Mental shortcuts without a calculator
Percentage increase and decrease: the multiplier
Reverse percentages: divide by the multiplier

12_Money_Simple_and_Compound_Interest.js.title: Money, Simple and Compound Interest
12_Money_Simple_and_Compound_Interest.js.subject: Mathematics
12_Money_Simple_and_Compound_Interest.js.course_label: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 · Number · Core + Extended

objectives.statement: Convert between currencies in both directions, and calculate gross pay, net pay and overtime pay.
Find profit or loss as an amount and as a percentage of the cost price, including discount and deposit calculations.
Calculate simple interest and compound interest without being given a formula, using the multiplier method for compound interest.
Compare simple and compound growth, and solve problems involving repeated percentage change at different rates.

prerequisites.statement: Convert a percentage to a decimal multiplier and use it to increase or decrease a quantity (from the previous Percentages lesson).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every calculation in this lesson — currency, wages, profit, and both kinds of interest — is built from the SAME multiplier idea; without it, compound interest in particular has no way to get started.

prerequisites.statement: Use a power/index on a calculator (e.g. evaluate $1.025^3$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Compound interest over several years is calculated with a single power of the multiplier; without this calculator skill, a student is forced back into a slow year-by-year table even when a direct calculation is expected.

prerequisites.statement: Round a money answer to $2$ decimal places (the nearest cent or penny).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every answer in this lesson is a sum of money, and the exam expects the final answer rounded correctly, with the FULL calculator value carried through the working rather than a rounded intermediate value.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise that percentage profit/loss is measured against the cost price (from the previous Percentages lesson).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson's profit and discount examples reuse that convention directly; without it, 'percentage profit' has no fixed meaning and could be measured against either price given in a question.

diagnostic_items.question: A price rises by $12\%$. By what number do you multiply it, and by what number do you multiply for a $12\%$ fall?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $1.12$ for the rise, $0.88$ for the fall.

common_wrong_answers.answer: $0.12$ for the rise and $-0.12$ for the fall.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Gives the percentage itself (as a decimal) instead of the full multiplier, forgetting to combine it with the starting $100\%$.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Confirms that the multiplier method from the previous lesson is still solid before it gets reused, without correction, inside the compound-interest formula.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Rebuild the multiplier as '$100\%\pm$ the change': $100\%+12\%=112\%=1.12$ for the rise, $100\%-12\%=88\%=0.88$ for the fall.

diagnostic_items.question: Why is compound interest greater than simple interest at the same rate after $2$ or more years, but equal after exactly $1$ year?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: After $1$ year there is no earlier interest yet to add, so both methods give the same result. From year $2$ onward, compound interest is calculated on a bigger amount each year (the previous interest is included), so it grows faster than simple interest, which is always calculated on the same, original principal.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Compound interest is always bigger, because 'compound' sounds like more.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Has learned the conclusion (compound $>$ simple) without the mechanism (interest-on-interest) that explains WHY, which makes the year-$1$ exception invisible to them.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner understands the MECHANISM of compounding (a growing base), rather than just memorising 'compound interest is bigger'.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Build a short year-by-year table for a concrete example and highlight the exact row (year $1$) where the two methods still agree, then the first row (year $2$) where they start to differ.

diagnostic_items.question: A shopkeeper sells an item at a $10\%$ profit. Is the selling price $1.1$ times the cost price or $1.1$ times the selling price? Explain.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $1.1$ times the COST price. Profit is always measured on what was paid (the cost price), so the selling price $=$ cost price $\times1.1$.

common_wrong_answers.answer: $1.1$ times the selling price, since that's the final price customers pay.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Confuses the two roles in the sentence: the selling price is the OUTPUT of the multiplication, not a quantity multiplied by itself.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner can state which quantity the multiplier is applied TO, not just that a multiplier of $1.1$ is involved somewhere.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write the relationship as an explicit equation, $\text{selling price}=\text{cost price}\times1.1$, and substitute a concrete cost price to see which number the $1.1$ actually multiplies.

diagnostic_items.question: You change euros to a currency whose rate is €$1=15$ units. Should the number you get be larger or smaller than the number of euros?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Larger: the rate is $1\to15$, so each euro is worth $15$ of the new currency, and multiplying by $15$ makes the number bigger.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Smaller, because converting currencies usually 'loses value'.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Confuses the everyday idea of a conversion fee or loss in VALUE with the NUMBER printed on the currency, which depends purely on the stated rate, not on any general sense that conversions lose money.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Rehearses the direction-sensing skill (which currency gives the bigger NUMBER) that every currency conversion in this lesson depends on.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Rewrite the rate as a sentence ('$1$ euro buys $15$ units') and ask which currency has the bigger number attached to $1$ unit of the other.

diagnostic_items.question: Explain why a $20\%$ increase followed by a $20\%$ decrease leaves you with less than you started with.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The combined multiplier is $1.2\times0.8=0.96$, a $4\%$ overall FALL: the $20\%$ decrease is taken from the larger, already-increased amount, so it removes more than the $20\%$ increase added.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It should leave you with exactly the same amount, since $+20\%$ and $-20\%$ are opposite.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Treats the two percentage changes as acting on the SAME fixed base, rather than recognising that the second change acts on the NEW, already-changed amount.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This Extended diagnostic directly previews the repeated-percentage-change section: it checks whether the learner already senses that successive percentage changes multiply rather than cancel, before the formal multiplier method for repeated change is taught.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Work through a concrete value (e.g. $100\to120\to96$) to show the mechanism explicitly, then generalise to the rule 'multiply the multipliers, never add the percentages'.

theory_blocks.title: Money problems are percentage problems in disguise
theory_blocks.body: Almost every money problem is a percentage problem in disguise. Increasing an amount by $r\%$ means multiplying it by $1+\tfrac{r}{100}$; decreasing it by $r\%$ means multiplying by $1-\tfrac{r}{100}$. [[blue:**Compound interest is simply that multiplication repeated once for every year**]] — the whole new idea in this lesson is applying a multiplier more than once, not a new kind of multiplier.
