theory_blocks.title: Which way does a currency rate go?
theory_blocks.body: Write the exchange rate as "$1$ unit of the FIRST currency $=x$ units of the SECOND", then decide which currency you HAVE and which you WANT. Changing into the currency with the BIGGER number in the rate: **multiply** by the rate. Changing back into the currency with the number $1$: **divide** by the rate. A quick sense check: if US\$ are worth LESS than €, a euro amount becomes a LARGER dollar number.

theory_blocks.title: Gross pay, net pay and overtime
theory_blocks.body:
**Gross pay** is the total earned before anything is taken away. **Net pay** is what is left after deductions such as tax and pension:
$$\text{net pay}=\text{gross pay}-\text{deductions}.$$
**Overtime** is paid at a higher rate for hours beyond the basic week: *time and a half* means $1.5\times$ the basic hourly rate, *double time* means $2\times$. In **piece work** the pay depends on the number of articles made, not on the time taken.

theory_blocks.title: Profit, loss, discount and deposit
theory_blocks.body:
If the selling price is greater than the cost price there is a **profit**; if it is smaller there is a **loss**:
$$\text{profit}=\text{selling price}-\text{cost price},\qquad \text{percentage profit}=\frac{\text{profit}}{\text{cost price}}\times100\%.$$
A **discount** is a reduction in the normal price; a **deposit** is a first payment, often a percentage of the price, with the rest paid later. Percentage profit or loss is always taken on the COST price, unless the question says otherwise.

theory_blocks.title: Two slips with profit and discount
theory_blocks.body: [[red:Working out percentage profit as a percentage of the SELLING price]] is wrong: the comparison must be with [[green:what the shop PAID, the cost price]]. Another common slip is to take a $15\%$ discount and then "add $15\%$ back" to check — a $15\%$ fall followed by a $15\%$ rise does NOT return to the start, because the second percentage is of a different (smaller) base.

theory_blocks.title: Simple interest
theory_blocks.body:
When you save money, the bank pays you **interest**; when you borrow, you pay it. In **simple interest** the same amount is paid every year, always calculated on the ORIGINAL sum (the **principal**).
$$\text{simple interest}=P\times\frac{R}{100}\times T,\qquad \text{total amount}=P+\text{interest}.$$
This formula is NOT given in the exam, but it rebuilds easily: find one year's interest ($R\%$ of $P$) and multiply by the number of years $T$.

theory_blocks.title: Compound interest: the multiplier method
theory_blocks.body:
With **compound interest** the interest earned each year is added to the account, so next year's interest is calculated on a BIGGER amount: you earn "interest on interest". At $r\%$ compound interest, the amount after one year is $\text{amount}\times\left(1+\tfrac r{100}\right)$; after $n$ years the same multiplication has been done $n$ times:
$$\text{amount after }n\text{ years}=P\times\left(1+\frac{r}{100}\right)^{n},\qquad \text{compound interest}=\text{final amount}-P.$$

theory_blocks.title: Compound interest must beat simple interest after year 1
theory_blocks.body: Compound interest must be LARGER than simple interest at the same rate over more than one year. For \$4\,000 at $2.5\%$ for $3$ years, simple interest would be $4000\times0.025\times3=\$300$, and the compound interest, $\$307.56$, is bigger — if your compound-interest answer comes out smaller than or equal to the simple-interest value for the same data (beyond year $1$), you have made a slip. Keep the full calculator value until the last step and round only then.

theory_blocks.title: Repeated percentage change at different rates
theory_blocks.body:
Compound interest is one example of a **repeated percentage change**. The rate need NOT be the same every time, and the changes need not all be increases: you multiply the quantity by one multiplier for EACH change.

1. Turn each percentage change into a multiplier ($+8\%\to1.08$, $-5\%\to0.95$).
2. Multiply the starting value by ALL the multipliers, in any order.
3. For the OVERALL percentage change, multiply the multipliers together and convert back: (overall multiplier $-1$) $\times100\%$.

theory_blocks.title: Percentages in a sequence do not add
theory_blocks.body: Adding percentages is wrong: a rise of $10\%$ followed by a fall of $10\%$ is NOT zero change. $1.1\times0.9=0.99$, so there is an overall FALL of $1\%$. The second percentage is taken of a different amount, so the two changes do not cancel — and in general, several percentage changes in sequence never simply add or subtract.

theory_blocks.title: Finding the rate from an overall multiplier
theory_blocks.body:
Sometimes the starting value and the final value are given and the RATE is what you have to find. Growth over $n$ equal periods at the same rate multiplies by $b^{\,n}$, so work backwards:

1. Divide the final value by the starting value to get the **overall multiplier** $b^{\,n}$.
2. Take the $n$th root to get the multiplier for ONE period: $b=\sqrt[n]{b^{\,n}}$.
3. Turn that one-period multiplier back into a rate: $r=(b-1)\times100$.

For two periods this is a square root, for three a cube root. Never read the rate straight off the overall multiplier: [[red:an overall multiplier of $1.1025$ over $2$ years is NOT $10.25\%$ per year]] — it is [[green:$\sqrt{1.1025}=1.05$, that is $5\%$ per year]].

keywords.definition: The amount of one currency that is equivalent to one unit of another currency.
The total amount earned before any deductions are taken away.
Gross pay minus deductions such as tax and pension.
Pay at a higher rate for hours worked beyond the basic week, e.g. time and a half or double time.
The original sum of money invested or borrowed, before any interest is added.
Interest calculated as the same fixed amount every year, always on the original principal.
Interest calculated each year on the principal PLUS all interest already added, so it grows faster than simple interest.
Finding a new value after a percentage change by multiplying by $1\pm r/100$, applied repeatedly for compound growth.
A sequence of percentage changes, not necessarily at the same rate or in the same direction, combined by multiplying their multipliers together.
An initial payment, often a percentage of the full price, with the remainder paid later.

worked_examples.statement: Currency. The exchange rate is $\text{€}1=\text{US\$}1.08$. (a) Convert €$250$ to US dollars. (b) A camera costs US\$$540$ in New York. How much is that in euros?
reasoning: (a) €1 buys US\$1.08, so going from euros to dollars means multiplying by $1.08$.
(b) Dollars are being changed BACK into euros, so divide by $1.08$.
worked_examples.interpretation: The direction of the conversion decides multiply or divide; checking the reverse calculation confirms the direction was chosen correctly.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Multiplying in part (b) as well, which would give a euro amount far too large.

worked_examples.statement: Wages. Lena earns \$$12$ per hour for a basic week of $36$ hours. Last week she also worked $5$ hours of overtime at time and a half. Deductions are $20\%$ of her gross pay. Find her net pay.
reasoning: Find basic pay: rate $\times$ basic hours.
Find the overtime rate ($1.5\times12$) and overtime pay (rate $\times5$ hours).
Add basic and overtime pay to get gross pay.
Net pay is gross pay $\times$ ($100\%-20\%$).
worked_examples.solution: Basic pay: $36\times12=\$432$. Overtime rate: $1.5\times12=\$18$/h, so overtime pay is $5\times18=\$90$. Gross pay: $432+90=\$522$. Net pay is $80\%$ of gross: $0.8\times522=\$417.60$.
worked_examples.interpretation: A wage calculation with overtime is just two separate rate calculations (basic and overtime) added together, followed by one ordinary percentage-decrease calculation for the deductions.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Applying the $1.5\times$ overtime multiplier to the WHOLE week's hours instead of only the $5$ overtime hours.

worked_examples.statement: Profit and discount. A shop buys a bicycle for \$$240$ and sells it for \$$312$. (a) Find the percentage profit. (b) In a sale the selling price is reduced by $15\%$. Find the sale price and say whether the shop still makes a profit.
reasoning: (a) Profit $=$ selling price $-$ cost price, then divide by the COST price.
(b) The sale price is $85\%$ of the original selling price; compare the result with the cost price to decide on profit or loss.
worked_examples.solution: (a) Profit $=312-240=\$72$, so percentage profit $=\dfrac{72}{240}\times100=30\%$. (b) $0.85\times312=\$265.20$. This is more than the \$240 cost price, so there is still a profit of $265.20-240=\$25.20$.
worked_examples.interpretation: A sale discount is applied to the SELLING price, but whether a profit remains must still be checked against the (unchanged) cost price — two different reference prices are in play in the same question.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing by $312$ in part (a) instead of $240$, or in part (b) assuming the sale automatically means a loss without actually comparing $\$265.20$ with the cost price.

worked_examples.statement: Simple interest. \$$2\,500$ is invested at $3.2\%$ simple interest per year. Find (a) the interest after $4$ years, (b) the total amount, (c) the number of years needed to earn \$$400$ of interest.
reasoning: (a) Find one year's interest, then multiply by the number of years.
(b) Add the interest to the principal.
(c) Divide the target interest by one year's interest.
worked_examples.solution: (a) Interest each year: $2500\times0.032=\$80$. After $4$ years: $4\times80=\$320$. (b) Total amount: $2500+320=\$2\,820$. (c) Each year adds \$80, so $400\div80=5$ years.
worked_examples.interpretation: Simple interest grows by the SAME fixed amount every year, so questions about a number of years or a target interest are solved with ordinary multiplication or division, never a power.
worked_examples.common_mistake: In part (c), dividing $400$ by the PRINCIPAL ($2500$) instead of by one year's interest ($80$).

worked_examples.statement: Compound interest. \$$4\,000$ is invested at $2.5\%$ compound interest per year. Find the amount after $3$ years and the interest earned.
reasoning: The multiplier is $1.025$.
Apply the multiplier three times (once per year), either as a year-by-year table or directly as a power.
worked_examples.solution: Using the multiplier directly: $4000\times1.025^3=\$4\,307.56$ (to the nearest cent), so the interest is $4307.56-4000=\$307.56$.
worked_examples.interpretation: A year-by-year table and the direct power $1.025^3$ are the SAME calculation; the power is simply a shortcut once the pattern of repeated multiplication is understood.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Calculating $4000\times1.025\times3=\$12\,300$ (treating the power as an ordinary multiplication by $3$), which is absurdly large; another slip is using simple interest ($4000+3\times100=\$4\,300$), which is too small because it ignores interest on interest.

worked_examples.statement: Different rates. \$$5\,000$ is invested for $3$ years. The interest rates for the three years are $2\%$, $3.5\%$ and $4\%$. Find the final amount and the overall percentage increase.
reasoning: Convert each rate to its own multiplier: $1.02$, $1.035$, $1.04$.
Multiply the principal by all three multipliers.
Multiply the three multipliers together to get the OVERALL multiplier, then convert to a percentage.
worked_examples.solution: $5000\times1.02\times1.035\times1.04=\$5\,489.64$. The overall multiplier is $1.02\times1.035\times1.04=1.09793$, an overall increase of $9.793\%\approx9.79\%$ (3 s.f.) — a little MORE than $2+3.5+4=9.5\%$, because of the interest on interest.
worked_examples.interpretation: When the rate changes each period, the SAME multiply-the-multipliers method still works — compound interest at a fixed rate is just the special case where all the multipliers happen to be equal.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Adding the three rates ($2+3.5+4=9.5\%$) and using a single multiplier of $1.095$ for the whole calculation, instead of multiplying the three separate multipliers.

worked_examples.statement: Up then down. The price of a jacket is increased by $8\%$, and then reduced by $5\%$ in a sale. What is the overall percentage change?
reasoning: Convert each change to its own multiplier: $1.08$ for $+8\%$, $0.95$ for $-5\%$.
Multiply the two multipliers together and convert the result back to a percentage change.
worked_examples.solution: $1.08\times0.95=1.026$. The overall change is $+2.6\%$, an increase of $2.6\%$.
worked_examples.interpretation: A mixed sequence of an increase and a decrease is handled by exactly the same multiply-the-multipliers rule as two increases or two decreases — the sign of each individual change is already built into its multiplier.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Subtracting the percentages ($8\%-5\%=3\%$) instead of multiplying the multipliers, which happens to look close here but is not the correct method and fails badly for larger percentages.

worked_examples.statement: Finding the rate. \$$4\,000$ is invested at $r\%$ compound interest per year and grows to \$$4\,630.50$ after $3$ years. Find $r$.
knowns: $n=3$ equal yearly periods at the same rate
reasoning: Divide the final amount by the principal to get the overall multiplier for the three years.
Take the CUBE root, because the same one-year multiplier has been applied three times.
Subtract $1$ and multiply by $100$ to turn the one-year multiplier back into a percentage rate.
worked_examples.solution: Overall multiplier $=4\,630.50\div4\,000=1.157625$. One-year multiplier $=\sqrt[3]{1.157625}=1.05$. So $r=(1.05-1)\times100=5$, that is $5\%$ per year. Check: $4\,000\times1.05^{3}=\$4\,630.50$.
worked_examples.interpretation: The $n$th root undoes the $n$th power, so it undoes $n$ periods of compounding in one step. Dividing the overall percentage increase by $3$ would not work either: $15.7625\%\div3=5.254\%$, which is too big, because each year's interest also earns interest.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reading the rate straight off the overall multiplier ($1.157625$, giving '$15.7625\%$ per year') instead of taking the cube root first.

guided_exercises.statement: Priya earns $\pounds11$ per hour for a basic week of $30$ hours, plus $4$ hours of overtime at double time. Deductions are $18\%$ of her gross pay. Find her net pay.
hints: Find the basic pay and the overtime pay separately, using the correct overtime rate, before adding them.
Net pay is gross pay multiplied by the complement of the deduction percentage ($100\%-18\%$).
guided_exercises.full_solution: Basic pay $=30\times11=\pounds330$. Overtime rate $=2\times11=\pounds22$/h; overtime pay $=4\times22=\pounds88$. Gross pay $=330+88=\pounds418$. Net pay $=0.82\times418=\pounds342.76$.
common_errors: Using the basic rate ($\pounds11$) for the overtime hours instead of double it, or applying the deduction percentage before adding the overtime pay.

guided_exercises.statement: \$$1\,500$ is invested at $4\%$ compound interest per year. Find the amount after $2$ years, and compare it with the simple interest that would be earned over the same $2$ years.
hints: For compound interest, apply the multiplier $1.04$ twice (as a power).
For simple interest, use $P\times R\%\times T$ with the SAME principal, rate and time, and compare the two interest amounts.
guided_exercises.answer: Compound amount $\$1\,622.40$ (interest $\$122.40$); simple interest $\$120$. Compound interest is $\$2.40$ more.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Compound: $1500\times1.04^2=\$1\,622.40$, interest $=\$122.40$. Simple: $1500\times0.04\times2=\$120$. Compound interest is larger by $122.40-120=\$2.40$, confirming the 'compound beats simple after year 1' check.
common_errors: Computing the compound amount as $1500\times1.04\times2$ instead of $1500\times1.04^2$.

guided_exercises.statement: A company's sales increase by $6\%$ in the first year and then fall by $4\%$ in the second year. Find the overall percentage change in sales over the two years.
hints: Convert each year's change to its own multiplier.
Multiply the two multipliers together, then convert the combined multiplier back to a percentage change — do not subtract the two percentages.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Multipliers: $1.06$ and $0.96$. Combined: $1.06\times0.96=1.0176$, an overall increase of $1.76\%$ (not $6\%-4\%=2\%$).
common_errors: Subtracting the percentages ($6\%-4\%=2\%$) instead of multiplying the two multipliers.

exercises.statement: The exchange rate is €$1=$ US\$$1.08$. (a) Convert €$250$ to US\$. (b) Convert US\$$432$ to euros. (c) A coat costs US\$$135$ in New York. What is its price in euros?
common_errors: Multiplying instead of dividing in parts (b) and (c), where dollars are being changed back into euros.

exercises.statement: Amara earns \$$9.60$ per hour for a $35$-hour week. She also works $6$ hours of overtime at time and a half. (a) Find her gross pay. (b) $22\%$ of her gross pay is deducted. Find her net pay.
common_errors: Using the basic rate instead of time-and-a-half ($1.5\times9.60=14.40$) for the overtime hours.

exercises.statement: A phone is bought for \$$240$ and sold for \$$312$. Find the profit and the percentage profit.
exercises.full_solution: Profit $=312-240=\$72$. Percentage profit $=72\div240\times100=30\%$.
common_errors: Dividing the profit by $312$ (the selling price) instead of $240$ (the cost price).

exercises.statement: A coat costing \$$120$ is sold in a sale with a $35\%$ discount. Find the discount and the sale price.
exercises.full_solution: Discount $=0.35\times120=\$42$. Sale price $=120-42=\$78$.
common_errors: Giving the discount amount ($\$42$) as the final sale price.

exercises.statement: A television has a cash price of \$$640$. It can be bought with a $15\%$ deposit followed by $12$ monthly payments of \$$48.50$. Find the total paid, and how much more this is than the cash price.
exercises.answer: Total $\$678$; $\$38$ more than the cash price.
exercises.full_solution: Deposit $=0.15\times640=\$96$. Payments $=12\times48.50=\$582$. Total $=96+582=\$678$, which is $678-640=\$38$ more than the cash price.
common_errors: Forgetting to add the deposit to the $12$ monthly payments when finding the total paid.

exercises.statement: Find the simple interest on \$$1\,800$ invested for $5$ years at $4\%$ per year, and the total amount at the end.
common_errors: Giving the total amount ($\$2\,160$) when only the interest was asked for, or vice versa.

exercises.statement: How many years does it take \$$500$ to earn \$$90$ simple interest at $3\%$ per year?
exercises.full_solution: One year's interest $=500\times0.03=\$15$. $90\div15=6$ years.
common_errors: Dividing $90$ by the principal $500$ instead of by one year's interest.

exercises.statement: \$$6\,000$ is invested at $3\%$ compound interest per year. Find the amount after $2$ years and the interest earned.
common_errors: Computing $6000\times1.03\times2$ (the simple-interest pattern) instead of $6000\times1.03^2$.

exercises.statement: \$$2\,000$ is invested for $3$ years at $5\%$ per year. Find how much more interest is earned with compound interest than with simple interest.
exercises.full_solution: Simple interest $=2000\times0.05\times3=\$300$. Compound: $2000\times1.05^3=2315.25$, interest $=\$315.25$. Difference $=315.25-300=\$15.25$.
common_errors: Comparing the two FINAL AMOUNTS instead of the two INTEREST amounts, or vice versa, when the question asks specifically for the difference in interest.

exercises.statement: Sam invests \$$850$ at $2.4\%$ simple interest per year. Find the total in his account after $3$ years.
common_errors: Forgetting to add the interest to the principal, leaving the interest ($\$61.20$) as the final answer.

exercises.statement: The price of a bike is increased by $12\%$ and then reduced by $10\%$. Find the overall percentage change.
exercises.full_solution: $1.12\times0.9=1.008$: an increase of $0.8\%$.
common_errors: Subtracting the two percentages ($12\%-10\%=2\%$) instead of multiplying the multipliers.

exercises.statement: \$$5\,000$ is invested for three years at interest rates of $2\%$, $3.5\%$ and $4\%$ in the three years. Show that the final amount is \$$5\,489.64$ to the nearest cent.
exercises.full_solution: $5000\times1.02\times1.035\times1.04=5489.64$ (to the nearest cent).
common_errors: Using a single average rate for all three years instead of each year's own multiplier.

exercises.statement: Find the overall percentage increase when a sum is invested for $5$ years at $4\%$ compound interest per year. Give your answer to $3$ significant figures.
common_errors: Giving the multiplier itself ($1.22$) instead of converting it to a percentage INCREASE.

exercises.statement: \$$1\,000$ is invested at $6\%$ compound interest per year. Find the smallest whole number of years after which the amount exceeds \$$1\,500$.
common_errors: Stopping at $6$ years because $1.4185$ looks 'close enough' to $1.5$, instead of checking the NEXT whole year as well.

exercises.statement: The compound interest earned in $2$ years at $4\%$ per year is \$$326.40$. Find the sum invested.
common_errors: Dividing $326.40$ by $0.04\times2$ (the simple-interest rate), instead of by the correct compound factor $1.04^2-1$.

exercises.statement: A tourist changes £$800$ into euros at £$1=$€$1.17$. She spends €$600$ and changes the rest back into pounds at €$1=$£$0.85$. How many pounds does she receive?
common_errors: Dividing by $0.85$ instead of multiplying (confusing the two different conversion rates given in the two directions).

exercises.statement: A jacket costs \$$120$. In a sale its price is reduced by $15\%$. (a) Find the sale price. (b) Rohan says that adding $15\%$ of the sale price back on will bring the price back to \$$120$. Show that he is wrong.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Sale price $=0.85\times120=\$102$. (b) $15\%$ of \$$102$ is $0.15\times102=\$15.30$, so adding it back gives $102+15.30=\$117.30$, which is less than \$$120$. The discount was $15\%$ of \$$120$, which is \$$18$, but the increase is only $15\%$ of the smaller amount \$$102$. To undo the discount properly, divide by the multiplier: $102\div0.85=\$120$.
common_errors: Assuming that a $p\%$ decrease is undone by a $p\%$ increase, when the two percentages are taken of different base amounts.

exam_questions.statement:
Tomas earns $\pounds10.50$ per hour for a basic week of $32$ hours. Last week he worked an extra $6$ hours of overtime at time and a half.
(a) Calculate his gross pay for the week. [3]
(b) $19\%$ of his gross pay is deducted for tax and pension. Calculate his net pay. [2]
(c) The following week his gross pay is $\pounds485.10$. Find this as a percentage of the gross pay calculated in part (a). [1]
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for the overtime rate $1.5\times10.50$; M1 for basic pay plus overtime pay; A1 for $\pounds441$
(b) M1 for the multiplier $0.81$ applied to the gross pay; A1 for $\pounds357.21$
common_errors: In (a), applying the overtime rate to all $38$ hours instead of only the $6$ overtime hours.

exam_questions.statement:
\$$3\,200$ is invested for $4$ years.
(a) Calculate the simple interest earned if the rate is $3.5\%$ per year. [2]
(b) Calculate the compound interest earned over the same $4$ years if the rate is also $3.5\%$ per year, compounded annually. [3]
(c) Explain, without further calculation, why your answer to (b) must be greater than your answer to (a). [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\$448$ (b) $\$472.07$ (to the nearest cent) (c) Because compound interest earns interest on the previously-added interest as well as on the principal.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $3200\times0.035\times4=\$448$. (b) $3200\times1.035^4-3200=3672.07\ldots-3200=\$472.07$ (to the nearest cent). (c) After the first year both methods agree, but from the second year onward compound interest is calculated on a growing amount (principal plus all interest added so far), while simple interest is always calculated on the same, unchanged principal — so compound interest accumulates faster over more than one year.
mark_scheme: (b) M1 for the multiplier $1.035^4$; M1 for subtracting $3200$ from the final amount; A1 for $\$472.07$ (accept $\$472.06$ or $\$472.08$ from early rounding, but the full-precision value should be used)
(c) B1 for identifying that compound interest is earned on previous interest as well as the principal; B1 for stating that this effect only appears from the second year onward
common_errors: In (b), computing $3200\times1.035\times4$ (the simple-interest pattern) instead of the power $1.035^4$.

exam_questions.statement:
A shop's weekly sales were \$$8\,000$. In the next three weeks, sales rose by $5\%$, then fell by $3\%$, then rose by $2\%$.
(a) Calculate the sales after the three weeks. [3]
(b) Find the overall percentage change in sales over the three weeks, to $3$ significant figures. [2]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $8000\times1.05\times0.97\times1.02=8310.96$. (b) Overall multiplier $=1.05\times0.97\times1.02=1.03887$, an increase of $3.89\%$ (3 s.f.) — not $5-3+2=4\%$ exactly, because of the compounding effect.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for forming all three multipliers ($1.05$, $0.97$, $1.02$); M1 for multiplying them together with the starting value; A1 for $\$8\,310.96$ or $\$8\,310$ (3 s.f.)
(b) M1 for $(1.03887-1)\times100$ or equivalent; A1 for $3.89\%$
common_errors: Adding and subtracting the percentages directly ($5-3+2=4\%$) and treating that as exact, rather than multiplying the multipliers and finding the small compounding difference.

challenge_questions.statement: Money invested at $5\%$ per year doubles in value after some time. Show that this takes $20$ years with simple interest but only $15$ years with compound interest (the first whole number of years after which the amount is more than double).
challenge_questions.full_solution: Simple: $5\%$ per year adds $5\%$ of the ORIGINAL each year, so doubling needs $100\div5=20$ years exactly. Compound: $1.05^{14}=1.98<2$ but $1.05^{15}=2.079>2$, so $15$ years.
common_errors: Assuming compound interest doubles in exactly half the time simple interest does, rather than checking successive whole years.

challenge_questions.statement: A price is increased by $10\%$ and then decreased by $10\%$. (a) Show that the overall change is a decrease of $1\%$. (b) What single percentage increase, to $3$ significant figures, would take the new price back to the original?
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) $1.1\times0.9=0.99$, a $1\%$ decrease. (b) Need a multiplier of $1\div0.99=1.0101\ldots$, an increase of $1.01\%$ (3 s.f.).
common_errors: In (b), suggesting a $1\%$ increase (the SAME size as the net fall), which would only bring the price to $0.99\times1.01=0.9999$, still slightly short of the original.

challenge_questions.statement: \$$8\,000$ is invested for $2$ years at $r\%$ compound interest per year, and grows to \$$8\,820$. Find $r$.
common_errors: Dividing $8820\div8000$ to get the TOTAL multiplier $1.1025$ and reading off $r=10.25$ directly, forgetting to take the square root first since two years of compounding have occurred.

challenge_questions.statement: Nadia invests at $4\%$ SIMPLE interest per year and Omar invests the same sum at $3\%$ COMPOUND interest per year. Show that after $19$ years Nadia has more, and find the first whole year in which Omar has more.
challenge_questions.answer: Omar first has more after $20$ years.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Nadia after $n$ years: $1+0.04n$ times the sum; Omar: $1.03^n$. At $n=19$: $1.76$ against $1.03^{19}=1.7535$, so Nadia is still ahead. At $n=20$: $1.80$ against $1.03^{20}=1.8061$, so Omar is first ahead after $20$ years.
common_errors: Assuming the compound investment (Omar) overtakes immediately just because compound interest 'eventually wins', without checking the actual crossover year by substitution.

challenge_questions.statement: A currency shop gives US\$$1.05$ for each euro it buys, and charges US\$$1.12$ for each euro it SELLS. A traveller changes €$500$ to dollars and immediately changes all the dollars back to euros. How many euros are lost, and what percentage of the original €$500$ is this?
challenge_questions.full_solution: $500\times1.05=\text{US\$}525$ (buying dollars with euros, at the 'buys' rate). $525\div1.12=\text{€}468.75$ (converting back, at the 'sells' rate). Loss $=500-468.75=\text{€}31.25$, which is $31.25\div500\times100=6.25\%$ of €$500$.
common_errors: Using the SAME rate for both conversions, missing the fact that a currency exchange uses a different rate for buying than for selling — this spread is how the shop makes its profit.

mcq.stem: A trader buys an item for \$$150$ and sells it for \$$198$. What is the percentage profit?

options.why_wrong: This divides the profit by the SELLING price ($198$) instead of the cost price ($150$).
This expresses the selling price as a percentage of the cost price, rather than finding the PROFIT as a percentage of the cost price.
This divides the profit ($48$) by $100$ directly, without relating it to the cost price at all.

mcq.explanation: Profit $=198-150=48$. Percentage profit $=48\div150\times100=32\%$.

mcq.stem: A jacket is reduced by $20\%$ to $\pounds64$ in a sale. A student 'checks' this by adding $20\%$ of $\pounds64$ back on, getting $\pounds76.80$. Why does this NOT reproduce the original price?

options.text: Because the student made an arithmetic error in computing $20\%$ of $64$
options.why_wrong: The arithmetic ($20\%$ of $64=12.80$) is correct; the METHOD of adding it back is what fails, since the original discount was of a different, larger base.

options.text: Because percentage discounts cannot be reversed at all
options.why_wrong: Discounts CAN be reversed correctly — by dividing by the discount's multiplier ($\div0.8$) — just not by adding a percentage of the sale price back on.

options.text: Because $20\%$ should have been subtracted again instead of added
options.why_wrong: Subtracting again would move the price further from the original, not closer to it.

options.text: Because the $20\%$ discount was taken from the larger original price, not from the smaller sale price

mcq.explanation: The correct original price is $64\div0.8=\pounds80$. Adding $20\%$ of the SALE price ($64$) only adds $\pounds12.80$, not the full $\pounds16$ that was actually removed from the larger original price.

mcq.stem: \$$3\,000$ is invested at $5\%$ COMPOUND interest for $3$ years. Which calculation correctly finds the TOTAL amount?

options.why_wrong: This is the SIMPLE interest formula (and it gives only the interest, not the total), used where compound interest requires a power of the multiplier instead.
This applies a single multiplier of $1.15$ (as if $5\%\times3=15\%$ were added all at once), rather than compounding the $5\%$ three separate times.
This adds the principal to the multiplier itself rather than multiplying by it.

mcq.explanation: Compound interest requires the multiplier to be applied as a POWER: $3000\times1.05^3=\$3\,472.88$ (to the nearest cent).

mcq.stem: Which exchange-rate calculation correctly converts US\$$680$ back into pounds, if $\pounds1=$ US\$$1.36$?

options.why_wrong: Multiplying moves further AWAY from pounds (the number-$1$ currency); this is the correct operation for the opposite direction, pounds to dollars.
This divides the rate by the amount, the wrong way round, and gives a tiny, meaningless number.
Currency conversion is always a multiplication or division by the rate, never a subtraction.

mcq.explanation: Dollars are the bigger-number currency in the rate, so converting back to pounds (the number-$1$ currency) means dividing: $680\div1.36=\pounds500$.

mcq.stem: A price increases by $12\%$ and is then decreased by $12\%$. Compared with the original, the final price is:

options.why_wrong: This assumes a rise and an equal fall always cancel exactly, but the combined multiplier $1.12\times0.88=0.9856$ is below $1$.
A rise followed by a fall of the SAME percentage always finishes lower, never higher: the fall is taken of the larger, risen price, so it removes more than the rise added.
This reuses the $12\%$ figure directly, but the actual overall fall ($1.44\%$) is much smaller than $12\%$.

mcq.explanation: Combined multiplier $=1.12\times0.88=0.9856$, a $1.44\%$ overall FALL.

mcq.stem: A population rises by $3\%$, then rises again by $5\%$, in two successive years. The overall percentage increase over the two years is:

options.why_wrong: This simply adds the two percentages ($3\%+5\%$), ignoring that the second rise is calculated on an already-increased population.
This multiplies the two percentages ($3\times5$) rather than combining the two MULTIPLIERS correctly.
This averages the two percentages, which has no mathematical basis for combining successive percentage changes.

mcq.explanation: Combined multiplier $=1.03\times1.05=1.0815$, an overall increase of $8.15\%$ — slightly more than $3+5=8\%$ because of the compounding effect.

flashcards.front: Net pay
flashcards.back: $\text{net pay}=\text{gross pay}-\text{deductions}$.

flashcards.front: Overtime: time and a half, double time
flashcards.back: Time and a half $=1.5\times$ basic rate; double time $=2\times$ basic rate.

flashcards.front: Simple interest formula
flashcards.back: $\text{simple interest}=P\times\dfrac{R}{100}\times T$ — the SAME amount every year, on the original principal.

flashcards.front: Compound interest: amount after $n$ years
flashcards.back: $\text{amount}=P\left(1+\dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{n}$; interest $=$ amount $-P$.

flashcards.front: Simple vs. compound interest — when do they first differ?
flashcards.back: They are EQUAL after exactly $1$ year; from year $2$ onward compound interest is bigger, because it earns interest on the interest already added.

flashcards.front: True or false: compound interest can be found with $P\times R\%\times n$.
flashcards.back: False — that is the SIMPLE interest formula. Compound interest needs the multiplier raised to the power $n$: $P\times(1+r/100)^n-P$.

flashcards.front: Percentage profit/loss — as a percentage of which price?
flashcards.back: Always the COST price, unless the question states otherwise — never the selling price.

flashcards.front: Does a $p\%$ discount, with $p\%$ of the NEW price added back, return to the original?
flashcards.back: No — the original discount was of a larger base. To reverse correctly, divide by the discount's multiplier instead.

flashcards.front: Combining several percentage changes in sequence
flashcards.back: Multiply ALL the individual multipliers together; never add or subtract the percentages.

flashcards.front: Overall multiplier from a combined sequence of changes — how to get a percentage from it?
flashcards.back: (overall multiplier $-1)\times100\%$ — positive means an overall increase, negative means an overall decrease.

flashcards.front: You know the compound interest earned over $2$ years and the rate — how do you find the principal $P$?
flashcards.back: Interest $=P\left[(1+r/100)^2-1\right]$; rearrange to $P=\dfrac{\text{interest}}{(1+r/100)^2-1}$.

flashcards.front: Currency conversion direction
flashcards.back: Multiply to convert TOWARDS the bigger-number currency in the rate; divide to convert BACK.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Percentage profit (or loss) is calculated as a percentage of the SELLING price.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The selling price is often the more prominent, final number in a question (what the customer actually pays), so it feels like the natural base to compare against.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: For a bicycle bought for $\$240$ and sold for $\$312$, the learner computes $72\div312\times100=23.1\%$ instead of $72\div240\times100=30\%$.
misconceptions.correct_model: Percentage profit or loss is always $\dfrac{\text{profit (or loss)}}{\text{COST price}}\times100\%$ — the comparison must be with what was actually PAID, unless a question explicitly states otherwise.
misconceptions.remediation: Before dividing, label which of the two given prices is the cost price (what the trader paid) and underline it as the one that goes on the bottom of the fraction.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A percentage discount, followed by 'adding the same percentage back' (of the discounted price), returns an item to its original price.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Addition undoing a subtraction is a deeply familiar pattern from ordinary arithmetic, and it is easy to apply that pattern to percentages without checking that the two percentage changes act on DIFFERENT base amounts.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: After a $15\%$ discount, the learner 'checks' their sale price by adding $15\%$ of the SALE price back on, and is surprised when this does not reproduce the original price.
misconceptions.correct_model: A $p\%$ discount followed by adding $p\%$ of the NEW (smaller) price back on does NOT return to the original, because $p\%$ of a smaller amount is a smaller amount of money than $p\%$ of the original; the two percentages are measured against different bases.
misconceptions.remediation: To check a discount calculation, REVERSE it properly: divide the sale price by the discount's multiplier (e.g. $\div0.85$ for a $15\%$ discount) rather than adding a percentage of the sale price back on.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Compound interest can be found the same way as simple interest, by multiplying the principal by the rate and the number of years ($P\times R\%\times n$), just with a bigger final step.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The simple-interest formula is learned first and is a comfortable, linear pattern; recognising that compound interest needs a fundamentally different structure (a POWER, not a product) requires noticing that each year's interest is calculated on a different, growing amount.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: For \$4\,000 at $2.5\%$ compound interest for $3$ years, the learner computes $4000\times0.025\times3=\$300$ (the SIMPLE interest formula) and calls it the compound interest, instead of $4000\times1.025^3-4000=\$307.56$.
misconceptions.correct_model: Compound interest requires the multiplier to be applied REPEATEDLY (as a power): $\text{final amount}=P\times\left(1+\tfrac{r}{100}\right)^n$, and the interest is final amount minus $P$ — not $P\times r\%\times n$, which is the simple-interest formula.
misconceptions.remediation: Before calculating, ask 'is the interest added to the account before the NEXT year's interest is worked out?' — if yes, a power is needed, never a straight multiplication by the number of years.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: When a quantity changes by several different percentages in sequence, the overall change is found by ADDING the percentages together.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Adding several numbers given in a question is often the first operation that comes to mind, and it works correctly for quantities that change by a fixed AMOUNT each time — it is easy to apply the same instinct to percentages, which change by a fixed FRACTION of a moving base instead.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: For rates of $2\%$, $3.5\%$ and $4\%$ over three years, the learner computes an overall change of $2+3.5+4=9.5\%$ instead of the correct $9.79\%$ (from multiplying the three multipliers).
misconceptions.correct_model: Combine a sequence of percentage changes by converting EACH ONE to its own multiplier and MULTIPLYING all the multipliers together; the overall percentage change is then found from the combined multiplier, and it is always slightly more than the sum of the individual percentages (for a sequence of increases) because of the interest-on-interest effect.
misconceptions.remediation: Write out each multiplier separately before combining anything, multiply them in a single calculator expression, and only convert the final combined multiplier back to a percentage at the very end.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calculating percentage profit against the selling price instead of the cost price.
common_mistakes.why: The selling price is often the more prominent final number in a question.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Label the cost price explicitly before dividing, and always put it on the bottom of the fraction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Computing compound interest with the simple-interest formula ($P\times R\%\times n$).
common_mistakes.why: The simple-interest pattern is learned first and is a comfortable, linear shortcut.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask whether interest is added to the account before the next year's interest is calculated; if so, use the power $(1+r/100)^n$, never a straight multiplication by the number of years.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding or subtracting percentages directly when several changes happen in sequence.
common_mistakes.why: Addition of given numbers is often the first instinct, and it happens to work for changes by a fixed AMOUNT, not a fixed PERCENTAGE.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always convert each change to its own multiplier first and multiply the multipliers together.

exam_notes: The formulas for simple and compound interest are NOT given in the exam, unlike density or pressure; they must be known and rebuilt from the multiplier idea.
If a question says 'calculate the compound interest', give the INTEREST (final amount minus principal), not the final amount — read the command word carefully.
Compound interest for more than $2$ or $3$ years needs a calculator; keep the full, unrounded value through the working and round only the final answer, usually to $2$ decimal places for money.
Always show the multiplier and the power explicitly (e.g. '$1.025^3$') as a separate line of working: this is where the method mark sits, even if the final arithmetic then goes wrong.
For a repeated-percentage-change question with different rates, write out each year's multiplier separately before combining them — a marker can award method marks for this step alone.

summary.big_idea: Nearly every money calculation is the multiplier method from percentages applied once (currency, wages, a single discount) or repeatedly (compound interest, repeated percentage change) — and 'repeatedly' always means multiplying several multipliers together, never adding or subtracting the percentages themselves.
key_points: Currency conversion: multiply towards the bigger-number currency, divide to come back; net pay $=$ gross pay $-$ deductions; percentage profit/loss is always measured against the COST price.
Simple interest ($P\times R/100\times T$) adds the SAME amount every year; neither interest formula is given in the exam.
Compound interest ($P(1+r/100)^n$) is the multiplier applied REPEATEDLY as a power; it equals simple interest after exactly $1$ year, then grows faster from year $2$ onward.
A sequence of percentage changes, even at different rates or in different directions, is combined by MULTIPLYING the individual multipliers, never by adding or subtracting the percentages.
Extended: for a given overall multiplier spread over $n$ equal periods, the per-period rate is found by taking the $n$th root of the multiplier.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Compound growth is the ordinary percentage multiplier applied once per period, so combine several periods by MULTIPLYING their multipliers together — never by adding or subtracting the percentages, and never by using the simple-interest formula when the interest itself is reinvested.

13_Exponential_Growth_and_Decay.json.title: Exponential Growth and Decay
13_Exponential_Growth_and_Decay.json.subject: Mathematics
13_Exponential_Growth_and_Decay.json.course_label: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 · Number · Extended only

objectives.statement: Write the multiplier for a percentage increase or decrease, or for doubling, halving or tripling, and use the model $\text{value}=a\times b^{n}$ to predict a value after $n$ periods.
Model and calculate exponential growth in context (population, bacteria, prices), interpreting the result sensibly for the quantity involved.
Model and calculate exponential decay and depreciation in context, and explain why a quantity decaying by a constant percentage never reaches exactly zero.
Find an unknown constant percentage rate from two given values, or an unknown number of periods by trial and improvement, and explain how exponential change differs from linear change.

prerequisites.statement: Convert a percentage increase or decrease into a decimal multiplier (from the Percentages lesson).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The multiplier $b$ is the single building block of every calculation in this lesson; without it there is no way to even start the model $a\times b^n$.

prerequisites.statement: Use the compound-interest model $P\times(1+r/100)^n$ (from the Money, Simple and Compound Interest lesson).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Exponential growth and decay are the SAME model as compound interest, written with a general starting value $a$ and multiplier $b$ instead of a principal and a rate; recognising this means almost nothing new has to be learned, only generalised.

prerequisites.statement: Evaluate a power and an $n$th root on a calculator (e.g. $1.03^{10}$ and $\sqrt[3]{0.614125}$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Predicting a future value needs a power; finding an unknown rate needs the matching root — without fluent calculator use for both, neither direction of this lesson's work is possible.

prerequisites.statement: Build and read a simple table of values from a rule (e.g. substitute $n=1,2,3,\ldots$ into an expression).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding an unknown number of periods by trial and improvement means generating successive values in a table and reading off where the target is crossed; without this skill, the search has no organised method.

diagnostic_items.question: What multiplier corresponds to a $6\%$ fall per year?

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Confuses the percentage figure itself (as a decimal) with the full multiplier, which must still include the starting $100\%$.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Confirms the multiplier skill from Percentages is solid before it is reused, unquestioned, inside a power.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Rebuild the multiplier as '$100\%$ minus the fall': $100\%-6\%=94\%=0.94$.

diagnostic_items.question: Why can a quantity that decays by $10\%$ every year never reach exactly zero?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Each year the value is multiplied by $0.9$, and a positive number multiplied by $0.9$ is still positive; it only ever gets smaller, approaching zero without ever landing on it.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It eventually becomes so small that it rounds to zero, so effectively it does reach zero.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Confuses a practical rounding convenience with the exact mathematical behaviour of the model, which never produces zero at any finite $n$.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks the conceptual understanding that repeated multiplication by a positive number less than $1$ shrinks a quantity indefinitely without ever reaching zero — the key distinguishing feature from linear decay.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Compute several terms of $100\times0.9^n$ for increasing $n$ and observe that every single term, however small, is still strictly positive.

diagnostic_items.question: A population is $P$ now and doubles every $5$ years. How many periods are there in $20$ years, and what is the population then?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $20\div5=4$ periods, so the population is $P\times2^4=16P$.

common_wrong_answers.answer: $20$ periods, since the question gives $20$ years.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Uses the number of YEARS directly as the number of periods, instead of first dividing by the length of one period (here, $5$ years).

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Rehearses the single most common source of a hugely wrong answer in this lesson: forgetting to convert the given time into the correct number of PERIODS before applying the power.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Always write 'one period $=\ldots$' explicitly first, then divide the total time given by that period length before raising the multiplier to a power.

diagnostic_items.question: Is a fall of $20\%$ each year for $3$ years the same as a single fall of $60\%$? Explain.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No. $0.8^3=0.512$, so the value falls to $51.2\%$ of the original, a fall of $48.8\%$ — not $60\%$. Each $20\%$ is taken of a smaller amount than the one before, so the falls do not simply add.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, because $20\%\times3=60\%$.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Treats exponential (repeated percentage) decay as if it were linear, adding the percentages instead of multiplying the multipliers.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This is the single most important diagnostic in the lesson: it directly previews the lesson's central caveat, that exponential change is never found by adding or multiplying the raw percentage by the number of periods.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Compute the combined multiplier $0.8\times0.8\times0.8=0.8^3=0.512$ explicitly, step by step, and compare it with the (wrong) shortcut $1-3\times0.2=0.4$.

theory_blocks.title: Linear adds, exponential multiplies
theory_blocks.body: [[blue:**Linear**]] change adds the same *amount* each step. [[orange:**Exponential**]] change multiplies by the same *factor* each step. Because each step multiplies the PREVIOUS result, exponential growth speeds up as the quantity gets bigger, and exponential decay slows down as the quantity gets smaller — without ever reaching zero.

theory_blocks.title: The exponential model
theory_blocks.body:
If a quantity starts at $a$ and is multiplied by the same number $b$ in every time period, then after $n$ periods
$$\text{value}=a\times b^{\,n}.$$
$b$ is the **multiplier** (growth or decay factor). For a percentage change of $r\%$:
$$b=1+\frac{r}{100}\ \text{(growth, }b>1\text{)},\qquad b=1-\frac{r}{100}\ \text{(decay, }0<b<1\text{)}.$$
Doubling has $b=2$, tripling $b=3$, halving $b=0.5$.

| Change per period | Multiplier $b$ | Type |
|---|---|---|
| $+8\%$ | $1.08$ | growth |
| $+2.5\%$ | $1.025$ | growth |
| $-15\%$ | $0.85$ | decay |
| $-0.5\%$ | $0.995$ | decay |
| doubles | $2$ | growth |
| halves | $0.5$ | decay |

theory_blocks.title: This is the compound interest formula, generalised
theory_blocks.body: $a\times b^n$ is exactly the compound-interest formula from the previous lesson, $P\times(1+r/100)^n$, with $a$ in place of $P$ and $b$ in place of $1+r/100$ — interest is just ONE context of exponential growth, alongside population, bacteria and depreciation. $n$ counts **periods**, not necessarily years: if a quantity changes every $20$ minutes, one period is $20$ minutes, not one year or one minute.

theory_blocks.title: Find the length of a period before anything else
theory_blocks.body: Always identify the length of one *period* first, and convert the TOTAL time given in the question into a number of periods by dividing. Working in minutes when the multiplier applies per $20$ minutes is the most common cause of a huge, wrong answer. The starting value $a$ is the value when $n=0$: the point where the graph would meet the vertical axis.

theory_blocks.title: Depreciation and exponential decay
theory_blocks.body: **Depreciation** is the fall in the value of an object (such as a car or machine) over time. If the value falls by $r\%$ per period, the multiplier is $1-r/100$. The value is multiplied by a number smaller than $1$ each period, so it gets smaller every period but never becomes exactly zero.

theory_blocks.title: Decay is not a straight line to zero
theory_blocks.body: A car bought for $\$18\,500$ that loses $15\%$ of its value each year [[red:does NOT lose the same number of dollars each year]]: it loses $\$2\,775$ in year $1$ but only $\$1\,449$ in year $5$, because each $15\%$ is taken of a smaller base. If a quantity lost the same *amount* each year it would follow a straight line (linear change) and would eventually reach exactly zero; a constant *percentage* loss never does.

assets.caption: A car worth $\$18\,500$ losing $15\%$ of its value each year (red curve), compared with losing the same $\$2\,775$ every year (dashed straight line). The straight line reaches $\$0$ after $6\tfrac23$ years, while the curve goes on falling and is still worth $\$3\,642$ after $10$ years.
assets.purpose: Show that a constant percentage loss gives a curve that never reaches zero, unlike a constant money loss.

theory_blocks.title: Finding the rate or the time
theory_blocks.body:
**Finding the rate.** Divide the final value by the starting value to get $b^n$, then take the $n$th root (or recognise a familiar power). Convert $b$ into a percentage: growth rate $=(b-1)\times100\%$.

**Finding the time.** At Extended level this is done by **trial and improvement**: compute the value for successive whole numbers of periods until the target is passed. Record each value so you can show the two values either side of the target.

theory_blocks.title: Three slips that wreck an exponential calculation
theory_blocks.body: Multiplying by $r$ instead of $1\pm r/100$: a $3\%$ increase is $\times1.03$, not $\times3$ or $\times0.03$. Using '$n\times$ percentage' as if change were linear: a fall of $15\%$ a year for $4$ years is NOT a fall of $60\%$ — the actual overall fall is $1-0.85^4=47.8\%$. Rounding the multiplier or an intermediate value: rounding $1.03^{10}$ to $1.34$ before multiplying by $24\,000$ gives $32\,160$, not the correct $32\,254$.

theory_blocks.title: Sanity-check the direction of change
theory_blocks.body: Use the direction of change as a sanity check: for growth the answer must be *bigger* than the start, and for decay *smaller* but still positive. Also check by working one or two steps by hand: $24\,000\times1.03=24\,720$ should be a plausible first step towards the final answer $32\,254$.

theory_blocks.title: Comparing exponential and linear change
theory_blocks.body:
| Year | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Linear: add \$100 a year | 500 | 700 | 900 | 1100 | 1300 |
| Exponential: $\times1.2$ a year | 500 | 720 | 1037 | 1493 | 2150 |

Both plans add $\$100$ in the first year (from $500$ to $600$). After that, the exponential quantity adds $\$120$, then $\$144$, then $\$173$, and so on, while the linear quantity keeps adding only $\$100$ every year. The gap widens every year — this is why compound interest and population growth become dramatic over long periods, even when the starting rate looks modest.

assets.caption: The two plans in the table drawn on the same axes. Adding $\$100$ a year gives a straight line; multiplying by $1.2$ a year gives a curve that climbs more and more steeply. Both are at $\$600$ after one year, but after $8$ years the line is at $\$1\,300$ and the curve at about $\$2\,150$.
assets.purpose: Show the widening gap between linear and exponential growth as a graph.

theory_blocks.title: The graph of an exponential model
theory_blocks.body:
Plotting $\text{value}=a\times b^{\,n}$ against $n$ always gives a **curve**, never a straight line.

- It meets the vertical axis at the starting value $a$, the value when $n=0$.
- For **growth** ($b>1$) the curve rises, and rises ever more steeply: equal steps along the $n$-axis give bigger and bigger jumps.
- For **decay** ($0<b<1$) the curve falls steeply at first and then flattens out, getting closer and closer to the horizontal axis without ever touching it.

To draw one, make a table of values for whole-number $n$, plot the points and join them with a [[green:smooth curve]] — never with a ruler. To read from one, go up from the $n$-axis to the curve and across to the value axis; to answer 'after how long?', go across from the value and down. Read to within half a small square.

keywords.definition: The rule $\text{value}=a\times b^n$, where a quantity starting at $a$ is multiplied by the same factor $b$ every period.
The number $b$ by which a quantity is multiplied every period; also called the growth or decay factor.
Repeated multiplication by a factor greater than $1$, so the quantity increases and the increase itself grows larger each period.
Repeated multiplication by a factor between $0$ and $1$, so the quantity decreases, approaching but never reaching zero.
The fall in the value of an object, such as a car or machine, over time, often modelled as exponential decay.
The fixed length of time (or number of events) after which a quantity is multiplied by the multiplier once.
Computing successive values of an exponential expression for whole numbers of periods to find when a target value is first crossed.
Change by the same fixed amount every period, as opposed to exponential change, which is by the same fixed factor.

worked_examples.statement: Population growth. The population of a town is $24\,000$ and grows by $3\%$ each year. Estimate the population after $10$ years.
reasoning: Growth of $3\%$ per year gives multiplier $b=1.03$.
Apply the model value $=a\times b^n$ with $a=24\,000$, $n=10$.
worked_examples.solution: $24\,000\times1.03^{10}=32\,253.99\ldots\approx32\,300$ (3 s.f.). Population is a count of people, so a rounded value makes sense, and the question says 'estimate' because real populations do not follow the model exactly.
worked_examples.interpretation: The exponential model gives a mathematical prediction; the word 'estimate' in the question is a signal to round sensibly for the quantity being counted, since the model is only an approximation of real population behaviour.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Rounding the multiplier to $1.3$ or the power to a rounded intermediate value before multiplying, which changes the answer noticeably.

worked_examples.statement: Bacteria. A culture starts with $500$ bacteria. The number doubles every $20$ minutes. How many are there after $3$ hours?
reasoning: Convert the total time into the SAME units as one period: $3$ hours $=180$ minutes.
Find the number of periods: $180\div20=9$.
Apply the model with $b=2$, $n=9$.
worked_examples.interpretation: The period is $20$ minutes, not $1$ hour or $1$ minute, so the FIRST and most important step is converting the given time into the correct number of periods before any power is applied.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using $n=3$ (treating each HOUR as one period) instead of $n=9$ (the correct number of $20$-minute periods), which would give a far smaller, wrong answer.

worked_examples.statement: Depreciation. A car costs $\$18\,500$ and loses $15\%$ of its value each year. (a) Find its value after $4$ years. (b) After how many whole years is it first worth less than $\$8\,000$?
reasoning: (a) The multiplier is $1-0.15=0.85$; apply the model directly with $n=4$.
(b) Trial and improvement: build a table of the value for successive whole years, keeping full calculator values, until the target is passed.
worked_examples.interpretation: A direct power answers 'what is the value after a GIVEN number of years'; a question asking 'after how many years' instead needs the reverse search, trial and improvement, since there is no simple algebraic way to isolate $n$ at this level.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Stopping at the first year where the value LOOKS close to $\$8\,000$ (year $5$, at $\$8\,208.55$) without checking that it is still ABOVE the target, instead of continuing to the next whole year.

worked_examples.statement: Finding the rate. The value of a machine falls from $\$12\,000$ to $\$9\,720$ in $2$ years, decreasing by the same percentage each year. Find the annual percentage decrease.
reasoning: Let the yearly multiplier be $b$. Write the equation $12\,000\times b^2=9\,720$.
Divide to isolate $b^2$, then take the square root to find $b$.
Convert $b$ into a percentage decrease.
worked_examples.solution: $b^2=\dfrac{9720}{12000}=0.81$, so $b=\sqrt{0.81}=0.9$. The multiplier $0.9$ means a decrease of $10\%$ per year.
worked_examples.interpretation: Finding an unknown RATE reverses the usual direction of the model: instead of substituting $b$ and finding the value, the two values are used to find $b$ itself, via division then a root.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Taking $9720\div12000=0.81$ and reading this directly as the annual multiplier, forgetting that $0.81$ is the multiplier applied TWICE (squared), so a square root is still needed.

worked_examples.statement: Finding the time. A colony of $800$ fungi grows by $25\%$ each day. After how many days does it first exceed $5\,000$?
reasoning: The multiplier is $1.25$.
Compute $800\times1.25^n$ for successive whole values of $n$ until the value exceeds $5\,000$.
worked_examples.solution: After $8$ days: $800\times1.25^8=4\,768.4\ldots<5\,000$. After $9$ days: $800\times1.25^9=5\,960.5\ldots>5\,000$. The colony first exceeds $5\,000$ after $\mathbf{9\ days}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: As with the depreciation example, 'after how many days' at Extended level is answered by trial and improvement, showing the value on BOTH sides of the target so the examiner can see the crossing point was located correctly.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Solving $800\times1.25^n=5000$ by attempting algebra beyond the syllabus (e.g. logarithms) instead of the expected trial-and-improvement method.

worked_examples.statement: Comparing the two kinds of change. Plan A starts at $\$500$ and adds $\$100$ every year. Plan B starts at $\$500$ and multiplies by $1.2$ every year. Show that both plans give the same value after year $1$, but that Plan B overtakes Plan A's rate of growth from year $2$ onward, and find the amount EACH plan adds in year $4$ alone.
reasoning: Compute each plan's value at $n=0,1$ to confirm they agree after year $1$.
Compute each plan's value at $n=3$ and $n=4$ and subtract to find the amount added in year $4$ alone, for each plan.
worked_examples.solution: At $n=0$: both are $\$500$. At $n=1$: Plan A is $500+100=\$600$; Plan B is $500\times1.2=\$600$ — equal. At $n=3$: Plan A $=\$800$, Plan B $=500\times1.2^3=\$864$. At $n=4$: Plan A $=\$900$, Plan B $=500\times1.2^4=\$1\,036.80$. Plan A always adds exactly $\$100$ in year $4$ ($900-800$); Plan B adds $1036.80-864=\$172.80$ in year $4$ alone — far more than its very first year's addition of only $\$100$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Both plans look identical for exactly one year, which is precisely why relying on only the first year's data can hide a huge later difference between linear and exponential growth.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming that because the two plans agree after year $1$, they will continue to grow by similar amounts in later years as well.

guided_exercises.statement: A savings scheme starts with $\$1\,200$ and grows by $4.5\%$ each year. Find the value after $6$ years, to the nearest dollar.
hints: Write the multiplier for a $4.5\%$ growth first, as a decimal.
Apply the model value $=a\times b^n$ with $a=1200$, $n=6$, keeping the full calculator value until the last step.
common_errors: Using the multiplier $0.045$ or $4.5$ instead of $1.045$.

guided_exercises.statement: A forklift truck is bought for $\$22\,000$ and loses $18\%$ of its value each year. After how many whole years is it first worth less than $\$10\,000$?
hints: Find the multiplier for an $18\%$ fall, and build a table of the value for $n=1,2,3,\ldots$ until the value passes below the target.
Keep the full calculator value at every row of the table, and show the two years either side of the crossing point.
common_errors: Stopping the search as soon as a value looks 'close' to the target, instead of checking it is actually on the correct side of it.

guided_exercises.statement: A sum of $\$8\,000$ grows at $r\%$ per year, compounded annually, and is worth $\$9\,261$ after $3$ years. Find $r$.
hints: Write the equation $8000\times b^3=9261$ and isolate $b^3$ first.
Take the CUBE root of $b^3$ to find $b$, since the growth happened over $3$ periods.
common_errors: Taking a square root instead of a cube root, forgetting that the growth happened over $3$ periods, not $2$.

exercises.statement: Write the multiplier for (a) an $8\%$ increase; (b) a $20\%$ decrease; (c) a $2.5\%$ increase; (d) a $0.5\%$ decrease.
common_errors: Writing $0.08$, $0.2$, $0.025$ or $0.005$ (the raw decimal of the percentage) instead of including the starting $1$.

exercises.statement: The population of a village is $15\,000$ and increases by $4\%$ each year. Find the population after $5$ years, to the nearest whole number.
common_errors: Rounding $1.04^5$ before multiplying by $15\,000$, giving a slightly inaccurate final value.

exercises.statement: A machine bought for $\$25\,000$ loses $12\%$ of its value each year. Find its value after $3$ years.
common_errors: Using the multiplier $0.12$ instead of $0.88$.

exercises.statement: A culture contains $200$ bacteria and the number doubles every hour. Write an expression for the number after $t$ hours, and find the number after $8$ hours.
common_errors: Forgetting to write the general expression first and jumping straight to a single numeric answer without showing the model.

exercises.statement: A population of $60$ rabbits trebles every year. Find the population after $4$ years.
exercises.full_solution: Multiplier $=3$. $60\times3^4=4\,860$.
common_errors: Multiplying $60\times4\times3$ (treating it as linear growth by a factor of $3$ each year) instead of raising $3$ to the power $4$.

exercises.statement: A house valued at $\$240\,000$ increases in value by $3.5\%$ per year. Find its value after $6$ years to the nearest $\$100$, and the overall percentage increase to $3$ significant figures.
exercises.full_solution: $240\,000\times1.035^6=295\,021.28\ldots\approx\$295\,000$ (nearest \$100). Overall multiplier $=1.035^6=1.22926\ldots$, an increase of $22.9\%$ (3 s.f.).
common_errors: Giving the overall percentage increase as $6\times3.5\%=21\%$ instead of correctly compounding.

exercises.statement: A car bought for $\$16\,000$ is worth $\$9\,826$ after $3$ years. Assuming it loses the same percentage each year, find the annual percentage depreciation.
exercises.full_solution: $9826\div16000=0.614125=0.85^3$, so the multiplier is $0.85$: a depreciation of $15\%$ per year.
common_errors: Dividing $9826\div16000$ and treating the result ($0.614125$) directly as the annual multiplier, forgetting to take the cube root since $3$ years have passed.

exercises.statement: A sum of $\$5\,000$ grows at $r\%$ per year and is worth $\$6\,655$ after $3$ years. Find $r$.
common_errors: Dividing $1.331$ by $3$ and multiplying by $100$ to get $44.4$ as the rate (treating the model as if it were linear, rather than taking a cube root).

exercises.statement: The population of a town of $30\,000$ falls by $6\%$ each year. After how many whole years will it first be below $20\,000$?
common_errors: Checking only one year and assuming it is correct, instead of confirming the value at the YEAR BEFORE it is still above the target.

exercises.statement: A sample of $640$ g of a substance halves in mass every $3$ days. (a) Find the mass after $15$ days. (b) Using $\text{mass}=640\times0.5^{t/3}$, find the mass after $7$ days, to $3$ significant figures.
common_errors: In (b), using $t=7$ directly as the exponent instead of $t/3$, which gives a far smaller, wrong mass.

exercises.statement: Plan A adds $\$50$ each year to $\$500$. Plan B increases $\$500$ by $8\%$ each year. After how many whole years is Plan B first worth more than Plan A?
exercises.full_solution: Year 6: Plan A $=\$800$, Plan B $=500\times1.08^6=\$793.44$ (B still behind). Year 7: Plan A $=\$850$, Plan B $=500\times1.08^7=\$856.91$ (B now ahead). So Plan B is first worth more after $7$ years.
common_errors: Comparing only the RATES (an $8\%$ increase 'sounds' bigger than a fixed $\$50$) instead of calculating and comparing actual values year by year.

exercises.statement: The value of a car falls by $20\%$ each year. Show that after $3$ years it has lost $48.8\%$ of its original value.
exercises.full_solution: $0.8^3=0.512$, so the value is $51.2\%$ of the original, a loss of $100\%-51.2\%=48.8\%$ (not $3\times20\%=60\%$).
common_errors: Giving $60\%$ (adding the three $20\%$ falls directly) instead of compounding them correctly.

exercises.statement:
The graph shows the value $V$ dollars of a car, $n$ years after it was bought.
(a) Write down the value of the car when it was new.
(b) Use the graph to estimate the value of the car after $5$ years.
(c) Use the graph to estimate how many years it takes for the value to fall to half of its value when new.
(d) The value falls by the same percentage each year. Use the values at $n=0$ and $n=1$ to find this percentage.
exercises.full_solution: (a) The curve meets the vertical axis at $V=8\,000$, so the car cost $\$8\,000$. (b) Going up from $n=5$ to the curve and across gives $V\approx2\,600$ (the model gives $8\,000\times0.8^{5}=\$2\,621.44$). (c) Half of $\$8\,000$ is $\$4\,000$; going across from $V=4\,000$ to the curve and down gives $n\approx3.1$, so a little over $3$ years. (d) At $n=0$, $V=8\,000$ and at $n=1$, $V=6\,400$, so the multiplier is $6\,400\div8\,000=0.8$ and the value falls by $20\%$ each year.
common_errors: Reading the first year's fall as $\$1\,600$ and then assuming the car loses $\$1\,600$ EVERY year, which would make it worthless after $5$ years; the loss is a constant percentage, not a constant amount.
In (c), reading the half-value time as exactly $3$ years without checking that the curve is still just above $\$4\,000$ there.

exam_questions.statement:
A van is bought for $\$28\,000$. It depreciates by $22\%$ each year.
(a) Find its value after $3$ years, correct to the nearest dollar. [2]
(b) Find, by trial and improvement, the first whole year in which the van's value falls below half of its original price. Show the values in the two years either side of this point. [4]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $28\,000\times0.78^3=13\,287.45\ldots\approx\$13\,287$. (b) Half the original price is $\$14\,000$. $n=2$: $28\,000\times0.78^2=17\,035.2>14\,000$. $n=3$: $28\,000\times0.78^3=13\,287.45\ldots<14\,000$. So the value first falls below half the original price in year $3$.
mark_scheme: (b) B1 for identifying the target value $\$14\,000$; M1 for computing the value at $n=2$; M1 for computing the value at $n=3$; A1 for correctly identifying year $3$ with both surrounding values shown
common_errors: In (b), checking only year 3 without also showing year 2 is still above the target, losing the method mark for a full trial-and-improvement argument.

exam_questions.statement:
The number of members of an online club grows from $4\,000$ to $6\,912$ over $4$ years, by the same percentage each year.
(a) Find the annual percentage growth rate. [3]
(b) Use your rate to predict the number of members after a further $2$ years (that is, $6$ years from the start). [2]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $b^4=6912\div4000=1.728$, so $b=\sqrt[4]{1.728}=1.14653\ldots$, a growth rate of $14.653\ldots\%\approx14.7\%$ (3 s.f.). (b) $4000\times1.14653\ldots^6=9\,086.06\ldots\approx9\,086$ members (or, equivalently, $6912\times1.14653\ldots^2$).
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for $6912\div4000$ $(=1.728)$; M1 for taking the correct $4$th root; A1 for $14.7\%$ (accept $14.65\%$ or better)
(b) M1 for applying the multiplier correctly for a further $2$ periods from either the start or from year $4$; A1 for a value consistent with the rate found in (a)
common_errors: In (a), taking the square root instead of the 4th root, forgetting that the growth happened over 4 periods.

exam_questions.statement:
A quantity decays by $25\%$ each year.
(a) Explain, without doing any further calculation, why it can never reach exactly zero. [1]
(b) Show that after $5$ years it has lost more than $75\%$ of its original value, but after $4$ years it has not yet lost $75\%$. [3]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Each year the value is multiplied by $0.75$, a positive number, and a positive number multiplied by a positive number stays positive, however small. (b) $0.75^4=0.3164\ldots$ (a loss of $68.4\%$, not yet $75\%$); $0.75^5=0.2373\ldots$ (a loss of $76.3\%$, more than $75\%$).
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) The multiplier $0.75$ is positive, so repeated multiplication by it can only ever shrink a positive value towards zero, never reach or cross it. (b) $0.75^4=0.31640625$, a loss of $68.359\ldots\%<75\%$. $0.75^5=0.2373046875$, a loss of $76.26\ldots\%>75\%$. So the $75\%$ loss threshold is crossed between year $4$ and year $5$.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for a correct explanation referencing repeated multiplication by a positive multiplier
(b) M1 for computing $0.75^4$ and comparing with $25\%$ remaining; M1 for computing $0.75^5$ and comparing; A1 for both correct conclusions stated clearly
common_errors: Comparing the multiplier values ($0.75^4$ and $0.75^5$) directly with $75\%$ instead of converting them correctly into a percentage LOSS first.

challenge_questions.statement: Show that a quantity growing at $6\%$ per year takes $12$ years to double (the first whole year after which the value is more than double), and explain why it has not yet doubled after $11$ years.
challenge_questions.answer: $12$ years; after $11$ years the value is only $1.898$ times the start.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $1.06^{11}=1.898\ldots<2$ and $1.06^{12}=2.012\ldots>2$, so $12$ years. After $11$ years the value is only $1.898$ times the start, not yet double.
common_errors: Using the 'rule of 70' or a similar estimate instead of directly testing successive whole years as the question requires.

challenge_questions.statement: City A has $2.0$ million people and grows by $2\%$ per year. City B has $2.6$ million people and its population falls by $1\%$ per year. After how many whole years will A first have a larger population than B? Show the values at the crucial years.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $A=2.0\times1.02^n$, $B=2.6\times0.99^n$ (millions). At $n=8$: $A=2.343$, $B=2.399$ ($A$ still behind). At $n=9$: $A=2.390$, $B=2.375$ ($A$ now ahead). So A first has a larger population after $9$ years.
common_errors: Assuming City A overtakes as soon as its growth 'feels' faster, without checking the actual crossover year by substitution.

challenge_questions.statement: A value falls by $10\%$ each year. After how many whole years will it first be less than $1\%$ of its original value?
common_errors: Underestimating how many periods are needed, because a $10\%$ fall sounds fast but shrinks a quantity only slowly once the base itself has become small.

challenge_questions.statement: A car loses $20\%$ of its value in the first year and $15\%$ of its value in each later year. Its value after $4$ years is $\$14\,739$. Find its original price.
common_errors: Applying the SAME $15\%$ rate to all $4$ years (ignoring that the first year uses a different, $20\%$ rate), which gives the wrong combined multiplier.

challenge_questions.statement: A price falls by $20\%$ each year for $5$ years and then rises by $20\%$ each year for the next $5$ years. Show that it does not return to its original value, and find the overall percentage change to $3$ significant figures.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Combined multiplier $=0.8^5\times1.2^5=0.96^5=0.81537\ldots$, which is not $1$. The overall change is a decrease of $18.5\%$ (3 s.f.).
common_errors: Assuming a fall followed by an equal-sized, equal-length rise must cancel out exactly and return to the original value.

mcq.stem: What multiplier corresponds to a $7\%$ decrease per year?

options.why_wrong: This uses the raw percentage as a decimal directly, rather than building the full multiplier $1-0.07$.
This is the multiplier for a $7\%$ INCREASE, not a decrease — the sign of the change has been reversed.
This gives the change itself as a negative decimal, but a multiplier must still include the original $100\%$, i.e. the full value $1-0.07=0.93$.

mcq.stem: A quantity of $400$ grows by $5\%$ each year for $3$ years. Which calculation correctly finds the value after $3$ years?

options.why_wrong: This applies a single multiplier of $1.15$, as if $5\%\times3=15\%$ could simply be added all at once, instead of compounding the $5\%$ three separate times.
This is the SIMPLE-interest-style pattern (a fixed amount added every year), treating exponential change as if it were linear.
This raises the raw rate $0.05$ (instead of the multiplier $1.05$) to the power $3$, which shrinks the value dramatically instead of growing it.

mcq.explanation: The multiplier is $1.05$, applied as a power for $3$ periods: $400\times1.05^3$.

mcq.stem: A quantity falls by $10\%$ each year for $5$ years. The overall percentage fall is:

options.why_wrong: This adds the five $10\%$ falls directly ($5\times10\%$), treating the change as linear rather than compounding.
This reuses the per-year rate as if it were the overall rate, ignoring that the fall happened over $5$ separate years.
$59.0\%$ is the fraction that REMAINS ($0.9^5=0.59049$), not the fall; the fall is $100\%-59.0\%=41.0\%$.

mcq.explanation: $0.9^5=0.59049$, so $59.0\%$ of the original REMAINS, meaning the overall fall is $100\%-59.0\%=41.0\%$ (3 s.f.) — noticeably less than the linear guess of $50\%$.

mcq.stem: A value grows from $\$7\,000$ to $\$9\,317.50$ over $3$ years, by the same percentage each year. The annual growth rate is closest to:

options.why_wrong: This reports the TOTAL increase over $3$ years ($\approx33.1\%$) as if it were the annual rate, instead of finding the per-year multiplier with a cube root.
This divides the total percentage increase by $3$ ($33.1\div3$), treating the growth as linear instead of compounding.
This divides the overall multiplier $1.331$ by $3$ (giving $0.444$) rather than taking its cube root.

mcq.explanation: $9317.50\div7000\approx1.331=1.1^3$, so the multiplier is about $1.1$, an annual growth rate of about $10\%$.

mcq.stem: To find $24\,000\times1.03^{10}$ accurately, which approach is correct?

options.text: Enter the whole expression into the calculator in one go, or keep every digit the calculator gives for $1.03^{10}$, and round only the FINAL answer
Round $1.03^{10}$ to $1.34$ first, then multiply by $24\,000$
options.why_wrong: Rounding the multiplier before the final multiplication introduces a noticeable error once it has been raised to a high power; it gives $32\,160$ instead of the correct $32\,254$.

options.text: Work out $24\,000\times1.03=24\,720$ first, then multiply THAT by $1.03^{10}$
options.why_wrong: This changes the structure of the calculation entirely (it multiplies in one year's growth twice over), rather than correctly raising the multiplier itself to the power $10$.

options.text: Any rounding is fine as long as it happens somewhere before the final answer
options.why_wrong: Rounding part-way through an exponential calculation is a genuine source of noticeable final-answer error, precisely because the rounded value gets raised to a further power or multiplied again.

mcq.explanation: Full, unrounded values must be kept until the very last step; rounding the multiplier or any intermediate result before completing the calculation changes the final answer measurably once powers are involved.

mcq.stem: A laptop depreciates by a constant $20\%$ each year. Which statement is TRUE?

options.text: It loses the same number of dollars every year, and eventually its value reaches exactly $\$0$
