exercises.statement: The highest temperature ever recorded was $58\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ (in Libya). The lowest temperature ever recorded was $-88\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ (in Antarctica). What is the temperature difference?
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A business bank account shows a balance of \$105. State the balance after each of the following transactions is applied in turn, saying whether it is positive or negative: (a) a rent payment of \$140 (b) a car insurance payment of \$283 (c) a salary payment of \$230 (d) a food bill payment of \$72 (e) a transfer into the account of \$250.
exercises.full_solution: Start at \$105 and apply each transaction in turn. (a) $105-140=-35$ (negative). (b) $-35-283=-318$ (negative). (c) $-318+230=-88$ (negative). (d) $-88-72=-160$ (negative). (e) $-160+250=90$ (positive).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The roof of a building is 130 m above ground level. An underground car park beneath the building has a floor 35 m below ground level. Calculate the vertical distance between the roof and the floor of the car park.
exercises.full_solution: Distance $=130+35=165$ m, since the roof is above ground level and the car-park floor is below it, so the two distances add.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A submarine is at a depth of 165 m below sea level. The sea floor at that point is 860 m below sea level. Calculate the distance between the submarine and the sea floor.
exercises.full_solution: Distance $=860-165=695$ m, found by subtracting the submarine's depth from the total depth of the sea floor.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Round the following numbers to the nearest 1000: (a) 68786 (b) 74245 (c) 89000 (d) 4020 (e) 99500 (f) 999999
exercises.full_solution: To round to the nearest 1000, look at the hundreds digit: 5 or more rounds up, less than 5 rounds down. (a) 68786 → 69000. (b) 74245 → 74000. (c) 89000 is already a multiple of 1000 → 89000. (d) 4020 → 4000. (e) 99500 → 100000 (hundreds digit is 5, rounds up). (f) 999999 → 1000000.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Round the following numbers to the nearest 100: (a) 78540 (b) 6858 (c) 14099 (d) 8084 (e) 950 (f) 2984
exercises.full_solution: Look at the tens digit to decide whether to round up or down. (a) 78540 → 78500. (b) 6858 → 6900. (c) 14099 → 14100. (d) 8084 → 8100. (e) 950 → 1000 (tens digit 5 rounds up). (f) 2984 → 3000.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Round the following numbers to the nearest 10: (a) 485 (b) 692 (c) 8847 (d) 83 (e) 4 (f) 997
exercises.full_solution: Look at the units digit to decide whether to round up or down. (a) 485 → 490 (units digit 5 rounds up). (b) 692 → 690. (c) 8847 → 8850. (d) 83 → 80. (e) 4 → 0 (rounds down since 4 < 5). (f) 997 → 1000.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.full_solution: Look at the second decimal digit to decide whether the first decimal digit rounds up: (a) 5.58→5.6 (b) 0.73→0.7 (c) 11.86→11.9 (d) 157.39→157.4 (e) 4.04→4.0 (f) 15.045→15.0 (second digit 4 rounds down) (g) 2.95→3.0 (second digit 5 rounds up, carrying) (h) 0.98→1.0 (carries) (i) 12.049→12.0.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.full_solution: Look at the third decimal digit to decide whether the second decimal digit rounds up: (a) 6.473→6.47 (b) 9.587→9.59 (c) 16.476→16.48 (d) 0.088→0.09 (e) 0.014→0.01 (f) 9.3048→9.30 (g) 99.996→100.00 (carries through) (h) 0.0048→0.00 (i) 3.0037→3.00.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the following to the number of significant figures (s.f.) shown in brackets: (a) 48599 (1 s.f.) (b) 48599 (3 s.f.) (c) 6841 (1 s.f.) (d) 7538 (2 s.f.) (e) 483.7 (1 s.f.) (f) 2.5728 (3 s.f.) (g) 990 (1 s.f.) (h) 2045 (2 s.f.) (i) 14.952 (3 s.f.)
exercises.full_solution: Keep the stated number of significant digits from the most significant figure, rounding the last one kept using the next digit: (a) 48599→50000 (1 s.f., since the second sig. digit 8 rounds the first digit 4 up to 5). (b) 48599→48600 (3 s.f.). (c) 6841→7000 (1 s.f.). (d) 7538→7500 (2 s.f.). (e) 483.7→500 (1 s.f.). (f) 2.5728→2.57 (3 s.f.). (g) 990→1000 (1 s.f., rounds up). (h) 2045→2000 (2 s.f.). (i) 14.952→15.0 (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the following to the number of significant figures (s.f.) shown in brackets: (a) 0.08562 (1 s.f.) (b) 0.5932 (1 s.f.) (c) 0.942 (2 s.f.) (d) 0.954 (1 s.f.) (e) 0.954 (2 s.f.) (f) 0.00305 (1 s.f.) (g) 0.00305 (2 s.f.) (h) 0.00973 (2 s.f.) (i) 0.00973 (1 s.f.)
exercises.full_solution: Leading zeros are never significant, so counting significant figures starts at the first non-zero digit: (a) 0.08562→0.09 (1 s.f.). (b) 0.5932→0.6 (1 s.f.). (c) 0.942→0.94 (2 s.f.). (d) 0.954→1 (1 s.f., rounds up through the 9; writing 1.0 would show 2 s.f.). (e) 0.954→0.95 (2 s.f.). (f) 0.00305→0.003 (1 s.f.). (g) 0.00305→0.0031 (2 s.f.). (h) 0.00973→0.0097 (2 s.f.). (i) 0.00973→0.01 (1 s.f., rounds up).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the following, giving your answer to an appropriate degree of accuracy: (a) $23.456\times17.89$ (b) $0.4\times12.62$ (c) $18\times9.24$ (d) $76.24\div3.2$ (e) $7.6^2$ (f) $16.42^3$ (g) $\frac{2.3\times3.37}{4}$ (h) $\frac{8.31}{2.02}$ (i) $9.2\div4^2$
exercises.answer: (a) ≈419.6 (b) ≈5.0 (c) ≈166.3 (d) ≈23.8 (e) ≈57.8 (f) ≈4427.1 (g) ≈1.9 (h) ≈4.1 (i) ≈0.6 (all to 1 d.p., a sensible degree of accuracy for calculator answers)
exercises.full_solution: Each value is computed on a calculator and then rounded to 1 decimal place, which is an appropriate level of accuracy for these calculations (for these calculations). (a) $23.456\times17.89=419.62784\to419.6$. (b) $0.4\times12.62=5.048\to5.0$. (c) $18\times9.24=166.32\to166.3$. (d) $76.24\div3.2=23.825\to23.8$. (e) $7.6^2=57.76\to57.8$. (f) $16.42^3=4427.101\ldots\to4427.1$. (g) $\frac{2.3\times3.37}{4}=1.93775\to1.9$. (h) $\frac{8.31}{2.02}=4.1139\ldots\to4.1$. (i) $9.2\div16=0.575\to0.6$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Without using a calculator, estimate the answers to the following: (a) $62\times19$ (b) $270\times12$ (c) $55\times60$ (d) $4950\times28$ (e) $0.8\times0.95$ (f) $0.184\times475$
exercises.answer: (a) ≈1200 (b) ≈3000 (c) ≈3600 (d) ≈150000 (e) ≈0.8 (f) ≈100 (one reasonable set of estimates obtained by rounding each number to 1 significant figure; the exact values are 1178, 3240, 3300, 138600, 0.76 and 87.4 respectively, confirming the estimates are the right order of magnitude)
exercises.full_solution: Round each number to one significant figure (or another convenient nearby value) and multiply. (a) $62\times19\approx60\times20=1200$. (b) $270\times12\approx300\times10=3000$. (c) $55\times60\approx60\times60=3600$. (d) $4950\times28\approx5000\times30=150000$. (e) $0.8\times0.95\approx0.8\times1=0.8$. (f) $0.184\times475\approx0.2\times500=100$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Without using a calculator, estimate the answers to the following: (a) $3946\div18$ (b) $8287\div42$ (c) $906\div27$ (d) $5520\div13$ (e) $48\div0.12$ (f) $610\div0.22$
exercises.answer: (a) ≈200 (b) ≈200 (c) ≈30 (d) ≈500 (e) ≈500 (f) ≈3000 (one reasonable set of estimates; exact values are 219.2, 197.3, 33.6, 424.6, 400 and 2772.7 respectively, showing the estimates are of the right order of magnitude)
exercises.full_solution: Round each number to a convenient nearby value and divide. (a) $3946\div18\approx4000\div20=200$. (b) $8287\div42\approx8000\div40=200$. (c) $906\div27\approx900\div30=30$. (d) $5520\div13\approx5000\div10=500$. (e) $48\div0.12\approx50\div0.1=500$. (f) $610\div0.22\approx600\div0.2=3000$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Without using a calculator, estimate the answers to the following: (a) $78.45+51.02$ (b) $168.3-87.09$ (c) $2.93\times3.14$ (d) $84.2\div19.5$ (e) $\frac{4.3\times752}{15.6}$ (f) $\frac{(9.8)^3}{(2.2)^2}$ (g) $\frac{\sqrt[3]{78}\times6}{5^3}$ (h) $\frac{38\times6^3}{\sqrt[4]{9900}}$ (i) $\sqrt[4]{25}\times\sqrt[4]{25}$
exercises.full_solution: Round each number to a convenient value. (a) $78.45+51.02\approx78+51=129\approx130$. (b) $168.3-87.09\approx168-87=81$. (c) $2.93\times3.14\approx3\times3=9$. (d) $84.2\div19.5\approx84\div20=4.2$. (e) $\frac{4.3\times752}{15.6}\approx\frac{4\times750}{15}=\frac{3000}{15}=200$. (f) $\frac{9.8^3}{2.2^2}\approx\frac{10^3}{2^2}=\frac{1000}{4}=250$. (g) using $\sqrt[3]{64}=4$ as a nearby cube: $\frac{4\times6}{125}=\frac{24}{125}\approx0.2$. (h) using $\sqrt[4]{10000}=10$: $\frac{38\times216}{10}=\frac{8208}{10}\approx820$. (i) $\sqrt[4]{25}\times\sqrt[4]{25}=(\sqrt[4]{25})^2=\sqrt{25}=5$ exactly — no estimation is even needed, the laws of indices give an exact value.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Using estimation, identify which of the following are definitely incorrect. Explain your reasoning clearly. (a) $95\times212=20140$ (b) $44\times17=748$ (c) $689\times413=28457$ (d) $142656\div8=17832$ (e) $77.9\times22.6=2512.54$ (f) $\frac{8.42\times46}{0.2}=19366$
exercises.answer: (a) and (b) and (d) are correct (consistent with a sensible estimate). (c), (e) and (f) are definitely incorrect.
exercises.full_solution: Estimate each calculation using rounded values and compare with the given answer. (a) $95\times212\approx100\times200=20000$, close to 20140 — plausible (and indeed exactly correct). (b) $44\times17\approx40\times20=800$, close to 748 — plausible (exactly correct). (c) $689\times413\approx700\times400=280000$, but the given answer 28457 is about ten times too small — definitely incorrect (the correct value is 284557, so a digit/decimal place has been lost). (d) $142656\div8\approx140000\div8=17500$, close to 17832 — plausible (exactly correct). (e) $77.9\times22.6\approx80\times20=1600$, far below the given 2512.54 — definitely incorrect (correct value is 1760.54). (f) $\frac{8.42\times46}{0.2}\approx\frac{8\times46}{0.2}=\frac{368}{0.2}=1840$, far below the given 19366 — definitely incorrect (correct value is 1936.6, so the given answer is ten times too large, a misplaced decimal point).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Estimate the shaded areas of the following shapes. Do not work out an exact answer. (a) A rectangle 17.2 m by 6.2 m. (b) An L-shaped figure: overall width 9.7 m, overall height 4.8 m, with a rectangular notch of width 3.1 m cut from the bottom-left corner, the remaining upper-left part having height 2.6 m. (c) A rectangle 28.8 cm by 16.3 cm with a smaller rectangular hole of 11 cm by 4.4 cm cut out of it.
exercises.answer: (a) ≈100 m² (e.g. $17\times6=102$) (b) ≈40–44 m² (c) ≈410–436 cm² (estimates obtained by rounding each dimension; exact values are 106.64 m², 39.74 m² and 421.04 cm² respectively, confirming the estimates are reasonable)
exercises.full_solution: (a) Round $17.2\to17$ and $6.2\to6$: area $\approx17\times6=102\,\text{m}^2$. (b) The shape is a $9.7\times4.8$ rectangle with a notch of width 3.1 m and height $4.8-2.6=2.2$ m removed; rounding, $10\times5-3\times2=50-6=44\,\text{m}^2$. (c) Round $28.8\to30$, $16.3\to16$, hole $11\times4.4\to11\times4$: area $\approx30\times16-11\times4=480-44=436\,\text{cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Estimate the volume of each of the solids below. Do not work out an exact answer. (a) A cuboid measuring 10.5 cm by 9 cm by 2.2 cm. (b) A cuboid measuring 38 cm by 19 cm by 6 cm. (c) An L-shaped prism of depth 11 cm. Its L-shaped cross-section is 20 cm high and 24 cm wide overall, and both arms of the L are 4 cm thick.
exercises.answer: (a) ≈180 cm³ (b) ≈4800 cm³ (c) ≈1600 cm³ (exact values 207.9 cm³, 4332 cm³ and 1760 cm³, confirming the estimates are reasonable)
exercises.full_solution: Round each dimension to 1 significant figure (or another convenient value) and multiply. (a) $10.5\to10$, $9\to9$, $2.2\to2$: volume $\approx10\times9\times2=180\,\text{cm}^3$ (exact: $10.5\times9\times2.2=207.9\,\text{cm}^3$). (b) $38\to40$, $19\to20$, $6\to6$: volume $\approx40\times20\times6=4800\,\text{cm}^3$ (exact: $38\times19\times6=4332\,\text{cm}^3$). (c) Split the L-shaped cross-section into a vertical arm $4\times20$ and a horizontal arm $(24-4)\times4=20\times4$: area $\approx80+80=160\,\text{cm}^2$. Multiply by the depth, $11\to10$: volume $\approx160\times10=1600\,\text{cm}^3$ (exact: $160\times11=1760\,\text{cm}^3$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Each of the following numbers is expressed to the nearest whole number. (i) Give the upper and lower bounds of each. (ii) Using $x$ as the number, express the range in which the number lies as an inequality. (a) 6 (b) 83 (c) 152 (d) 1000 (e) 100
exercises.full_solution: A number rounded to the nearest whole number can be up to 0.5 less or 0.5 more than the stated value (with the upper bound not actually reached). (a) $6\to5.5\le x<6.5$. (b) $83\to82.5\le x<83.5$. (c) $152\to151.5\le x<152.5$. (d) $1000\to999.5\le x<1000.5$. (e) $100\to99.5\le x<100.5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Each of the following numbers is correct to one decimal place. (i) Give the upper and lower bounds of each. (ii) Using $x$ as the number, express the range in which the number lies as an inequality. (a) 3.8 (b) 15.6 (c) 1.0 (d) 10.0 (e) 0.3
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Each of the following numbers is correct to two significant figures. (i) Give the upper and lower bounds of each. (ii) Using $x$ as the number, express the range in which the number lies as an inequality. (a) 4.2 (b) 0.84 (c) 420 (d) 5000 (e) 0.045 (f) 25000
exercises.full_solution: The bound half-unit equals half of the place value of the last significant digit. (a) $4.2$: unit 0.1, so $4.15\le x<4.25$. (b) $0.84$: unit 0.01, so $0.835\le x<0.845$. (c) $420$: unit 10, so $415\le x<425$. (d) $5000$ (2 s.f.): unit 100, so $4950\le x<5050$. (e) $0.045$: unit 0.001, so $0.0445\le x<0.0455$. (f) $25000$ (2 s.f.): unit 1000, so $24500\le x<25500$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The mass of a sack of vegetables is given as 5.4 kg. (a) Illustrate the lower and upper bounds of the mass on a number line. (b) Using $M$ kg for the mass, express the range of values in which $M$ must lie as an inequality.
exercises.answer: Lower bound 5.35 kg, upper bound 5.45 kg; $5.35\le M<5.45$.
exercises.full_solution: 5.4 kg is given to 1 d.p., so the true mass can be up to 0.05 kg less or more. (a) On a number line, mark a solid dot at 5.35 and an open circle at 5.45, with the line shaded between them. (b) $5.35\le M<5.45$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: At a school sports day, the winning time for the 100 m race was given as 11.8 seconds. (a) Illustrate the lower and upper bounds of the time on a number line. (b) Using $T$ seconds for the time, express the range of values in which $T$ must lie as an inequality.
exercises.answer: Lower bound 11.75 s, upper bound 11.85 s; $11.75\le T<11.85$.
exercises.full_solution: 11.8 s is given to 1 d.p., so the bound half-unit is 0.05 s either side. (a) On a number line, mark a solid dot at 11.75 and an open circle at 11.85. (b) $11.75\le T<11.85$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The capacity of a swimming pool is given as 620 m³ correct to two significant figures. (a) Calculate the lower and upper bounds of the pool's capacity. (b) Using $x$ cubic metres for the capacity, express the range of values in which $x$ must lie as an inequality.
exercises.answer: Lower bound 615 m³, upper bound 625 m³; $615\le x<625$.
exercises.full_solution: 620 to 2 s.f. has its last significant digit in the tens place, so the bound half-unit is 5 m³ either side. (a) Lower bound $=615\,\text{m}^3$, upper bound $=625\,\text{m}^3$. (b) $615\le x<625$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A farmer measures the dimensions of his rectangular field to the nearest 10 m. The length is recorded as 630 m and the width is recorded as 400 m. (a) Calculate the lower and upper bounds of the length. (b) Using $W$ metres for the width, express the range of values in which $W$ must lie as an inequality.
exercises.answer: (a) Lower bound 625 m, upper bound 635 m. (b) $395\le W<405$.
exercises.full_solution: Each measurement is given to the nearest 10 m, so the bound half-unit is 5 m either side. (a) Length $630\to625\le\text{length}<635$, i.e. lower bound 625 m, upper bound 635 m. (b) Width $400\to395\le W<405$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate lower and upper bounds for the following calculations, if each of the numbers is given to the nearest whole number: (a) $14\times20$ (b) $135\times25$ (c) $100\times50$ (d) $\frac{40}{10}$ (e) $\frac{33}{11}$ (f) $\frac{125}{15}$ (g) $\frac{12\times65}{16}$ (h) $\frac{101\times28}{69}$ (i) $\frac{250\times7}{100}$ (j) $\frac{44}{3^2}$ (k) $\frac{578}{17\times22}$ (l) $\frac{1000}{4\times(3+8)}$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate lower and upper bounds for the following calculations, if each of the numbers is given to 1 decimal place: (a) $2.1+4.7$ (b) $6.3\times4.8$ (c) $10.0\times14.9$ (d) $17.6-4.2$ (e) $\frac{8.5+3.6}{6.8}$ (f) $\frac{7.7-6.2}{3.5}$ (g) $\frac{(16.4)^2}{(3.0-0.3)^2}$ (h) $\frac{100.0}{(50.0-40.0)^2}$ (i) $(0.1-0.2)^2$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate lower and upper bounds for the following calculations, if each of the numbers is given to 2 significant figures: (a) $64\times320$ (b) $1.7\times0.65$ (c) $4800\times240$ (d) $\frac{54000}{600}$ (e) $\frac{4.2}{0.031}$ (f) $\frac{100}{5.2}$ (g) $\frac{6.8\times42}{120}$ (h) $\frac{100.0}{4.5\times6.0}$ (i) $\frac{180}{7.3-4.5}$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The masses to the nearest 0.5 kg of two parcels are 1.5 kg and 2.5 kg. Calculate the lower and upper bounds of their combined mass.
exercises.answer: Lower bound 3.5 kg, upper bound 4.5 kg.
exercises.full_solution: Each mass is given to the nearest 0.5 kg, so each has bound half-unit 0.25 kg. $1.5\to1.25$–$1.75$; $2.5\to2.25$–$2.75$. Combined mass: lower $=1.25+2.25=3.5$ kg, upper $=1.75+2.75=4.5$ kg.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate upper and lower bounds for the perimeter of a rectangle with dimensions 6.8 cm by 4.2 cm, given that its dimensions are correct to 1 decimal place.
exercises.answer: Lower bound 21.8 cm, upper bound 22.2 cm.
exercises.full_solution: Each dimension has bound half-unit 0.05 cm: length $6.75$–$6.85$, width $4.15$–$4.25$. Perimeter $=2(l+w)$: lower $=2(6.75+4.15)=2(10.9)=21.8$ cm, upper $=2(6.85+4.25)=2(11.1)=22.2$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate upper and lower bounds for the perimeter of a rectangle with dimensions 4.86 m by 2.00 m, whose dimensions are accurate to 2 decimal places.
exercises.answer: Lower bound 13.70 m, upper bound 13.74 m.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate upper and lower bounds for the area of a rectangle with dimensions 10.0 cm by 7.5 cm, given that its dimensions are accurate to 1 decimal place.
exercises.answer: Lower bound 74.13 cm², upper bound 75.88 cm² (to 2 d.p.).
exercises.full_solution: Each dimension has bound half-unit 0.05 cm: length $9.95$–$10.05$, width $7.45$–$7.55$. Area: lower $=9.95\times7.45=74.1275$ cm², upper $=10.05\times7.55=75.8775$ cm².
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate upper and lower bounds for the area of a rectangle with dimensions 600 m by 120 m, whose dimensions are correct to 2 significant figures.
exercises.answer: Lower bound 68425 m², upper bound 75625 m².
exercises.full_solution: 600 (2 s.f.) has bound half-unit 5: 595–605. 120 (2 s.f.) has bound half-unit 5: 115–125. Area: lower $=595\times115=68425$ m², upper $=605\times125=75625$ m².
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The area of a rectangle is given as 55.8 cm² and its width as 4.2 cm, both correct to 1 decimal place. Calculate the upper and lower bounds for the length of the rectangle, giving your answers correct to 2 decimal places.
exercises.answer: Lower bound 13.12 cm, upper bound 13.46 cm (to 2 d.p.).
exercises.full_solution: Both measurements are given to 1 decimal place, so each has bound half-unit $0.05$: area $55.75$–$55.85$ cm², width $4.15$–$4.25$ cm. Length $=$ area $\div$ width, so the SMALLEST length comes from the smallest area divided by the largest width, and the LARGEST length from the largest area divided by the smallest width. Lower $=\dfrac{55.75}{4.25}=13.1176\ldots=13.12$ cm; upper $=\dfrac{55.85}{4.15}=13.4578\ldots=13.46$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Copy each of the following statements, and insert one of the symbols $=,>,<$ into the space to make the statement correct: (a) $7\times2 \ldots 8+7$ (b) $6^2 \ldots 9\times4$ (c) $5\times10 \ldots 7^2$ (d) $80\,\text{cm} \ldots 1\,\text{m}$ (e) $1000\,\text{litres} \ldots 1\,\text{m}^3$ (f) $48\div6 \ldots 54\div9$
exercises.full_solution: Evaluate both sides and compare. (a) $14<15$. (b) $36=36$. (c) $50>49$. (d) $80\,\text{cm}<100\,\text{cm}=1\,\text{m}$. (e) $1\,\text{m}^3=1000$ litres exactly, so they are equal. (f) $8>6$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The radius of a circle is given as 8.5 cm, correct to 1 decimal place. Calculate the upper and lower bounds for the circumference of the circle, giving your answers correct to 1 decimal place.
exercises.answer: Lower bound 53.1 cm, upper bound 53.7 cm (to 1 d.p.).
exercises.full_solution: The radius has bound half-unit $0.05$ cm, so $8.45\le r<8.55$. The circumference $C=2\pi r$ increases as $r$ increases, so the bounds of $r$ give the bounds of $C$ directly. Lower $=2\pi\times8.45=53.0929\ldots=53.1$ cm; upper $=2\pi\times8.55=53.7212\ldots=53.7$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Represent each of the following inequalities on a number line, where $x$ is a real number: (a) $x<2$ (b) $x\ge3$ (c) $x\le-4$ (d) $x\ge-2$ (e) $2<x<5$ (f) $-3<x<0$ (g) $-2\le x<2$ (h) $2\ge x\ge-1$
exercises.answer: Number-line sketches: (a) open circle at 2, shading/arrow to the left. (b) solid dot at 3, shading/arrow to the right. (c) solid dot at -4, shading/arrow to the left. (d) solid dot at -2, shading/arrow to the right. (e) open circles at 2 and 5, shading between. (f) open circles at -3 and 0, shading between. (g) solid dot at -2, open circle at 2, shading between. (h) equivalent to $-1\le x\le2$: solid dots at -1 and 2, shading between.
exercises.full_solution: An open circle marks a boundary value that is excluded (strict $<$ or $>$), a solid (filled) dot marks one that is included ($\le$ or $\ge$), and the shaded region/arrow shows all the values satisfying the inequality. Each part is drawn by locating the boundary value(s) on the line and choosing open or solid circles according to whether the inequality is strict.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The radius of a circle is given as 8.5 cm, correct to 1 decimal place. Calculate the upper and lower bounds for the area of the circle, giving your answers correct to 1 decimal place.
exercises.answer: Lower bound 224.3 cm², upper bound 229.7 cm² (to 1 d.p.).
exercises.full_solution: Again $8.45\le r<8.55$. The area $A=\pi r^2$ also increases as $r$ increases, so lower $=\pi\times8.45^2=\pi\times71.4025=224.3175\ldots=224.3$ cm²; upper $=\pi\times8.55^2=\pi\times73.1025=229.6582\ldots=229.7$ cm².
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write down the inequalities which correspond to the following number lines: (a) an open circle at 0, with the line shaded/arrowed to the right, continuing past 3. (b) an arrow shaded from the left continuing past 0, up to a solid dot at 3. (c) a solid dot at 0 and a solid dot at 4, with the line shaded solidly between them. (d) an open circle at $-4$ and a solid dot at $-1$, with the line shaded between them.
exercises.full_solution: Read off each boundary value and whether its circle is open (excluded) or solid (included), and the direction of the arrow/shading. (a) Open circle at 0, shaded to the right with no upper bound shown: $x>0$. (b) Shaded from the left with no lower bound, up to a solid dot at 3: $x\le3$. (c) Solid dots at both 0 and 4: $0\le x\le4$. (d) Open circle at $-4$, solid dot at $-1$: $-4<x\le-1$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The area of a circle is given as 400 cm², correct to 2 significant figures. Calculate the upper and lower bounds for the radius of the circle, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
exercises.answer: Lower bound 11.2 cm, upper bound 11.4 cm (to 3 s.f.).
exercises.full_solution: 400 correct to 2 significant figures has bound half-unit $5$, so $395\le A<405$ (in cm²). Rearranging $A=\pi r^2$ gives $r=\sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}$, which increases as $A$ increases. Lower $=\sqrt{\dfrac{395}{\pi}}=11.2130\ldots=11.2$ cm; upper $=\sqrt{\dfrac{405}{\pi}}=11.3540\ldots=11.4$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the following sentences using inequality signs: (a) The maximum capacity of an athletics stadium is 20000 people. (b) In a class, the tallest student is 180 cm and the shortest is 135 cm. (c) Five times a number plus 3 is less than 20. (d) The maximum temperature in May was 25°C. (e) A farmer has between 350 and 400 apples on each tree in his orchard. (f) In December, temperatures in Kenya were between 11°C and 28°C.
exercises.full_solution: Translate each phrase into symbols, using $\le/\ge$ for 'maximum/minimum' (since the stated extreme value is actually achieved) and the tightest sensible reading of 'between'. (a) Capacity $n$ cannot exceed 20000: $n\le20000$. (b) Height $h$ of a student lies between the shortest and tallest recorded: $135\le h\le180$ (cm). (c) 'Five times a number plus 3' is $5x+3$, and it is less than 20: $5x+3<20$. (d) Temperature $T$ never exceeded 25°C: $T\le25$. (e) The apple count $n$ is strictly between 350 and 400: $350<n<400$. (f) December temperatures $T$ (in °C) ranged inclusively from the recorded minimum to maximum: $11\le T\le28$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A cube has sides of length 2.0 cm, correct to 1 decimal place, and a mass of 100 g, correct to the nearest gram. Using density $=$ mass $\div$ volume, calculate the upper and lower bounds for the density of the cube, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
exercises.answer: Lower bound 11.5 g/cm³, upper bound 13.6 g/cm³ (to 3 s.f.).
exercises.full_solution: Side: bound half-unit $0.05$ cm, so $1.95\le l<2.05$. Mass: bound half-unit $0.5$ g, so $99.5\le m<100.5$. Volume $=l^3$, so $1.95^3=7.414875$ cm³ and $2.05^3=8.615125$ cm³ are the bounds of the volume. For a quotient, the LOWEST density is the smallest mass divided by the largest volume and the HIGHEST density is the largest mass divided by the smallest volume. Lower $=\dfrac{99.5}{8.615125}=11.5494\ldots=11.5$ g/cm³; upper $=\dfrac{100.5}{7.414875}=13.5538\ldots=13.6$ g/cm³.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the following decimals in order of magnitude, starting with the smallest: $6.0,\ 0.6,\ 0.66,\ 0.606,\ 0.06,\ 6.6,\ 6.606$.
exercises.full_solution: Compare the numbers by their value, lining up decimal places: 0.06 (smallest), then 0.6, then 0.606 (just above 0.6), then 0.66, then the numbers greater than 1: 6.0, 6.6, and finally 6.606 (largest).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The distance from the Earth to the Moon is given as 384 000 km, correct to 3 significant figures. A spacecraft covers this distance at an average speed of 3500 km/h, correct to 2 significant figures. Calculate the least and the greatest time the journey could take, giving your answers correct to the nearest hour.
exercises.answer: Least time 108 hours, greatest time 111 hours (to the nearest hour).
exercises.full_solution: Distance: 384 000 to 3 significant figures has bound half-unit $500$, so $383\,500\le d<384\,500$ (km). Speed: 3500 to 2 significant figures has bound half-unit $50$, so $3450\le s<3550$ (km/h). Time $=$ distance $\div$ speed, so the LEAST time is the smallest distance divided by the greatest speed and the GREATEST time is the largest distance divided by the slowest speed. Least $=\dfrac{383\,500}{3550}=108.028\ldots\approx108$ hours; greatest $=\dfrac{384\,500}{3450}=111.449\ldots\approx111$ hours.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the following fractions in order of magnitude, starting with the largest: $\frac12,\ \frac13,\ \frac6{13},\ \frac45,\ \frac7{18},\ \frac2{19}$.
exercises.full_solution: Convert each to a decimal to compare: $\frac12=0.5$, $\frac13\approx0.333$, $\frac6{13}\approx0.462$, $\frac45=0.8$, $\frac7{18}\approx0.389$, $\frac2{19}\approx0.105$. Ordering from largest to smallest: $\frac45(0.8) > \frac12(0.5) > \frac6{13}(0.462) > \frac7{18}(0.389) > \frac13(0.333) > \frac2{19}(0.105)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the following lengths in order of magnitude, starting with the smallest: $2\,\text{m},\ 60\,\text{cm},\ 800\,\text{mm},\ 180\,\text{cm},\ 0.75\,\text{m}$.
exercises.full_solution: Convert all lengths to centimetres: $2\,\text{m}=200\,\text{cm}$, $60\,\text{cm}=60\,\text{cm}$, $800\,\text{mm}=80\,\text{cm}$, $180\,\text{cm}=180\,\text{cm}$, $0.75\,\text{m}=75\,\text{cm}$. Ordering ascending: $60<75<80<180<200$, i.e. $60\,\text{cm} < 0.75\,\text{m} < 800\,\text{mm} < 180\,\text{cm} < 2\,\text{m}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the following masses in order of magnitude, starting with the largest: $4\,\text{kg},\ 3500\,\text{g},\ \frac34\,\text{kg},\ 700\,\text{g},\ 1\,\text{kg}$.
exercises.full_solution: Convert all masses to grams: $4\,\text{kg}=4000\,\text{g}$, $3500\,\text{g}=3500\,\text{g}$, $\frac34\,\text{kg}=750\,\text{g}$, $700\,\text{g}=700\,\text{g}$, $1\,\text{kg}=1000\,\text{g}$. Ordering descending: $4000>3500>1000>750>700$, i.e. $4\,\text{kg} > 3500\,\text{g} > 1\,\text{kg} > \frac34\,\text{kg} > 700\,\text{g}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the following volumes in order of magnitude, starting with the smallest: $1\,\text{l},\ 430\,\text{ml},\ 800\,\text{cm}^3,\ 120\,\text{cl},\ 150\,\text{cm}^3$.
exercises.full_solution: Convert all volumes to millilitres (noting $1\,\text{cm}^3=1\,\text{ml}$): $1\,\text{l}=1000\,\text{ml}$, $430\,\text{ml}=430\,\text{ml}$, $800\,\text{cm}^3=800\,\text{ml}$, $120\,\text{cl}=1200\,\text{ml}$, $150\,\text{cm}^3=150\,\text{ml}$. Ordering ascending: $150<430<800<1000<1200$, i.e. $150\,\text{cm}^3 < 430\,\text{ml} < 800\,\text{cm}^3 < 1\,\text{l} < 120\,\text{cl}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate the following (i) in your head, (ii) using a scientific calculator: (a) $8\times3+2$ (b) $4\div2+8$ (c) $12\times4-6$ (d) $4+6\times2$ (e) $10-6\div3$ (f) $6-3\times4$
exercises.full_solution: Apply the standard order of operations (multiplication/division before addition/subtraction). (a) $8\times3=24$, $+2=26$. (b) $4\div2=2$, $+8=10$. (c) $12\times4=48$, $-6=42$. (d) $6\times2=12$, $4+12=16$. (e) $6\div3=2$, $10-2=8$. (f) $3\times4=12$, $6-12=-6$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate the following: (a) $7\times2+3\times2$ (b) $12\div3+6\times5$ (c) $9+3\times8-1$ (d) $36-9\div3-2$ (e) $-14\times2-16\div2$ (f) $4+3\times7-6\div3$
exercises.full_solution: Do all multiplications/divisions first, then additions/subtractions left to right. (a) $14+6=20$. (b) $4+30=34$. (c) $9+24-1=32$. (d) $36-3-2=31$. (e) $-28-8=-36$. (f) $4+21-2=23$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate the following: (a) $(4+5)\times3$ (b) $8\times(12-4)$ (c) $3\times(-8+-3)-3$ (d) $(4+11)\div(7-2)$ (e) $4\times3\times(7+5)$ (f) $24\div3\div(10-5)$
exercises.full_solution: Evaluate the brackets first. (a) $9\times3=27$. (b) $8\times8=64$. (c) $3\times(-11)-3=-33-3=-36$. (d) $15\div5=3$. (e) $12\times12=144$. (f) $24\div3=8$, then $8\div5=1.6$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: In each case, copy the calculation and insert brackets where needed to make it correct, then check with a calculator: (a) $6\times2+1=18$ (b) $1+3\times5=16$ (c) $8+6\div2=7$ (d) $9+2\times4=44$ (e) $9\div3\times4+1=13$ (f) $3+2\times4-1=15$
exercises.answer: (a) $6\times(2+1)=18$ (b) $1+3\times5=16$ — already correct, no brackets needed (c) $(8+6)\div2=7$ (d) $(9+2)\times4=44$ (e) $9\div3\times4+1=13$ — already correct, no brackets needed (f) $(3+2)\times(4-1)=15$
exercises.full_solution:
Work out the standard (no-bracket) value of each expression, and compare it to the stated result; if they already agree, no brackets are needed, otherwise find where brackets make the two sides match. (a) standard value $=13
e18$; with brackets $6	imes(2+1)=6	imes3=18$ ✓. (b) standard value $=1+15=16$, already matches — no brackets needed. (c) standard value $=8+3=11
e7$; with brackets $(8+6)\div2=14\div2=7$ ✓. (d) standard value $=9+8=17
e44$; with brackets $(9+2)	imes4=11	imes4=44$ ✓. (e) standard value (left to right for $\div,	imes$) $=3	imes4+1=13$, already matches — no brackets needed. (f) standard value $=3+8-1=10
e15$; with brackets $(3+2)	imes(4-1)=5	imes3=15$ ✓.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The same four numbers, $12\div4-2+6$, give different results depending on where brackets are placed. For each target value, copy the calculation and insert brackets (if needed) so that it is correct: (a) $12\div4-2+6=7$ (b) $12\div4-2+6=12$ (c) $12\div4-2+6=-5$ (d) $12\div4-2+6=1.5$. Likewise for $4+5\times6-1$: (e) $4+5\times6-1=33$ (f) $4+5\times6-1=29$ (g) $4+5\times6-1=53$ (h) $4+5\times6-1=45$
exercises.answer: (a) $12\div4-2+6=7$ — already correct, no brackets needed (b) $12\div(4-2)+6=12$ (c) $12\div4-(2+6)=-5$ (d) $12\div(4-2+6)=1.5$ (e) $4+5\times6-1=33$ — already correct, no brackets needed (f) $4+5\times(6-1)=29$ (g) $(4+5)\times6-1=53$ (h) $(4+5)\times(6-1)=45$
exercises.full_solution: (a) Standard order gives $12\div4-2+6=3-2+6=7$, already matching — no brackets needed. (b) $12\div(4-2)+6=12\div2+6=6+6=12$. (c) $12\div4-(2+6)=3-8=-5$. (d) $12\div(4-2+6)=12\div8=1.5$. (e) Standard order gives $4+30-1=33$, already matching — no brackets needed. (f) $4+5\times(6-1)=4+5\times5=4+25=29$. (g) $(4+5)\times6-1=9\times6-1=54-1=53$. (h) $(4+5)\times(6-1)=9\times5=45$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the information on the following number lines as inequalities (the range shown runs from $-2$ to $2$): (a) a solid dot at $-1$, with an arrow pointing to the right. (b) shaded from the left past $-2$, up to an open circle at 2. (c) a solid dot at $-2$ and an open circle at 2, shaded between. (d) a solid dot at $-1$ and a solid dot at 1, shaded between.
exercises.full_solution: Read the type of circle (open = excluded, solid = included) at each boundary and the direction of shading. (a) Solid dot at $-1$ (included), unbounded to the right: $x\ge-1$. (b) Unbounded to the left, open circle at 2: $x<2$. (c) Solid dot at $-2$, open circle at 2: $-2\le x<2$. (d) Solid dots at both $-1$ and $1$: $-1\le x\le1$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Illustrate each of the following inequalities on a number line: (a) $x\ge3$ (b) $x<4$ (c) $0<x<4$ (d) $-3\le x<1$
exercises.answer: (a) Solid dot at 3, shaded/arrowed to the right. (b) Open circle at 4, shaded/arrowed to the left. (c) Open circles at 0 and 4, shaded between. (d) Solid dot at $-3$, open circle at 1, shaded between.
exercises.full_solution: Use a solid dot for an included boundary ($\le,\ge$) and an open circle for an excluded one ($<,>$), shading the region of the line that satisfies the inequality. (a) $x\ge3$: solid dot at 3, arrow right. (b) $x<4$: open circle at 4, arrow left. (c) $0<x<4$: open circles at 0 and 4, shading between. (d) $-3\le x<1$: solid dot at $-3$, open circle at 1, shading between.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the following fractions in order of magnitude, starting with the smallest: $\frac47,\ \frac3{14},\ \frac9{10},\ \frac12,\ \frac25$.
exercises.full_solution: Convert to decimals: $\frac47\approx0.571$, $\frac3{14}\approx0.214$, $\frac9{10}=0.9$, $\frac12=0.5$, $\frac25=0.4$. Ordering ascending: $\frac3{14}(0.214) < \frac25(0.4) < \frac12(0.5) < \frac47(0.571) < \frac9{10}(0.9)$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.full_solution:
Compare the standard (no-bracket) value with the stated target and insert brackets to reconcile them. (a) standard $=7-8=-1
e6$; with brackets $(7-4)	imes2=3	imes2=6$ ✓. (b) standard $=12+9+4=25
e33$; with brackets $12+3	imes(3+4)=12+3	imes7=12+21=33$ ✓. (c) standard $=5+30-4=31
e20$; with brackets $(5+5)	imes(6-4)=10	imes2=20$ ✓. (d) with brackets $(5+5)	imes6-4=60-4=56$ ✓.

exercises.statement: Evaluate the following: (a) $\frac34$ of 20 (b) $\frac45$ of 20 (c) $\frac49$ of 45 (d) $\frac58$ of 64 (e) $\frac3{11}$ of 66 (f) $\frac9{10}$ of 80 (g) $\frac57$ of 42 (h) $\frac89$ of 54 (i) $\frac78$ of 240 (j) $\frac45$ of 65
exercises.full_solution: To find a fraction of a number, divide by the denominator then multiply by the numerator. (a) $20\div4=5$, $5\times3=15$. (b) $20\div5=4$, $\times4=16$. (c) $45\div9=5$, $\times4=20$. (d) $64\div8=8$, $\times5=40$. (e) $66\div11=6$, $\times3=18$. (f) $80\div10=8$, $\times9=72$. (g) $42\div7=6$, $\times5=30$. (h) $54\div9=6$, $\times8=48$. (i) $240\div8=30$, $\times7=210$. (j) $65\div5=13$, $\times4=52$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Change the following mixed numbers into vulgar (improper) fractions: (a) $4\frac23$ (b) $3\frac35$ (c) $5\frac78$ (d) $2\frac56$ (e) $8\frac12$ (f) $9\frac57$ (g) $6\frac49$ (h) $4\frac14$ (i) $5\frac4{11}$ (j) $7\frac67$ (k) $4\frac3{10}$ (l) $11\frac3{13}$
exercises.full_solution: Multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator, keeping the same denominator: $w\frac{n}{d}=\frac{wd+n}{d}$. (a) $\frac{4\times3+2}{3}=\frac{14}{3}$. (b) $\frac{3\times5+3}{5}=\frac{18}{5}$. (c) $\frac{5\times8+7}{8}=\frac{47}{8}$. (d) $\frac{2\times6+5}{6}=\frac{17}{6}$. (e) $\frac{8\times2+1}{2}=\frac{17}{2}$. (f) $\frac{9\times7+5}{7}=\frac{68}{7}$. (g) $\frac{6\times9+4}{9}=\frac{58}{9}$. (h) $\frac{4\times4+1}{4}=\frac{17}{4}$. (i) $\frac{5\times11+4}{11}=\frac{59}{11}$. (j) $\frac{7\times7+6}{7}=\frac{55}{7}$. (k) $\frac{4\times10+3}{10}=\frac{43}{10}$. (l) $\frac{11\times13+3}{13}=\frac{146}{13}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Change the following improper (vulgar) fractions into mixed numbers: (a) $\frac{29}{4}$ (b) $\frac{33}{5}$ (c) $\frac{41}{6}$ (d) $\frac{53}{8}$ (e) $\frac{49}{9}$ (f) $\frac{17}{12}$ (g) $\frac{66}{7}$ (h) $\frac{33}{10}$ (i) $\frac{19}{2}$ (j) $\frac{73}{12}$
exercises.full_solution: Divide the numerator by the denominator: the quotient is the whole number part, and the remainder over the denominator is the fraction part. (a) $29=7\times4+1\Rightarrow7\frac14$. (b) $33=6\times5+3\Rightarrow6\frac35$. (c) $41=6\times6+5\Rightarrow6\frac56$. (d) $53=6\times8+5\Rightarrow6\frac58$. (e) $49=5\times9+4\Rightarrow5\frac49$. (f) $17=1\times12+5\Rightarrow1\frac5{12}$. (g) $66=9\times7+3\Rightarrow9\frac37$. (h) $33=3\times10+3\Rightarrow3\frac3{10}$. (i) $19=9\times2+1\Rightarrow9\frac12$. (j) $73=6\times12+1\Rightarrow6\frac1{12}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.full_solution: Write the whole-number part, then the fraction part using place value (tenths, hundredths or thousandths). (a) $4\frac5{10}=4.5$. (b) $6.3$. (c) $17.8$. (d) $3\frac7{100}=3.07$. (e) $9.27$. (f) $11.36$. (g) $4\frac6{1000}=4.006$. (h) $5.027$. (i) $4.356$. (j) $9.204$.

exercises.statement: Express each of the following as a fraction with denominator 100, then write them as percentages: (a) $\frac{29}{50}$ (b) $\frac{17}{25}$ (c) $\frac{11}{20}$ (d) $\frac3{10}$ (e) $\frac{23}{25}$ (f) $\frac{19}{50}$ (g) $\frac34$ (h) $\frac25$
exercises.full_solution: Multiply numerator and denominator by whatever makes the denominator 100, then read off the percentage. (a) $\frac{29}{50}\times\frac22=\frac{58}{100}=58\%$. (b) $\frac{17}{25}\times\frac44=\frac{68}{100}=68\%$. (c) $\frac{11}{20}\times\frac55=\frac{55}{100}=55\%$. (d) $\frac3{10}\times\frac{10}{10}=\frac{30}{100}=30\%$. (e) $\frac{23}{25}\times\frac44=\frac{92}{100}=92\%$. (f) $\frac{19}{50}\times\frac22=\frac{38}{100}=38\%$. (g) $\frac34\times\frac{25}{25}=\frac{75}{100}=75\%$. (h) $\frac25\times\frac{20}{20}=\frac{40}{100}=40\%$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate the answer to each of the following: (a) $3+5\times2-4$ (b) $12\div8+6\div4$
exercises.full_solution: Apply the order of operations (multiplication/division before addition/subtraction). (a) $5\times2=10$, so $3+10-4=9$. (b) $12\div8=1.5$ and $6\div4=1.5$, so $1.5+1.5=3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Copy these equations and put brackets in the correct places to make them correct: (a) $6\times4+6\div3=20$ (b) $9-3\times7+2=54$
exercises.full_solution: (a) Standard order gives $24+2=26\ne20$; placing brackets as $6\times(4+6)\div3=6\times10\div3=60\div3=20$ ✓. (b) Standard order gives $9-21+2=-10\ne54$; placing brackets as $(9-3)\times(7+2)=6\times9=54$ ✓.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Work out the remainders in the following divisions: (a) $72\div7$ (b) $430\div9$
exercises.full_solution: (a) The largest multiple of $7$ not greater than $72$ is $7\times10=70$, and $72-70=2$, so $72\div7=10$ remainder $2$. (b) The largest multiple of $9$ not greater than $430$ is $9\times47=423$ (the next one, $9\times48=432$, is too big), and $430-423=7$, so $430\div9=47$ remainder $7$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: (a) A length of rail track is $9\,\text{m}$ long. How many complete lengths will be needed to lay $1\,\text{km}$ of track? (b) How many $35$-cent stamps can be bought for $10$ dollars?
exercises.full_solution: (a) $1\,\text{km}=1000\,\text{m}$ and $1000\div9=111.1\ldots$. Whole lengths only: $111$ lengths reach only $111\times9=999\,\text{m}$, so one more length is needed and $112$ lengths must be used. (b) $10$ dollars $=1000$ cents and $1000\div35=28.57\ldots$. Buying $28$ stamps costs $28\times35=980$ cents, leaving $20$ cents, which is not enough for another stamp, so $28$ stamps can be bought.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Work out the following long divisions to $1$ d.p. (a) $7892\div7$ (b) $7892\div15$
exercises.full_solution: (a) $7\times1127=7889$, leaving a remainder of $3$, so $7892\div7=1127.428\ldots$; the next digit is $2$, so to $1$ d.p. the answer is $1127.4$. (b) $15\times526=7890$, leaving a remainder of $2$, so $7892\div15=526.133\ldots$; the next digit is $3$, so to $1$ d.p. the answer is $526.1$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Express the following fractions in their lowest terms: (a) $\frac5{10}$ (b) $\frac7{21}$ (c) $\frac8{12}$ (d) $\frac{16}{36}$ (e) $\frac{75}{100}$ (f) $\frac{81}{90}$
exercises.full_solution: Divide numerator and denominator by their highest common factor. (a) HCF(5,10)=5: $\frac12$. (b) HCF(7,21)=7: $\frac13$. (c) HCF(8,12)=4: $\frac23$. (d) HCF(16,36)=4: $\frac49$. (e) HCF(75,100)=25: $\frac34$. (f) HCF(81,90)=9: $\frac9{10}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate each of the following and write the answer as a fraction in its simplest form: (a) $\frac35+\frac45$ (b) $\frac3{11}+\frac7{11}$ (c) $\frac23+\frac14$ (d) $\frac35+\frac49$ (e) $\frac8{13}+\frac25$ (f) $\frac12+\frac23+\frac34$
exercises.full_solution: (a) $1\,\text{km}=1000\,\text{m}$ and $1000\div9=111.1\ldots$, so only $111$ whole lengths fit. They reach just $111\times9=999\,\text{m}$, which leaves $1\,\text{m}$ of track to lay, so one more length is needed: $112$ complete lengths must be used. (b) $10$ dollars $=1000$ cents and $1000\div35=28.57\ldots$. Buying $28$ stamps costs $28\times35=980$ cents, leaving $20$ cents, which is not enough for another stamp, so $28$ stamps can be bought.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate each of the following and write the answer as a fraction in its simplest form: (a) $\frac18+\frac38+\frac58$ (b) $\frac37+\frac57+\frac47$ (c) $\frac13+\frac12+\frac14$ (d) $\frac15+\frac13+\frac14$ (e) $\frac38+\frac35+\frac34$ (f) $\frac3{13}+\frac14+\frac12$
exercises.full_solution: Convert each to a common denominator before adding. (a) denom 8: $\frac{1+3+5}{8}=\frac98=1\frac18$. (b) denom 7: $\frac{3+5+4}{7}=\frac{12}{7}=1\frac57$. (c) denom 12: $\frac4{12}+\frac6{12}+\frac3{12}=\frac{13}{12}=1\frac1{12}$. (d) denom 60: $\frac{12}{60}+\frac{20}{60}+\frac{15}{60}=\frac{47}{60}$. (e) denom 40: $\frac{15}{40}+\frac{24}{40}+\frac{30}{40}=\frac{69}{40}=1\frac{29}{40}$. (f) denom 52: $\frac{12}{52}+\frac{13}{52}+\frac{26}{52}=\frac{51}{52}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate each of the following and write the answer as a fraction in its simplest form: (a) $\frac37-\frac27$ (b) $\frac45-\frac7{10}$ (c) $\frac89-\frac13$ (d) $\frac7{12}-\frac12$ (e) $\frac58-\frac25$ (f) $\frac34-\frac25+\frac7{10}$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate each of the following and write the answer as a fraction in its simplest form: (a) $\frac34+\frac15-\frac23$ (b) $\frac38+\frac7{11}-\frac12$ (c) $\frac45-\frac3{10}+\frac7{20}$ (d) $\frac9{13}+\frac13-\frac45$ (e) $\frac9{10}-\frac15-\frac14$ (f) $\frac89-\frac13-\frac12$
