exercises.statement: Evaluate each of the following and write the answer as a fraction in its simplest form: (a) $2\frac12+3\frac14$ (b) $3\frac35+1\frac7{10}$ (c) $6\frac12-3\frac25$ (d) $8\frac58-2\frac13$ (e) $5\frac78-4\frac34$ (f) $3\frac14-2\frac59$
exercises.full_solution: Convert to improper fractions (or combine whole and fractional parts separately), then use a common denominator. (a) $\frac52+\frac{13}{4}=\frac{10}{4}+\frac{13}{4}=\frac{23}{4}=5\frac34$. (b) $\frac{18}{5}+\frac{17}{10}=\frac{36}{10}+\frac{17}{10}=\frac{53}{10}=5\frac3{10}$. (c) $\frac{13}{2}-\frac{17}{5}=\frac{65}{10}-\frac{34}{10}=\frac{31}{10}=3\frac1{10}$. (d) $\frac{69}{8}-\frac73=\frac{207}{24}-\frac{56}{24}=\frac{151}{24}=6\frac7{24}$. (e) $\frac{47}{8}-\frac{19}{4}=\frac{47}{8}-\frac{38}{8}=\frac98=1\frac18$. (f) $\frac{13}{4}-\frac{23}{9}=\frac{117}{36}-\frac{92}{36}=\frac{25}{36}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate each of the following and write the answer as a fraction in its simplest form: (a) $2\frac12+1\frac14+1\frac38$ (b) $2\frac45+3\frac18+1\frac3{10}$ (c) $4\frac12-1\frac14-3\frac58$ (d) $6\frac12-2\frac34-3\frac25$ (e) $2\frac47-3\frac14-1\frac35$ (f) $4\frac7{20}-5\frac12+2\frac25$
exercises.full_solution: Convert each mixed number to an improper fraction, combine over a common denominator, then convert back. (a) denom 8: $\frac{20}{8}+\frac{10}{8}+\frac{11}{8}=\frac{41}{8}=5\frac18$. (b) denom 40: $\frac{112}{40}+\frac{125}{40}+\frac{52}{40}=\frac{289}{40}=7\frac9{40}$. (c) denom 8: $\frac{36}{8}-\frac{10}{8}-\frac{29}{8}=-\frac38$. (d) denom 20: $\frac{130}{20}-\frac{55}{20}-\frac{68}{20}=\frac7{20}$. (e) denom 140: $2\frac47=\frac{18}{7}=\frac{360}{140}$, $3\frac14=\frac{13}{4}=\frac{455}{140}$, $1\frac35=\frac85=\frac{224}{140}$, so $\frac{360}{140}-\frac{455}{140}-\frac{224}{140}=-\frac{319}{140}=-2\frac{39}{140}$. (f) denom 20: $\frac{87}{20}-\frac{110}{20}+\frac{48}{20}=\frac{25}{20}=\frac54=1\frac14$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the reciprocal of each of the following: (a) $\frac18$ (b) $\frac7{12}$ (c) $\frac35$ (d) $1\frac12$ (e) $3\frac34$ (f) 6
exercises.full_solution: Invert each fraction (writing whole/mixed numbers as fractions first). (a) $\frac18\to8$. (b) $\frac7{12}\to\frac{12}{7}$. (c) $\frac35\to\frac53$. (d) $1\frac12=\frac32\to\frac23$. (e) $3\frac34=\frac{15}{4}\to\frac4{15}$. (f) $6=\frac61\to\frac16$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate the following: (a) $\frac38\times\frac49$ (b) $\frac23\times\frac9{10}$ (c) $\frac57\times\frac4{15}$ (d) $\frac34$ of $\frac89$ (e) $\frac56$ of $\frac3{10}$ (f) $\frac78$ of $\frac25$
exercises.full_solution: Multiply numerators and denominators, cancelling common factors. (a) $\frac{3\times4}{8\times9}=\frac{12}{72}=\frac16$. (b) $\frac{2\times9}{3\times10}=\frac{18}{30}=\frac35$. (c) $\frac{5\times4}{7\times15}=\frac{20}{105}=\frac4{21}$. (d) $\frac{3\times8}{4\times9}=\frac{24}{36}=\frac23$. (e) $\frac{5\times3}{6\times10}=\frac{15}{60}=\frac14$. (f) $\frac{7\times2}{8\times5}=\frac{14}{40}=\frac7{20}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate the following: (a) $\frac58\div\frac34$ (b) $\frac56\div\frac13$ (c) $\frac45\div\frac7{10}$ (d) $1\frac23\div\frac25$ (e) $\frac37\div2\frac17$ (f) $1\frac14\div1\frac78$
exercises.full_solution: Multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor. (a) $\frac58\times\frac43=\frac{20}{24}=\frac56$. (b) $\frac56\times3=\frac{15}{6}=\frac52=2\frac12$. (c) $\frac45\times\frac{10}{7}=\frac{40}{35}=\frac87=1\frac17$. (d) $\frac53\times\frac52=\frac{25}{6}=4\frac16$. (e) $\frac37\times\frac{7}{15}=\frac{21}{105}=\frac15$. (f) $\frac54\times\frac8{15}=\frac{40}{60}=\frac23$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate the following: (a) $\frac34\times\frac45$ (b) $\frac78\times\frac23$ (c) $\frac34\times\frac47\times\frac3{10}$ (d) $\frac45\div\frac23\times\frac7{10}$ (e) $\frac12$ of $\frac34$ (f) $4\frac12\div3\frac19$
exercises.full_solution: (a) $\frac{12}{20}=\frac35$. (b) $\frac{14}{24}=\frac7{12}$. (c) $\frac{36}{280}=\frac9{70}$. (d) working left to right: $\frac45\div\frac23=\frac45\times\frac32=\frac{12}{10}=\frac65$; then $\frac65\times\frac7{10}=\frac{42}{50}=\frac{21}{25}$. (e) $\frac38$. (f) $\frac92\div\frac{28}{9}=\frac92\times\frac9{28}=\frac{81}{56}=1\frac{25}{56}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate the following: (a) $\left(\frac38\times\frac45\right)+\left(\frac12\text{ of }\frac35\right)$ (b) $\left(1\frac12\times3\frac34\right)-\left(2\frac35\div1\frac12\right)$ (c) $\left(\frac35\text{ of }\frac49\right)+\left(\frac49\text{ of }\frac35\right)$ (d) $\left(1\frac13\times2\frac58\right)^2$
exercises.full_solution: (a) $\frac38\times\frac45=\frac{12}{40}=\frac3{10}$; $\frac12\times\frac35=\frac3{10}$; sum $=\frac6{10}=\frac35$. (b) $1\frac12\times3\frac34=\frac32\times\frac{15}4=\frac{45}{8}=5.625$; $2\frac35\div1\frac12=\frac{13}5\div\frac32=\frac{13}5\times\frac23=\frac{26}{15}\approx1.733$; difference $=\frac{45}{8}-\frac{26}{15}=\frac{675}{120}-\frac{208}{120}=\frac{467}{120}=3\frac{47}{120}$. (c) note both terms are equal: $2\times\left(\frac35\times\frac49\right)=2\times\frac{12}{45}=2\times\frac4{15}=\frac8{15}$. (d) $1\frac13\times2\frac58=\frac43\times\frac{21}8=\frac{84}{24}=\frac72$; squared $=\frac{49}4=12\frac14$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Change the following fractions to decimals: (a) $\frac34$ (b) $\frac45$ (c) $\frac9{20}$ (d) $\frac{17}{50}$ (e) $\frac13$ (f) $\frac38$ (g) $\frac7{16}$ (h) $\frac29$ (i) $\frac7{11}$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Change the following mixed numbers to decimals: (a) $2\frac34$ (b) $3\frac35$ (c) $4\frac7{20}$ (d) $6\frac{11}{50}$ (e) $5\frac23$ (f) $6\frac78$ (g) $5\frac9{16}$ (h) $4\frac29$ (i) $5\frac37$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Change the following decimals to fractions: (a) 0.5 (b) 0.7 (c) 0.6 (d) 0.75 (e) 0.825 (f) 0.05 (g) 0.050 (h) 0.402 (i) 0.0002
exercises.full_solution: Write each decimal over the appropriate power of 10, then simplify. (a) $\frac5{10}=\frac12$. (b) $\frac7{10}$. (c) $\frac6{10}=\frac35$. (d) $\frac{75}{100}=\frac34$. (e) $\frac{825}{1000}=\frac{33}{40}$. (f) $\frac5{100}=\frac1{20}$. (g) $0.050=0.05=\frac1{20}$ (the trailing zero does not change the value). (h) $\frac{402}{1000}=\frac{201}{500}$. (i) $\frac2{10000}=\frac1{5000}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Change the following decimals to mixed numbers: (a) 2.4 (b) 6.5 (c) 8.2 (d) 3.75 (e) 10.55 (f) 9.204 (g) 15.455 (h) 30.001 (i) 1.0205
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Convert each of the following recurring decimals to fractions in their simplest form: (a) $0.\dot3$ (b) $0.\dot7$ (c) $0.\dot4\dot2$ (d) $0.\dot6\dot5$
exercises.full_solution: For a single repeating digit, let $x$ equal the decimal, multiply by 10, and subtract; for a two-digit repeating block, multiply by 100. (a) $x=0.333\ldots$, $10x=3.333\ldots$, so $9x=3\Rightarrow x=\frac39=\frac13$. (b) $9x=7\Rightarrow x=\frac79$. (c) $x=0.424242\ldots$, $100x=42.4242\ldots$, $99x=42\Rightarrow x=\frac{42}{99}=\frac{14}{33}$. (d) $99x=65\Rightarrow x=\frac{65}{99}$ (already in lowest terms, since $\gcd(65,99)=1$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Convert each of the following recurring decimals to fractions in their simplest form: (a) $0.0\dot5$ (b) $0.0\dot6\dot2$ (c) $1.0\dot2$ (d) $4.00\dot3\dot8$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Without using a calculator, work out the sum $0.1\dot5+0.0\dot4$ by converting each decimal to a fraction first. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Without using a calculator, evaluate $0.2\dot7-0.10\dot6$ by converting each decimal to a fraction first. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: There are 200 birds in a flock. 120 of them are female. What percentage of the flock are: (a) female? (b) male?
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write these fractions as percentages: (a) $\frac78$ (b) $\frac{11}{15}$ (c) $\frac7{24}$ (d) $\frac17$
exercises.full_solution: Multiply each fraction by 100%. (a) $\frac78\times100=87.5\%$. (b) $\frac{11}{15}\times100=73.33\ldots\%$. (c) $\frac7{24}\times100=29.1\overline6\%$. (d) $\frac17\times100=14.2857\ldots\%$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Convert the following percentages to decimals: (a) 39% (b) 47% (c) 83% (d) 7% (e) 2% (f) 20%
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Convert the following decimals to percentages: (a) 0.31 (b) 0.67 (c) 0.09 (d) 0.05 (e) 0.2 (f) 0.75
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the percentage equivalent of the following fractions: (a) $\frac14$ (b) $\frac23$ (c) $\frac58$ (d) $1\frac45$ (e) $4\frac9{10}$ (f) $3\frac78$
exercises.full_solution: Convert each to an improper fraction if needed and multiply by 100%. (a) $\frac14\times100=25\%$. (b) $\frac23\times100=66.67\%$. (c) $\frac58\times100=62.5\%$. (d) $\frac95\times100=180\%$. (e) $\frac{49}{10}\times100=490\%$. (f) $\frac{31}8\times100=387.5\%$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the decimal equivalent of the following: (a) $\frac34$ (b) 80% (c) $\frac15$ (d) 7% (e) $1\frac78$ (f) $\frac16$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate the following: (a) 25% of 80 (b) 80% of 125 (c) 62.5% of 80 (d) 30% of 120 (e) 90% of 5 (f) 25% of 30
exercises.full_solution: Multiply each quantity by the percentage written as a decimal. (a) $0.25\times80=20$. (b) $0.8\times125=100$. (c) $0.625\times80=50$. (d) $0.3\times120=36$. (e) $0.9\times5=4.5$. (f) $0.25\times30=7.5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Evaluate the following: (a) 17% of 50 (b) 50% of 17 (c) 65% of 80 (d) 80% of 65 (e) 7% of 250 (f) 250% of 7
exercises.full_solution: Note that '$p\%$ of $n$' equals '$n\%$ of $p$', since both equal $\frac{p\times n}{100}$. (a)/(b) $0.17\times50=0.5\times17=8.5$. (c)/(d) $0.65\times80=0.8\times65=52$. (e)/(f) $0.07\times250=2.5\times7=17.5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: In a class of 30 students, 20% have black hair, 10% have blonde hair and 70% have brown hair. Calculate the number of students with: (a) black hair (b) blonde hair (c) brown hair.
exercises.full_solution: Multiply 30 by each percentage. (a) $0.2\times30=6$. (b) $0.1\times30=3$. (c) $0.7\times30=21$. (Check: $6+3+21=30$.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A survey conducted among 120 school children looked at which type of meat they preferred. 55% said they preferred lamb, 20% said they preferred chicken, 15% preferred duck and 10% turkey. Calculate the number of children in each category.
exercises.full_solution: Multiply 120 by each percentage: lamb $=0.55\times120=66$; chicken $=0.2\times120=24$; duck $=0.15\times120=18$; turkey $=0.1\times120=12$. (Check: $66+24+18+12=120$.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A survey was carried out in a school to see what nationality its students were. Of the 220 students in the school, 65% were Australian, 20% were Pakistani, 5% were Greek and 10% belonged to other nationalities. Calculate the number of students of each nationality.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A shopkeeper keeps a record of the number of items he sells in one day. Of the 150 items he sold, 46% were newspapers, 24% were pens, 12% were books while the remaining 18% were other items. Calculate the number of each item he sold.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Express the first quantity as a percentage of the second: (a) 24 out of 50 (b) 46 out of 125 (c) 7 out of 20 (d) 45 out of 90 (e) 9 out of 20 (f) 16 out of 40 (g) 13 out of 39 (h) 20 out of 35
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A hockey team plays 42 matches. It wins 21, draws 14 and loses the rest. Express each of these results as a percentage of the total number of games played.
exercises.full_solution: Losses $=42-21-14=7$. Wins: $\frac{21}{42}\times100=50\%$. Draws: $\frac{14}{42}\times100=33.33\%$. Losses: $\frac{7}{42}\times100=16.67\%$. (Check: these sum to 100%.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Four candidates stood in an election: A received 24500 votes, B received 18200 votes, C received 16300 votes, D received 12000 votes. Express each of these as a percentage of the total votes cast.
exercises.answer: A: $\approx34.5\%$, B: $\approx25.6\%$, C: $\approx23.0\%$, D: $\approx16.9\%$ (all to 1 d.p.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A car manufacturer produces 155000 cars a year, available in six colours. Numbers sold: Red 55000, Blue 48000, White 27500, Silver 10200, Green 9300, Black 5000. Express each of these as a percentage of the total number of cars produced, to 1 d.p.
exercises.answer: Red: 35.5%, Blue: 31.0%, White: 17.7%, Silver: 6.6%, Green: 6.0%, Black: 3.2%
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Increase the following by the given percentage: (a) 150 by 25% (b) 230 by 40% (c) 7000 by 2% (d) 70 by 250% (e) 80 by 12.5% (f) 75 by 62%
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Decrease the following by the given percentage: (a) 120 by 25% (b) 40 by 5% (c) 90 by 90% (d) 1000 by 10% (e) 80 by 37.5% (f) 75 by 42%
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: In the following questions the first number is increased to become the second number. Calculate the percentage increase in each case: (a) $50\to60$ (b) $75\to135$ (c) $40\to84$ (d) $30\to31.5$ (e) $18\to33.3$ (f) $4\to13$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: In the following questions the first number is decreased to become the second number. Calculate the percentage decrease in each case: (a) $50\to25$ (b) $80\to56$ (c) $150\to142.5$ (d) $3\to0$ (e) $550\to352$ (f) $20\to19$
exercises.full_solution: Percentage decrease $=\frac{\text{old}-\text{new}}{\text{old}}\times100\%$. (a) $\frac{25}{50}\times100=50\%$. (b) $\frac{24}{80}\times100=30\%$. (c) $\frac{7.5}{150}\times100=5\%$. (d) $\frac3{3}\times100=100\%$. (e) $\frac{198}{550}\times100=36\%$. (f) $\frac1{20}\times100=5\%$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A farmer increases the yield on his farm by 15%. If his previous yield was 6500 tonnes, what is his present yield?
exercises.full_solution: New yield $=6500\times1.15=7475$ tonnes.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The cost of a computer in a computer store is reduced by 12.5% in a sale. If the computer was priced at \$7800, what is its price in the sale?
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A winter coat is priced at \$100. In the sale, its price is reduced by 25%. (a) Calculate the sale price of the coat. (b) After the sale, its price is increased by 25% again. Calculate the coat's price after the sale.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $100\times0.75=\$75$. (b) $75\times1.25=\$93.75$ — note this is less than the original \$100, because the 25% increase is applied to the smaller, already-discounted price.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A farmer takes 250 chickens to be sold at a market. In the first hour, he sells 8% of his chickens. In the second hour, he sells 10% of those that were left. (a) How many chickens has he sold in total? (b) What percentage of the original number did he manage to sell in the two hours?
exercises.full_solution: First hour: $0.08\times250=20$ sold, leaving $250-20=230$. Second hour: $0.10\times230=23$ sold. (a) Total sold $=20+23=43$. (b) $\frac{43}{250}\times100=17.2\%$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The number of fish on a fish farm increases by approximately 10% each month. If there were originally 350 fish, calculate to the nearest 100 how many fish there would be after 12 months.
exercises.full_solution: After 12 months of compound 10% growth: $350\times1.1^{12}=350\times3.138\ldots\approx1098.4$, which rounds to 1100 fish to the nearest 100.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the value of $X$ in each of the following: (a) 40% of $X$ is 240 (b) 24% of $X$ is 84 (c) 85% of $X$ is 765 (d) 4% of $X$ is 10 (e) 15% of $X$ is 18.75 (f) 7% of $X$ is 0.105
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the value of $Y$ in each of the following: (a) 125% of $Y$ is 70 (b) 140% of $Y$ is 91 (c) 210% of $Y$ is 189 (d) 340% of $Y$ is 68 (e) 150% of $Y$ is 0.375 (f) 144% of $Y$ is $-54.72$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: In a geography textbook, 35% of the pages are coloured. If there are 98 coloured pages, how many pages are there in the whole book?
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A town has 3500 families who own a car. If this represents 28% of the families in the town, how many families are there in total?
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: In a test, Isabel scored 88%. If she got three questions incorrect, how many did she get correct?
exercises.full_solution: The 3 incorrect questions represent $100\%-88\%=12\%$ of the total, so the total number of questions is $3\div0.12=25$. She got correct $25-3=22$ questions.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Water expands when it freezes. If the increase in volume is 4%, what volume of water will make an iceberg of $12\,700\,000\,\text{m}^3$? Give your answer to three significant figures.
exercises.full_solution: The iceberg's volume is 104% of the original water volume $V$: $1.04V=12\,700\,000\Rightarrow V=\frac{12\,700\,000}{1.04}=12\,211\,538.46\ldots\,\text{m}^3\approx12\,200\,000\,\text{m}^3$ to 3 s.f.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find 40% of 1600 m.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A shop increases the price of a television set by 8%. If the present price is \$320, what is the new price?
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A car loses 55% of its value after four years. If it cost \$22500 when new, what is its value after the four years?
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Express the first quantity as a percentage of the second: (a) 40 cm, 2 m (b) 25 mins, 1 hour (c) 450 g, 2 kg (d) 3 m, 3.5 m (e) 70 kg, 1 tonne (f) 75 cl, 2.5 l
exercises.full_solution: Convert both quantities to the same unit before dividing. (a) $2\,\text{m}=200\,\text{cm}$: $\frac{40}{200}\times100=20\%$. (b) $1$ hour $=60$ min: $\frac{25}{60}\times100=41.67\%$. (c) $2\,\text{kg}=2000\,\text{g}$: $\frac{450}{2000}\times100=22.5\%$. (d) $\frac3{3.5}\times100=85.71\%$. (e) $1$ tonne $=1000\,\text{kg}$: $\frac{70}{1000}\times100=7\%$. (f) $2.5\,\text{l}=250\,\text{cl}$: $\frac{75}{250}\times100=30\%$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A house is bought for \$75000 and then resold for \$87000. Calculate the percentage profit.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A pair of shoes is priced at \$45. During a sale the price is reduced by 20%. (a) Calculate the sale price of the shoes. (b) What is the percentage increase in the price if after the sale it is once again restored to \$45?
exercises.full_solution: (a) Sale price $=45\times0.8=\$36$. (b) Increase needed $=45-36=\$9$; percentage increase $=\frac{9}{36}\times100=25\%$ (note this is larger than the original 20% decrease, since it is calculated on the smaller sale price).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A machine prints four books in 10 minutes. How many will it print in 2 hours?
exercises.full_solution: Rate $=\frac{4}{10}$ books per minute. In 2 hours $=120$ minutes: $\frac4{10}\times120=48$ books.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A farmer plants five apple trees in 25 minutes. If he continues to work at a constant rate, how long will it take him to plant 200 trees?
exercises.full_solution: Rate $=\frac{25}{5}=5$ minutes per tree. For 200 trees: $200\times5=1000$ minutes $=16\frac23$ hours.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A television set uses 3 units of electricity in 2 hours. How many units will it use in 7 hours? Give your answer to the nearest unit.
exercises.full_solution: Rate $=\frac32$ units per hour. In 7 hours: $\frac32\times7=10.5$, which rounds to 11 units to the nearest whole unit.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A bricklayer lays 1500 bricks in an 8-hour day. Assuming he continues to work at the same rate, calculate: (a) how many bricks he would expect to lay in a five-day week, (b) how long to the nearest hour it would take him to lay 10000 bricks.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $1500\times5=7500$ bricks. (b) Rate $=\frac{1500}{8}=187.5$ bricks per hour; time for 10000 bricks $=\frac{10000}{187.5}=53.33$ hours $\approx53$ hours.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A machine used to paint white lines on a road uses 250 litres of paint for each 8 km of road marked. Calculate: (a) how many litres of paint would be needed for 200 km of road, (b) what length of road could be marked with 4000 litres of paint.
exercises.full_solution: Rate $=\frac{250}{8}$ litres per km. (a) $\frac{250}{8}\times200=6250$ litres. (b) Length $=\frac{4000}{250}\times8=128$ km.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: An aircraft is cruising at 720 km/h and covers 1000 km. How far would it travel in the same period of time if the speed increased to 800 km/h?
exercises.full_solution: Time taken at 720 km/h for 1000 km: $t=\frac{1000}{720}$ hours. At 800 km/h, distance $=800\times\frac{1000}{720}=\frac{800000}{720}\approx1111.1$ km.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A production line travelling at 2 m/s labels 150 tins. In the same period of time how many will it label at: (a) 6 m/s (b) 1 m/s (c) 1.6 m/s?
exercises.full_solution: Rate $=\frac{150}{2}=75$ tins per (m/s) of speed, since the number labelled is directly proportional to speed over a fixed time period. (a) $75\times6=450$. (b) $75\times1=75$. (c) $75\times1.6=120$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A car travels at an average speed of 80 km/h for 6 hours. (a) How far will it travel in the 6 hours? (b) What average speed will it need to travel at in order to cover the same distance in 5 hours?
exercises.full_solution: (a) Distance $=80\times6=480$ km. (b) Speed needed $=\frac{480}{5}=96$ km/h.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Sand and gravel are mixed in the ratio 5:3 to form ballast. (a) How much gravel is mixed with 750 kg of sand? (b) How much sand is mixed with 750 kg of gravel?
exercises.full_solution: (a) $\frac35\times750=450$ kg of gravel. (b) $\frac53\times750=1250$ kg of sand.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A recipe uses 150 g butter, 500 g flour, 50 g sugar and 100 g currants to make 18 small cakes. (a) How much of each ingredient will be needed to make 72 cakes? (b) How many whole cakes could be made with 1 kg of butter?
exercises.answer: (a) Butter 600 g, flour 2000 g, sugar 200 g, currants 400 g. (b) 120 cakes.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Scale factor $=\frac{72}{18}=4$: butter $150\times4=600$ g, flour $500\times4=2000$ g, sugar $50\times4=200$ g, currants $100\times4=400$ g. (b) $1\,\text{kg}=1000$ g of butter makes $\frac{1000}{150}\times18=120$ cakes.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A paint mix uses red and white paint in a ratio of 1:12. (a) How much white paint will be needed to mix with 1.4 litres of red paint? (b) If a total of 15.5 litres of paint is mixed, calculate the amount of white paint and the amount of red paint used. Give your answers to the nearest 0.1 litre.
exercises.full_solution: (a) White $=1.4\times12=16.8$ litres. (b) The ratio $1:12$ gives 13 parts total; 1 part $=\frac{15.5}{13}\approx1.1923$ litres; red (1 part) $\approx1.2$ litres, white (12 parts) $\approx14.3$ litres (check: $1.2+14.3=15.5$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A tulip farmer sells sacks of mixed bulbs, packaged in a ratio of red to yellow of 8:5. (a) If a sack contains 200 red bulbs, calculate the number of yellow bulbs. (b) If a sack contains 351 bulbs in total, how many of each colour would you expect to find? (c) One sack is packaged with a bulb mixture in the ratio 7:5 by mistake. If the sack contains 624 bulbs, how many more yellow bulbs would you expect to have compared with a normal sack of 624 bulbs?
exercises.answer: (a) 125 yellow bulbs. (b) Red 216, yellow 135. (c) 20 more yellow bulbs.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $\frac58\times200=125$. (b) $8+5=13$ parts: red $=\frac8{13}\times351=216$, yellow $=\frac5{13}\times351=135$. (c) Normal ratio (8:5, 13 parts) on 624 bulbs gives yellow $=\frac5{13}\times624=240$; mistaken ratio (7:5, 12 parts) gives yellow $=\frac5{12}\times624=260$; difference $=260-240=20$ more yellow bulbs.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A pure fruit juice is made by mixing the juices of oranges and mangoes in the ratio of 9:2. (a) If 189 litres of orange juice are used, calculate the number of litres of mango juice needed. (b) If 605 litres of the juice are made, calculate the number of litres of orange juice and mango juice used.
exercises.answer: (a) 42 litres of mango juice. (b) Orange juice 495 litres, mango juice 110 litres.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $\frac29\times189=42$ litres. (b) $9+2=11$ parts; 1 part $=\frac{605}{11}=55$ litres; orange $=9\times55=495$ litres, mango $=2\times55=110$ litres.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Divide 150 in the ratio 2:3.
exercises.full_solution: $2+3=5$ parts; 1 part $=\frac{150}5=30$. So the shares are $2\times30=60$ and $3\times30=90$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Divide 72 in the ratio 2:3:4.
exercises.full_solution: $2+3+4=9$ parts; 1 part $=\frac{72}9=8$. Shares: $2\times8=16$, $3\times8=24$, $4\times8=32$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Divide 5 kg in the ratio 13:7.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Divide 45 minutes in the ratio 2:3.
exercises.full_solution: $2+3=5$ parts; 1 part $=\frac{45}5=9$ minutes. Shares: $2\times9=18$, $3\times9=27$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Divide 1 hour in the ratio 1:5.
exercises.full_solution: 1 hour $=60$ minutes; $1+5=6$ parts; 1 part $=10$ minutes. Shares: $1\times10=10$ minutes, $5\times10=50$ minutes.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: $\frac78$ of a can of drink is water, the rest is syrup. What is the ratio of water to syrup?
exercises.full_solution: Syrup fraction $=1-\frac78=\frac18$. Ratio water:syrup $=\frac78:\frac18=7:1$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: $\frac59$ of a litre carton of orange is pure orange juice, the rest is water. How many millilitres of each are in the carton?
exercises.full_solution: 1 litre $=1000$ ml. Orange juice $=\frac59\times1000=\frac{5000}9\approx555.6$ ml. Water $=\frac49\times1000=\frac{4000}9\approx444.4$ ml.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: 55% of students in a school are boys. (a) What is the ratio of boys to girls? (b) How many boys and how many girls are there if the school has 800 students?
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A piece of wood is cut in the ratio 2:3. What fraction of the length is the longer piece?
exercises.full_solution: Total parts $=2+3=5$; the longer piece is 3 parts, i.e. $\frac35$ of the total length.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: If the piece of wood in Question 9 is 80 cm long, how long is the shorter piece?
exercises.full_solution: The shorter piece is $\frac25$ of the length: $\frac25\times80=32$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A gas pipe is 7 km long. A valve is positioned in such a way that it divides the length of the pipe in the ratio 4:3. Calculate the distance of the valve from each end of the pipe.
exercises.answer: 4 km from one end, 3 km from the other.
exercises.full_solution: $4+3=7$ parts; 1 part $=\frac77=1$ km. Distances: $4\times1=4$ km from one end, $3\times1=3$ km from the other end.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The size of the angles of a quadrilateral are in the ratio 1:2:3:3. Calculate the size of each angle.
exercises.full_solution: Angles of a quadrilateral sum to $360^\circ$. Total parts $=1+2+3+3=9$; 1 part $=\frac{360}9=40^\circ$. Angles: $40^\circ, 80^\circ, 120^\circ, 120^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 3:5:4. Calculate the size of each angle.
exercises.full_solution: Angles of a triangle sum to $180^\circ$. Total parts $=3+5+4=12$; 1 part $=\frac{180}{12}=15^\circ$. Angles: $3\times15=45^\circ$, $5\times15=75^\circ$, $4\times15=60^\circ$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A millionaire leaves 1.4 million dollars in his will to be shared between his three children in the ratio of their ages. If they are 24, 28 and 32 years old, calculate to the nearest dollar the amount they will each receive.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A small company makes a profit of \$8000. This is divided between the directors in the ratio of their initial investments. If Alex put \$20000 into the firm, Maria \$35000 and Ahmet \$25000, calculate the amount of the profit they will each receive.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A teacher shares sweets among 8 students so that they get 6 each. How many sweets would they each have had if there had been 12 students?
exercises.full_solution: Total sweets $=8\times6=48$ (inverse proportion: more students means fewer sweets each). With 12 students: $\frac{48}{12}=4$ sweets each.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The table below represents the inversely proportional relationship between the speed and the time taken for a train to travel between two stations (speed $\times$ time = constant). Speed (km/h): 60, ?, ?, 120, 90, 50, 10. Time (h): 2, 3, 4, ?, ?, ?, ?. Copy and complete the table.
exercises.full_solution: Since speed $\times$ time is constant, the constant $=60\times2=120$ (km, the distance between the stations). For time $=3$: speed $=120\div3=40$. For time $=4$: speed $=120\div4=30$. For speed $=120$: time $=120\div120=1$. For speed $=90$: time $=120\div90=1\frac13$ h. For speed $=50$: time $=120\div50=2.4$ h. For speed $=10$: time $=120\div10=12$ h.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Six people can dig a trench in 8 hours. (a) How long would it take: (i) 4 people (ii) 12 people (iii) 1 person? (b) How many people would it take to dig the trench in: (i) 3 hours (ii) 16 hours (iii) 1 hour?
exercises.answer: (a)(i) 12 hours (ii) 4 hours (iii) 48 hours. (b)(i) 16 people (ii) 3 people (iii) 48 people.
exercises.full_solution: The total work is $6\times8=48$ person-hours (inverse proportion between people and time). (a) (i) $48\div4=12$ h. (ii) $48\div12=4$ h. (iii) $48\div1=48$ h. (b) (i) $48\div3=16$ people. (ii) $48\div16=3$ people. (iii) $48\div1=48$ people.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Chairs in a hall are arranged in 35 rows of 18. (a) How many rows would there be with 21 chairs to a row? (b) How many chairs would there be in each row if there were 15 rows?
exercises.full_solution: Total chairs $=35\times18=630$ (fixed total, inverse proportion between rows and chairs per row). (a) $630\div21=30$ rows. (b) $630\div15=42$ chairs per row.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A train travelling at 100 km/h takes 4 hours for a journey. How long would it take a train travelling at 60 km/h?
exercises.full_solution: Distance $=100\times4=400$ km. At 60 km/h: time $=\frac{400}{60}=6\frac23$ hours.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A worker in a sugar factory packs 24 cardboard boxes with 15 bags of sugar in each. If he had boxes which held 18 bags of sugar each, how many fewer boxes would be needed?
exercises.full_solution: Total bags $=24\times15=360$. With 18 bags per box: $360\div18=20$ boxes needed, which is $24-20=4$ fewer boxes.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A swimming pool is filled in 30 hours by two identical pumps. How much quicker would it be filled if five similar pumps were used instead?
exercises.answer: 18 hours quicker (filled in 12 hours instead of 30).
exercises.full_solution: Total pump-hours needed $=2\times30=60$. With 5 pumps: time $=60\div5=12$ hours, which is $30-12=18$ hours quicker.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Increase 100 by the following ratios: (a) 8:5 (b) 5:2 (c) 7:4 (d) 11:10 (e) 9:4 (f) 32:25
exercises.full_solution: Multiply 100 by each ratio (first term over second). (a) $100\times\frac85=160$. (b) $100\times\frac52=250$. (c) $100\times\frac74=175$. (d) $100\times\frac{11}{10}=110$. (e) $100\times\frac94=225$. (f) $100\times\frac{32}{25}=128$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Increase 70 by the following ratios: (a) 4:3 (b) 5:3 (c) 8:7 (d) 9:4 (e) 11:5 (f) 17:14
exercises.full_solution: Multiply 70 by each ratio. (a) $70\times\frac43=93.33$. (b) $70\times\frac53=116.67$. (c) $70\times\frac87=80$. (d) $70\times\frac94=157.5$. (e) $70\times\frac{11}5=154$. (f) $70\times\frac{17}{14}=85$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Decrease 60 by the following ratios: (a) 2:3 (b) 5:6 (c) 7:12 (d) 3:5 (e) 1:4 (f) 13:15
exercises.full_solution: Multiply 60 by each ratio. (a) $60\times\frac23=40$. (b) $60\times\frac56=50$. (c) $60\times\frac7{12}=35$. (d) $60\times\frac35=36$. (e) $60\times\frac14=15$. (f) $60\times\frac{13}{15}=52$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Decrease 30 by the following ratios: (a) 3:4 (b) 2:9 (c) 7:12 (d) 3:16 (e) 5:8 (f) 9:20
exercises.full_solution: Multiply 30 by each ratio. (a) $30\times\frac34=22.5$. (b) $30\times\frac29=6.67$. (c) $30\times\frac7{12}=17.5$. (d) $30\times\frac3{16}=5.625$. (e) $30\times\frac58=18.75$. (f) $30\times\frac9{20}=13.5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Increase 40 by a ratio of 5:4.
exercises.full_solution: $40\times\frac54=50$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Decrease 40 by a ratio of 4:5.
exercises.full_solution: $40\times\frac45=32$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Increase 150 by a ratio of 7:5.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Decrease 210 by a ratio of 3:7.
exercises.full_solution: $210\times\frac37=90$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A photograph measuring 8 cm by 6 cm is enlarged by a ratio of 11:4. What are the dimensions of the new print?
exercises.full_solution: Multiply each dimension by $\frac{11}4$: $8\times\frac{11}4=22$ cm, $6\times\frac{11}4=16.5$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A photocopier enlarges in the ratio 7:4. What would be the new size of a diagram measuring 16 cm by 12 cm?
exercises.full_solution: Multiply each dimension by $\frac74$: $16\times\frac74=28$ cm, $12\times\frac74=21$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A drawing measuring 10 cm by 16 cm needs to be enlarged. The dimensions of the enlargement need to be 25 cm by 40 cm. Calculate the enlargement needed and express it as a ratio.
exercises.answer: A ratio of 5:2 (i.e. a scale factor of 2.5).
exercises.full_solution: Scale factor $=\frac{25}{10}=\frac{40}{16}=2.5=\frac52$, so the enlargement ratio is 5:2.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A banner needs to be enlarged from its original format. The dimensions of the original are 4 cm tall by 25 cm wide. The enlarged banner needs to be at least 8 m wide but no more than 1.4 m tall. Calculate the minimum and maximum ratios of enlargement possible.
exercises.full_solution: Minimum enlargement (to reach at least 8 m $=800$ cm wide from 25 cm): $\frac{800}{25}=32$, i.e. ratio 32:1. Maximum enlargement (so height does not exceed 1.4 m $=140$ cm from 4 cm): $\frac{140}4=35$, i.e. ratio 35:1. So the enlargement ratio must be between 32:1 and 35:1 inclusive.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A rectangle measuring 7 cm by 4 cm is enlarged by a ratio of 2:1. (a) What is the area of: (i) the original rectangle? (ii) the enlarged rectangle? (b) By what ratio has the area been enlarged?
exercises.full_solution: (a)(i) $7\times4=28\,\text{cm}^2$. (ii) Enlarged rectangle is $14\,\text{cm}\times8\,\text{cm}$, area $=112\,\text{cm}^2$. (b) $\frac{112}{28}=4$, i.e. the area ratio is $4:1=2^2:1$ (the square of the linear ratio).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A square of side length 3 cm is enlarged by a ratio of 3:1. (a) What is the area of: (i) the original square? (ii) the enlarged square? (b) By what ratio has the area been enlarged?
exercises.full_solution: (a)(i) $3\times3=9\,\text{cm}^2$. (ii) Enlarged side $=9$ cm, area $=81\,\text{cm}^2$. (b) $\frac{81}9=9$, i.e. ratio $9:1=3^2:1$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A cuboid measuring 3 cm by 5 cm by 2 cm is enlarged by a ratio of 2:1. (a) What is the volume of: (i) the original cuboid? (ii) the enlarged cuboid? (b) By what ratio has the volume been increased?
exercises.full_solution: (a)(i) $3\times5\times2=30\,\text{cm}^3$. (ii) Enlarged cuboid is $6\times10\times4$, volume $=240\,\text{cm}^3$. (b) $\frac{240}{30}=8$, i.e. ratio $8:1=2^3:1$ (the cube of the linear ratio).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A cube of side 4 cm is enlarged by a ratio of 3:1. (a) What is the volume of: (i) the original cube? (ii) the enlarged cube? (b) By what ratio has the volume been increased?
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The triangle shown (a right-angled triangle with base 8 cm and height 4 cm) is to be reduced by a ratio of 1:2. (a) Calculate the area of the original triangle. (b) Calculate the area of the reduced triangle. (c) Calculate the ratio by which the area of the triangle has been reduced.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Area $=\frac12\times8\times4=16\,\text{cm}^2$. (b) Reduced triangle has base 4 cm and height 2 cm: area $=\frac12\times4\times2=4\,\text{cm}^2$. (c) $\frac{4}{16}=\frac14$, i.e. ratio $1:4=1^2:2^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: From questions 5-9, can you conclude what happens to two- and three-dimensional figures when they are either enlarged or reduced?
exercises.answer: When a 2D figure's linear dimensions are scaled by a ratio $k:1$, its area is scaled by $k^2:1$. When a 3D figure's linear dimensions are scaled by $k:1$, its volume is scaled by $k^3:1$.
exercises.full_solution: This follows from the pattern observed in Q5-Q9: a linear enlargement of ratio 2:1 gave an area ratio of 4:1 ($=2^2$) and a volume ratio of 8:1 ($=2^3$); a linear ratio of 3:1 gave an area ratio of 9:1 ($=3^2$) and a volume ratio of 27:1 ($=3^3$); a linear reduction of 1:2 gave an area ratio of 1:4 ($=1^2:2^2$). In general, area scales with the square, and volume with the cube, of the linear scale factor.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Aluminium has a density of $2900\,\text{kg/m}^3$. A construction company needs four cubic metres of aluminium. Calculate the mass of the aluminium needed.
exercises.full_solution: Mass $=$ density $\times$ volume $=2900\times4=11600$ kg.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A marathon race is 42195 m in length. The world record in 2016 was 2 hrs, 2 mins and 57 seconds, held by Dennis Kimetto of Kenya. (a) How many seconds in total did Kimetto take to complete the race? (b) Calculate his average speed in m/s for the race, to 2 d.p. (c) What average speed would the runner need to maintain to complete the marathon in under two hours?
exercises.answer: (a) 7377 seconds. (b) 5.72 m/s. (c) Just over $5.86\,\text{m/s}$ (more precisely, greater than $\frac{42195}{7200}\approx5.86\,\text{m/s}$).
exercises.full_solution: (a) $2\times3600+2\times60+57=7200+120+57=7377$ seconds. (b) Speed $=\frac{42195}{7377}=5.7194\ldots\approx5.72$ m/s. (c) Under 2 hours means under $7200$ seconds, so speed must exceed $\frac{42195}{7200}=5.8604\ldots\approx5.86$ m/s.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The approximate densities of four metals in g/cm³ are: Aluminium 2.9, Brass 8.8, Copper 9.3, Steel 8.2. A cube of an unknown metal has side lengths of 5 cm. The mass of the cube is 1.1 kg. (a) By calculating the cube's density, determine which metal the cube is likely to be made from. Another cube made of steel has a mass of 4.0 kg. (b) Calculate the length of each of the sides of the steel cube, to 1 d.p.
exercises.answer: (a) Density $=8.8\,\text{g/cm}^3$, so the cube is likely brass. (b) Side length $\approx7.9$ cm.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Volume of cube $=5^3=125\,\text{cm}^3$; mass $=1.1\,\text{kg}=1100$ g; density $=\frac{1100}{125}=8.8\,\text{g/cm}^3$, matching brass exactly. (b) For the steel cube: $4.0\,\text{kg}=4000$ g; volume $=\frac{4000}{8.2}=487.8\,\text{cm}^3$; side $=\sqrt[3]{487.8}\approx7.9$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Singapore is the country with the highest population density in the world. Its population is 5535000 and it has a total area of $719\,\text{km}^2$. (a) Calculate Singapore's population density. China is the country with the largest population. (b) Explain why China has not got the world's highest population density. (c) Find the area and population of your own country. Calculate your country's population density.
exercises.answer: (a) Approximately $7698\,\text{people/km}^2$. (b) Because population density is population divided by area — China's enormous land area (about $9.6$ million km²) means that even its very large population (around 1.4 billion) is spread much more thinly than Singapore's population over its tiny area, giving China a far lower density. (c) This part is open-ended and depends on the student's own country; no single numeric answer applies.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $\frac{5535000}{719}=7698.2\ldots\approx7698$ people per km². (b) Population density depends on the ratio of population to area, not on population alone; since China's area is vastly larger than Singapore's, its density (population $\div$ area) is much lower even though its total population is larger. (c) Not computable here as no specific country was given in this sub-part; a student would substitute their own country's population and area into density $=$ population $\div$ area.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A farmer has a rectangular field measuring 600 m $\times$ 800 m. He uses the field for grazing his sheep. (a) Calculate the area of the field in km². (b) 40 sheep graze in the field. Calculate the population density of sheep in the field, in sheep/km². (c) Guidelines for keeping sheep state that the maximum population density for grazing sheep is 180/km². Calculate the number of sheep the farmer is allowed to graze in his field.
exercises.answer: (a) $0.48\,\text{km}^2$. (b) $\approx83.3\,\text{sheep/km}^2$. (c) 86 sheep (maximum, since the number of sheep must be a whole number).
exercises.full_solution: (a) Area $=600\times800=480\,000\,\text{m}^2=\frac{480\,000}{1\,000\,000}=0.48\,\text{km}^2$. (b) Density $=\frac{40}{0.48}=83.33\,\text{sheep/km}^2$. (c) Maximum number $=180\times0.48=86.4$, which must be rounded down to 86 whole sheep to stay within the guideline.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The formula linking pressure ($P\,\text{N/m}^2$), force ($F$ N) and surface area ($A\,\text{m}^2$) is given as $P=F/A$. A square-based box exerts a force of 160 N on a floor. If the pressure on the floor is $1000\,\text{N/m}^2$, calculate the length, in cm, of each side of the base of the box.
exercises.full_solution: $A=\frac{F}{P}=\frac{160}{1000}=0.16\,\text{m}^2$. Since the base is square, side $=\sqrt{0.16}=0.4$ m $=40$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Using indices, simplify the following expressions: (a) $3\times3\times3$ (b) $2\times2\times2\times2\times2$ (c) $4\times4$ (d) $6\times6\times6\times6$ (e) $8\times8\times8\times8\times8\times8$ (f) $5$
exercises.full_solution: Each expression is a single number repeatedly multiplied by itself, so it is written as that number raised to the power equal to the count of factors. (a) three 3's $=3^3$. (b) five 2's $=2^5$. (c) two 4's $=4^2$. (d) four 6's $=6^4$. (e) six 8's $=8^6$. (f) a single factor of 5 is $5^1=5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify the following using indices: (a) $2\times2\times2\times3\times3$ (b) $4\times4\times4\times4\times4\times5\times5$ (c) $3\times3\times4\times4\times4\times5\times5$ (d) $2\times7\times7\times7\times7$ (e) $1\times1\times6\times6$ (f) $3\times3\times3\times4\times4\times6\times6\times6\times6\times6$
exercises.full_solution: Group repeated factors of each distinct base and count how many times each appears, writing each group as that base raised to the count. (a) three 2's and two 3's $=2^3\times3^2$. (b) five 4's and two 5's $=4^5\times5^2$. (c) two 3's, three 4's, two 5's $=3^2\times4^3\times5^2$. (d) one 2 and four 7's $=2\times7^4$. (e) two 1's and two 6's $=1^2\times6^2=6^2$. (f) three 3's, two 4's, five 6's $=3^3\times4^2\times6^5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write out the following in full: (a) $4^2$ (b) $5^7$ (c) $3^5$ (d) $4^3\times6^3$ (e) $7^2\times2^7$ (f) $3^2\times4^3\times2^4$
exercises.full_solution: Writing a power 'in full' means expanding it back into repeated multiplication, the reverse of index notation: the base is written as a factor as many times as the index states. (a) $4^2=4\times4$. (b) $5^7=5\times5\times5\times5\times5\times5\times5$ (seven 5's). (c) $3^5=3\times3\times3\times3\times3$ (five 3's). (d) $4^3\times6^3$ expands to three 4's times three 6's. (e) $7^2\times2^7$ expands to two 7's times seven 2's. (f) $3^2\times4^3\times2^4$ expands to two 3's, three 4's and four 2's.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Without using a calculator work out the value of the following: (a) $2^5$ (b) $3^4$ (c) $8^2$ (d) $6^3$ (e) $10^6$ (f) $4^4$ (g) $2^3\times3^2$ (h) $10^3\times5^3$
exercises.full_solution: Evaluate each power by repeated multiplication. (a) $2^5=2\times2\times2\times2\times2=32$. (b) $3^4=3\times3\times3\times3=81$. (c) $8^2=8\times8=64$. (d) $6^3=6\times6\times6=216$. (e) $10^6=1\,000\,000$. (f) $4^4=4\times4\times4\times4=256$. (g) $2^3\times3^2=8\times9=72$. (h) $10^3\times5^3=1000\times125=125\,000$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify the following using indices: (a) $3^2\times3^4$ (b) $8^5\times8^2$ (c) $5^2\times5^4\times5^3$ (d) $4^3\times4^5\times4^2$ (e) $2^1\times2^3$ (f) $6^2\times3^2\times3^3\times6^4$ (g) $4^5\times4^3\times5^5\times5^4\times6^2$ (h) $2^4\times5^7\times5^3\times6^2\times6^6$
exercises.full_solution: Using the first law of indices $a^m\times a^n=a^{m+n}$ for matching bases, and treating different bases separately: (a) $3^{2+4}=3^6$. (b) $8^{5+2}=8^7$. (c) $5^{2+4+3}=5^9$. (d) $4^{3+5+2}=4^{10}$. (e) $2^{1+3}=2^4$. (f) group base 6: $6^{2+4}=6^6$; base 3: $3^{2+3}=3^5$; result $6^6\times3^5$. (g) base 4: $4^{5+3}=4^8$; base 5: $5^{5+4}=5^9$; base 6: $6^2$; result $4^8\times5^9\times6^2$. (h) base 2: $2^4$; base 5: $5^{7+3}=5^{10}$; base 6: $6^{2+6}=6^8$; result $2^4\times5^{10}\times6^8$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Simplify the following: (a) $\dfrac{2^2\times2^4}{2^3}$ (b) $\dfrac{3^4\times3^2}{3^5}$ (c) $\dfrac{5^6\times5^7}{5^2\times5^8}$ (d) $\dfrac{(4^2)^5\times4^2}{4^7}$ (e) $\dfrac{4^4\times2^5\times4^2}{4^3\times2^3}$ (f) $\dfrac{6^3\times6^3\times8^5\times8^6}{8^6\times6^2}$ (g) $\dfrac{(5^5)^2\times(4^4)^3}{5^8\times4^9}$ (h) $\dfrac{(6^3)^4\times6^3\times4^9}{6^8\times4^8}$

exercises.statement: Without using a calculator, evaluate the following: (a) $2^3\times2^0$ (b) $5^2\div6^0$ (c) $5^2\times5^{-2}$ (d) $6^3\times6^{-3}$ (e) $(4^0)^2$ (f) $4^0\div2^2$

exercises.statement: Without using a calculator, evaluate the following: (a) $4^{-1}$ (b) $3^{-2}$ (c) $6\times10^{-2}$ (d) $5\times10^{-3}$ (e) $100\times10^{-2}$ (f) $10^{-3}$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Without using a calculator, evaluate the following: (a) $9\times3^{-2}$ (b) $16\times2^{-3}$ (c) $64\times2^{-4}$ (d) $4\times2^{-3}$ (e) $36\times6^{-3}$ (f) $100\times10^{-1}$
exercises.full_solution: Write each negative-index term as a fraction then multiply. (a) $9\times\frac{1}{9}=1$. (b) $16\times\frac18=2$. (c) $64\times\frac{1}{16}=4$. (d) $4\times\frac18=\frac12$. (e) $36\times\frac{1}{216}=\frac{36}{216}=\frac16$. (f) $100\times\frac{1}{10}=10$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Without using a calculator, evaluate the following: (a) $\dfrac{3}{2^{-2}}$ (b) $\dfrac{4}{2^{-3}}$ (c) $\dfrac{9}{5^{-2}}$ (d) $\dfrac{5}{4^{-2}}$ (e) $\dfrac{7^{-3}}{7^{-4}}$ (f) $\dfrac{8^{-6}}{8^{-8}}$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find the value of $x$ in each of the following: (a) $2^x=4$ (b) $2^x=16$ (c) $4^x=64$ (d) $10^x=1000$ (e) $5^x=625$ (f) $3^x=1$
exercises.full_solution: Express the right-hand side as a power of the same base as the left, then equate indices. (a) $4=2^2\Rightarrow x=2$. (b) $16=2^4\Rightarrow x=4$. (c) $64=4^3\Rightarrow x=3$. (d) $1000=10^3\Rightarrow x=3$. (e) $625=5^4\Rightarrow x=4$. (f) $1=3^0\Rightarrow x=0$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.full_solution: (a) $8=2^3\Rightarrow z-1=3\Rightarrow z=4$. (b) $27=3^3\Rightarrow z+2=3\Rightarrow z=1$. (c) $64=4^3\Rightarrow2z=3\Rightarrow z=1.5$. (d) $1=10^0\Rightarrow z+1=0\Rightarrow z=-1$. (e) $9^{(z-1)}=3^{2(z-1)}$, so $z=2(z-1)=2z-2\Rightarrow z=2$. (f) $125^z=5^{3z}$, so $z=3z\Rightarrow2z=0\Rightarrow z=0$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find the value of $n$ in each of the following: (a) $\left(\frac12\right)^n=8$ (b) $\left(\frac13\right)^n=81$ (c) $\left(\frac12\right)^n=32$ (d) $\left(\frac12\right)^n=4^{(n+1)}$ (e) $\left(\frac12\right)^{(n+1)}=2$ (f) $\left(\frac{1}{16}\right)^n=4$
exercises.full_solution: Rewrite $\left(\frac1a\right)^n=a^{-n}$ and match powers of the same prime base. (a) $8=2^3=(\frac12)^{-3}\Rightarrow n=-3$. (b) $81=3^4=(\frac13)^{-4}\Rightarrow n=-4$. (c) $32=2^5=(\frac12)^{-5}\Rightarrow n=-5$. (d) $(\frac12)^n=2^{-n}$ and $4^{(n+1)}=2^{2n+2}$, so $-n=2n+2\Rightarrow-3n=2\Rightarrow n=-\frac23$. (e) $(\frac12)^{(n+1)}=2^{-(n+1)}=2^1\Rightarrow-(n+1)=1\Rightarrow n=-2$. (f) $\frac{1}{16}=2^{-4}$ and $4=2^2$, so $(2^{-4})^n=2^2\Rightarrow-4n=2\Rightarrow n=-0.5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.full_solution: Express the right-hand side as a power of the same base, matching a negative or positive index as needed. (a) $27=3^3\Rightarrow-x=3\Rightarrow x=-3$. (b) $128=2^7\Rightarrow-x=7\Rightarrow x=-7$. (c) $64=2^6\Rightarrow-x+3=6\Rightarrow x=-3$. (d) $\frac{1}{16}=4^{-2}\Rightarrow-x=-2\Rightarrow x=2$. (e) $\frac{1}{256}=2^{-8}\Rightarrow-x=-8\Rightarrow x=8$. (f) $\frac{1}{81}=3^{-4}\Rightarrow-x+1=-4\Rightarrow x=5$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Which of the following are not in standard form? (a) $6.2\times10^5$ (b) $7.834\times10^{16}$ (c) $8.0\times10^5$ (d) $0.46\times10^7$ (e) $82.3\times10^6$ (f) $6.75\times10^1$
exercises.answer: Not in standard form: (d) $0.46\times10^7$ and (e) $82.3\times10^6$. The rest, (a), (b), (c) and (f), are in standard form.
exercises.full_solution: A number is in standard form $A\times10^n$ only if $1\le A<10$. (a) $A=6.2$: valid. (b) $A=7.834$: valid. (c) $A=8.0$: valid. (d) $A=0.46<1$: not valid. (e) $A=82.3\ge10$: not valid. (f) $A=6.75$: valid.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the following numbers in standard form: (a) $600\,000$ (b) $48\,000\,000$ (c) $784\,000\,000\,000$ (d) $534\,000$ (e) $7$ million (f) $8.5$ million
exercises.full_solution: Rewrite each number as $A\times10^n$ with $1\le A<10$, where $n$ is the number of places the decimal point moves left. (a) $600\,000=6\times10^5$. (b) $48\,000\,000=4.8\times10^7$. (c) $784\,000\,000\,000=7.84\times10^{11}$. (d) $534\,000=5.34\times10^5$. (e) $7$ million $=7\,000\,000=7\times10^6$. (f) $8.5$ million $=8\,500\,000=8.5\times10^6$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the following in standard form: (a) $68\times10^5$ (b) $720\times10^6$ (c) $8\times10^5$ (d) $0.75\times10^8$ (e) $0.4\times10^{10}$ (f) $50\times10^6$
exercises.full_solution: Adjust the coefficient so that $1\le A<10$ and compensate in the index. (a) $68\times10^5=6.8\times10^1\times10^5=6.8\times10^6$. (b) $720\times10^6=7.2\times10^2\times10^6=7.2\times10^8$. (c) $8\times10^5$ already has $1\le8<10$, so it is unchanged. (d) $0.75\times10^8=7.5\times10^{-1}\times10^8=7.5\times10^7$. (e) $0.4\times10^{10}=4\times10^{-1}\times10^{10}=4\times10^9$. (f) $50\times10^6=5\times10^1\times10^6=5\times10^7$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the following as ordinary numbers: (a) $3.8\times10^3$ (b) $4.25\times10^6$ (c) $9.003\times10^7$ (d) $1.01\times10^5$
exercises.full_solution: Move the decimal point to the right by the number of places given by the index, filling the gaps with zeros. (a) $3.8\times10^3=3800$. (b) $4.25\times10^6=4\,250\,000$. (c) $9.003\times10^7=90\,030\,000$. (d) $1.01\times10^5=101\,000$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Multiply the following and write your answers in standard form: (a) $200\times3000$ (b) $6000\times4000$ (c) $7\text{ million}\times20$ (d) $500\times6\text{ million}$ (e) $3\text{ million}\times4\text{ million}$ (f) $4500\times4000$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Light from the Sun takes approximately $8$ minutes to reach Earth. If light travels at a speed of $3\times10^8\,\text{m/s}$, calculate to three significant figures (s.f.) the distance from the Sun to the Earth.
exercises.full_solution: Work in seconds first: $8$ minutes $=8\times60=480\,\text{s}$. Distance $=$ speed $\times$ time $=(3\times10^8)\times480$. Writing $480=4.8\times10^2$ gives $(3\times4.8)\times10^{8+2}=14.4\times10^{10}=1.44\times10^{11}\,\text{m}$, which is already correct to three significant figures (about $144$ million km).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find the value of the following and write your answers in standard form: (a) $(4.4\times10^3)\times(2\times10^5)$ (b) $(6.8\times10^7)\times(3\times10^3)$ (c) $(4\times10^5)\times(8.3\times10^5)$ (d) $(5\times10^9)\times(8.4\times10^{12})$ (e) $(8.5\times10^6)\times(6\times10^{15})$ (f) $(5.0\times10^{12})^2$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find the value of the following and write your answers in standard form: (a) $(3.8\times10^8)\div(1.9\times10^6)$ (b) $(6.75\times10^9)\div(2.25\times10^4)$ (c) $(9.6\times10^{11})\div(2.4\times10^5)$ (d) $(1.8\times10^{12})\div(9.0\times10^7)$ (e) $(2.3\times10^{11})\div(9.2\times10^4)$ (f) $(2.4\times10^8)\div(6.0\times10^3)$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find the value of the following and write your answers in standard form: (a) $(3.8\times10^5)+(4.6\times10^4)$ (b) $(7.9\times10^9)+(5.8\times10^8)$ (c) $(6.3\times10^7)+(8.8\times10^5)$ (d) $(3.15\times10^9)+(7.0\times10^6)$ (e) $(5.3\times10^8)-(8.0\times10^7)$ (f) $(6.5\times10^7)-(4.9\times10^6)$ (g) $(8.93\times10^{10})-(7.8\times10^9)$ (h) $(4.07\times10^7)-(5.1\times10^6)$
exercises.full_solution: Adding or subtracting needs a common index: rewrite the number with the smaller index using the larger index, then add or subtract the coefficients. (a) $4.6\times10^4=0.46\times10^5$, so the sum is $(3.8+0.46)\times10^5=4.26\times10^5$. (b) $5.8\times10^8=0.58\times10^9$, giving $(7.9+0.58)\times10^9=8.48\times10^9$. (c) $8.8\times10^5=0.088\times10^7$, giving $(6.3+0.088)\times10^7=6.388\times10^7$. (d) $7.0\times10^6=0.007\times10^9$, giving $(3.15+0.007)\times10^9=3.157\times10^9$. (e) $8.0\times10^7=0.8\times10^8$, giving $(5.3-0.8)\times10^8=4.5\times10^8$. (f) $4.9\times10^6=0.49\times10^7$, giving $(6.5-0.49)\times10^7=6.01\times10^7$. (g) $7.8\times10^9=0.78\times10^{10}$, giving $(8.93-0.78)\times10^{10}=8.15\times10^{10}$. (h) $5.1\times10^6=0.51\times10^7$, giving $(4.07-0.51)\times10^7=3.56\times10^7$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.full_solution: Rewrite each small decimal as $A\times10^{-n}$ with $1\le A<10$, where $n$ is the number of places the decimal point moves right to reach $A$. (a) $0.0006=6\times10^{-4}$. (b) $0.000053=5.3\times10^{-5}$. (c) $0.000864=8.64\times10^{-4}$. (d) $0.000000088=8.8\times10^{-8}$. (e) $0.0000007=7\times10^{-7}$. (f) $0.0004145=4.145\times10^{-4}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the following numbers in standard form: (a) $68\times10^{-5}$ (b) $750\times10^{-9}$ (c) $42\times10^{-11}$ (d) $0.08\times10^{-7}$ (e) $0.057\times10^{-9}$ (f) $0.4\times10^{-10}$
exercises.full_solution: Adjust the coefficient to lie between 1 and 10, compensating the exponent accordingly. (a) $68\times10^{-5}=6.8\times10^{-4}$. (b) $750\times10^{-9}=7.5\times10^{-7}$. (c) $42\times10^{-11}=4.2\times10^{-10}$. (d) $0.08\times10^{-7}=8\times10^{-9}$. (e) $0.057\times10^{-9}=5.7\times10^{-11}$. (f) $0.4\times10^{-10}=4\times10^{-11}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write the following as ordinary numbers: (a) $8\times10^{-3}$ (b) $4.2\times10^{-4}$ (c) $9.03\times10^{-2}$ (d) $1.01\times10^{-5}$
exercises.full_solution: Move the decimal point left by the number of places given by the (positive) exponent. (a) $8\times10^{-3}=0.008$. (b) $4.2\times10^{-4}=0.00042$. (c) $9.03\times10^{-2}=0.0903$. (d) $1.01\times10^{-5}=0.0000101$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Deduce the value of $n$ in each of the following cases: (a) $0.00025=2.5\times10^n$ (b) $0.00357=3.57\times10^n$ (c) $0.00000006=6\times10^n$ (d) $0.004^2=1.6\times10^n$ (e) $0.00065^2=4.225\times10^n$ (f) $0.0002^n=8\times10^{-12}$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write these numbers in order of magnitude, starting with the largest: $3.2\times10^{-4}$, $6.8\times10^5$, $5.57\times10^{-9}$, $6.2\times10^3$, $5.8\times10^{-7}$, $6.741\times10^{-4}$, $8.414\times10^2$
exercises.full_solution: Compare the exponents first (larger exponent means a larger number for positive $A$), then compare coefficients where exponents tie among comparable sizes: as ordinary numbers these are approximately $680\,000$, $6200$, $841.4$, $0.0006741$, $0.00032$, $0.00000058$, $0.00000000557$ — giving the order $6.8\times10^5>6.2\times10^3>8.414\times10^2>6.741\times10^{-4}>3.2\times10^{-4}>5.8\times10^{-7}>5.57\times10^{-9}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.full_solution: Each equation asks for which root of the base gives the right-hand side. (a) $16^{1/2}=4\Rightarrow x=\frac12$. (b) $8^{1/3}=2\Rightarrow x=\frac13$. (c) $9^{1/2}=3\Rightarrow x=\frac12$. (d) $27^{1/3}=3\Rightarrow x=\frac13$. (e) $100^{1/2}=10\Rightarrow x=\frac12$. (f) $64^{1/6}=2\Rightarrow x=\frac16$.
